# =========================================================================
# business/dates.py
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Today's date. It is used by BUSINESS RULES (no booking
# in the past, a single UPCOMING appointment per patient): it therefore lives
# in the business layer. The web layer reuses it.
# =========================================================================
from datetime import date


# today's date, in the time zone of the server
def today() -> date:
    return date.today()

The current date is used for two business rules (no appointments in the past, only one upcoming appointment per patient): it belongs in the business layer. Isolating it in a function has another advantage: an automated test could replace it with a fixed date.

docs.title: 11.12.2. business/exception.py
docs.text:
# =========================================================================
# business/exception.py
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The exception raised by the business layer when a BUSINESS RULE is
# violated (login already taken, doctor who still has appointments, slot
# already booked...). It does not carry a text, but a translation
# KEY (e.g.: "ERRORS.LOGIN_TAKEN"): it is the web layer that will
# translate it into French or English when displaying the page
# (see i18n/fr.json, i18n/en.json).
#
# A BusinessException is not an anomaly: it is a normal response
# ("this login is already taken"), displayed to the user. Any other
# exception is a real anomaly, which ends up on the 500 error page.
# =========================================================================


class BusinessException(Exception):

    def __init__(self, key: str, params: dict[str, str] | None = None):
        super().__init__(key)
        # translation key of the message
        self.key = key
        # possible parameters of the message ({minutes}...)
        self.params = params or {}

The business layer exception does not carry text, as in Example 28, but rather a translation key ([ERRORS.LOGIN_TAKEN]) and any parameters: the business layer does not know in which language the user is viewing the page. The web layer will translate the key. [super().__init__(key)] passes the key to the constructor of the [Exception] class: this is the value that is displayed if the exception is logged.

A [BusinessException] is not an error: it is a normal response (“this username is already taken”), which is displayed to the user. Any other exception is a true error, which results in a 500 error page.

# =========================================================================
# business/business.py
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The CONTRACT of the business layer: reads, schedule, appointments, management
# of the doctors and of the clients.
#
# A Protocol describes the methods an object must have, without saying how
# they are written (the equivalent of an interface). BusinessService (the
# business layer) and ApplicationModel (the cache of the web layer) both
# comply with it. Python checks nothing at runtime: it is
# the analysis tools (that of VS Code, for example) that report a mismatch.
#
# T | None: a result that can be missing (a doctor who does not exist...).
# =========================================================================
from datetime import date
from typing import Protocol

from rdvmedecins.domain.schedule import DoctorDaySchedule
from rdvmedecins.entities import Client, Slot, Doctor, Appointment
from rdvmedecins.business.person_data import PersonData


class Business(Protocol):

    # ------------------------------------------------ reads
    def get_all_clients(self) -> list[Client]: ...

    def get_all_doctors(self) -> list[Doctor]: ...

    def get_all_slots(self, doctor_id: int) -> list[Slot]: ...

    def get_doctor_day_appointments(self, doctor_id: int, day: date) -> list[Appointment]: ...

    def get_client_by_id(self, id: int) -> Client | None: ...

    def get_doctor_by_id(self, id: int) -> Doctor | None: ...

    def get_appointment_by_id(self, id: int) -> Appointment | None: ...

    def get_slot_by_id(self, id: int) -> Slot | None: ...

    def get_doctor_day_schedule(self, doctor_id: int, day: date) -> DoctorDaySchedule | None: ...

    # the client (patient) whose user account is [user_id]
    def get_client_by_user_id(self, user_id: int) -> Client | None: ...

    # the appointments of a client, of today or future, with slot and doctor
    def get_client_upcoming_appointments(self, client_id: int) -> list[Appointment]: ...

    # ------------------------------------------------ appointments (ADMIN, DOCTOR, USER)
    # raises a BusinessException if:
    #  - the day is past ("ERRORS.PAST_DATE");
    #  - the patient already has an upcoming appointment ("ERRORS.PATIENT_HAS_UPCOMING_APPOINTMENT");
    #  - the slot is already taken on that day ("ERRORS.SLOT_ALREADY_BOOKED").
    def add_appointment(self, day: date, slot: Slot, client: Client) -> Appointment: ...

    def delete_appointment(self, appointment: Appointment) -> None: ...

    # ------------------------------------------------ doctors (ADMIN)
    # creates the doctor AND their user account (DOCTOR role)
    def add_doctor(self, data: PersonData) -> Doctor: ...

    # edits the doctor AND their user account
    def edit_doctor(self, id: int, data: PersonData) -> Doctor: ...

    # deletes the doctor, their slots AND their account - refused if they have appointments
    def delete_doctor(self, id: int) -> None: ...

    # ------------------------------------------------ clients
    # (the ADMIN; add_client is also used for the registration of a patient,
    # edit_client and delete_client by the patient for their own account)
    # creates the client AND their user account (USER role)
    def add_client(self, data: PersonData) -> Client: ...

    def edit_client(self, id: int, data: PersonData) -> Client: ...

    # deletes the client, their account AND all their appointments (past and future)
    def delete_client(self, id: int) -> None: ...
  • Line 23: The business layer contract: a list of its methods, along with their parameters and return values. A [Protocol] (standard module [typing]) is the [Python] equivalent of an interface: it describes the methods an object must have, without specifying how they are implemented. A class conforms to it as long as it has these methods, without having to declare it (this is known as structural typing, or *duck typing*: “if it walks like a duck…”). Two classes conform to it: [BusinessService], the business layer, and [ApplicationModel], the web layer cache (discussed later). [Python] does not check anything at runtime: it is the analysis tools, such as the one in [Visual Studio Code], that flag a discrepancy;
