docs.title: 11.12.5. business/service.py
docs.text:
The business layer implementation. This is the most important file in the application.

# =========================================================================
# business/service.py
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Implementation of the business layer.
#
# The management of the doctors and of the clients follows three business rules:
#
#   1. a person (doctor or client) and their user account ALWAYS go
#      together: they are created, edited and deleted together, in
#      the same TRANSACTION - either everything succeeds, or nothing is written;
#   2. the login is unique in the whole application, and two doctors (or
#      two clients) cannot have the same first and last names;
#   3. deletion:
#      - a DOCTOR who has appointments cannot be deleted (their
#        patients would lose their appointment without being warned): they must
#        first be cancelled. Their time slots disappear with them;
#      - a CLIENT, on the other hand, disappears with ALL their appointments (past and
#        future) - whether the deletion comes from the ADMIN or from the patient
#        themselves.
#
# And two rules for booking appointments, whatever the role of
# the one who books (ADMIN, DOCTOR or the patient themselves):
#   4. no appointment in the past;
#   5. a patient has only ONE upcoming appointment at a time.
#
# Doctors and clients follow exactly the same rules: the common code
# is written ONCE (private methods _xxx_person), and parameterized by a
# small "descriptor" that says what type of person we are dealing with.
#
# The TRANSACTIONS are opened by the _transaction method (at the end of the
# file), which also translates into BusinessException the errors that the database
# reports when the SQL statements are sent to it.
# =========================================================================
import re
from collections.abc import Callable
from dataclasses import dataclass
from datetime import date

from sqlalchemy.exc import IntegrityError
from sqlalchemy.orm import Session, sessionmaker
from sqlalchemy.orm.exc import StaleDataError

from rdvmedecins.auth.passwords import hash_password
from rdvmedecins.domain.schedule import DoctorDaySchedule, DoctorDaySlot
from rdvmedecins.entities import Client, Slot, Doctor, Person, Role, Appointment, User
from rdvmedecins.business import dates
from rdvmedecins.business.person_data import PersonData
from rdvmedecins.business.exception import BusinessException
from rdvmedecins.repositories.client_repository import ClientRepository
from rdvmedecins.repositories.slot_repository import SlotRepository
from rdvmedecins.repositories.doctor_repository import DoctorRepository
from rdvmedecins.repositories.person_repository import PersonRepository
from rdvmedecins.repositories.appointment_repository import AppointmentRepository
from rdvmedecins.repositories.user_repository import UserRepository


# everything that distinguishes a doctor from a client for the business rules
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Descriptor:
    dao: PersonRepository
    factory: type[Person]  # Doctor or Client
    role: Role  # DOCTOR or USER
    not_found_key: str  # message if the person does not exist
    already_exists_key: str  # message if the same first and last names already exist
    # optional (None): if present, the deletion is REFUSED as long as the
    # person has appointments (count_appointments > 0), with the message has_appointments_key
    count_appointments: Callable[[Session, int], int] | None
    has_appointments_key: str | None
    # optional: what must be deleted BEFORE the person (the rows that
    # reference it by a foreign key)
    before_delete: Callable[[Session, int], None] | None


# -----------------------------------------------------------------------
# Database errors -> BusinessException
#
# When a UNIQUE constraint refuses a write, SQLAlchemy raises an
# IntegrityError, whose [orig] attribute is the original error, that of the
# PyMySQL driver. Its message quotes the NAME of the constraint:
#   Duplicate entry 'Marie-PELISSIER' for key 'doctors.unq_doctors_first_name_last_name'
# (MySQL 8 prefixes the name with that of the table, MariaDB does not). This is
# why the SQL script NAMES all its constraints.
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------
CONSTRAINT_MESSAGES = {
    "unq_users_login": "ERRORS.LOGIN_TAKEN",
    "unq_doctors_first_name_last_name": "ERRORS.DOCTOR_ALREADY_EXISTS",
    "unq_clients_first_name_last_name": "ERRORS.PATIENT_ALREADY_EXISTS",
    "unq1_appointments": "ERRORS.SLOT_ALREADY_BOOKED",
}

CONSTRAINT = re.compile(r"for key '(?:[^'.]*\.)?([^']+)'")


class BusinessService:

    # all the dependencies are provided by the application factory
    # (see rdvmedecins/__init__.py): this is dependency injection "by
    # hand". sessions: the factory of the SQLAlchemy sessions.
    def __init__(self, sessions: sessionmaker, doctors: DoctorRepository,
                 clients: ClientRepository, slots: SlotRepository, appointments: AppointmentRepository,
                 users: UserRepository):
        self._sessions = sessions
        self._doctors = doctors
        self._clients = clients
        self._slots = slots
        self._appointments = appointments
        self._users = users

        self._doctor = Descriptor(
            dao=doctors, factory=Doctor, role=Role.DOCTOR,
            not_found_key="ERRORS.DOCTOR_NOT_FOUND",
            already_exists_key="ERRORS.DOCTOR_ALREADY_EXISTS",
            count_appointments=appointments.count_by_doctor,
            has_appointments_key="ERRORS.DOCTOR_HAS_APPOINTMENTS",
            # a doctor without appointments may still have time slots:
            # they make no sense without them, they are deleted with them (otherwise
            # the foreign key slots.doctor_id would forbid the deletion)
            before_delete=slots.delete_by_doctor)

        self._client = Descriptor(
            dao=clients, factory=Client, role=Role.USER,
            not_found_key="ERRORS.PATIENT_NOT_FOUND",
            already_exists_key="ERRORS.PATIENT_ALREADY_EXISTS",
            # no count_appointments: the deletion of a client is never refused;
            # their appointments (past and future) are deleted with them (otherwise
            # the foreign key appointments.client_id would forbid the deletion)
            count_appointments=None, has_appointments_key=None,
            before_delete=appointments.delete_by_client)

    # =======================================================================
    # reads: a session, for the time of the read; the objects read remain
    # usable afterwards (expire_on_commit=False, see rdvmedecins/__init__.py)
    # =======================================================================

    def _read[R](self, work: Callable[[Session], R]) -> R:
        with self._sessions() as session:
            return work(session)

    def get_all_clients(self) -> list[Client]:
        return self._read(self._clients.list)

    def get_all_doctors(self) -> list[Doctor]:
        return self._read(self._doctors.list)

    def get_all_slots(self, doctor_id: int) -> list[Slot]:
        return self._read(lambda s: self._slots.list_by_doctor(s, doctor_id))

    def get_doctor_day_appointments(self, doctor_id: int, day: date) -> list[Appointment]:
        return self._read(lambda s: self._appointments.doctor_day_appointments(s, doctor_id, day))

    def get_client_by_id(self, id: int) -> Client | None:
        return self._read(lambda s: self._clients.read(s, id))

    def get_doctor_by_id(self, id: int) -> Doctor | None:
        return self._read(lambda s: self._doctors.read(s, id))

    def get_appointment_by_id(self, id: int) -> Appointment | None:
        return self._read(lambda s: self._appointments.read(s, id))

    def get_slot_by_id(self, id: int) -> Slot | None:
        return self._read(lambda s: self._slots.read(s, id))

    def get_client_by_user_id(self, user_id: int) -> Client | None:
        return self._read(lambda s: self._clients.read_by_user(s, user_id))

    def get_client_upcoming_appointments(self, client_id: int) -> list[Appointment]:
        return self._read(lambda s: self._appointments.client_upcoming_appointments(s, client_id, dates.today()))

    # the schedule of a doctor on a given day: their slots, and for each one the
    # appointment booked on that day (None if it is free)
    def get_doctor_day_schedule(self, doctor_id: int, day: date) -> DoctorDaySchedule | None:
        doctor = self.get_doctor_by_id(doctor_id)
        if doctor is None:
            return None
        time_slots = self.get_all_slots(doctor_id)
        # slot no. -> appointment booked on this slot (a dictionary "comprehension")
        bookings = {a.slot_id: a for a in self.get_doctor_day_appointments(doctor_id, day)}
        doctor_day_slots = [DoctorDaySlot(slot, bookings.get(slot.id))
                            for slot in time_slots]
        return DoctorDaySchedule(doctor, day, doctor_day_slots)

    # =======================================================================
    # appointments
    # =======================================================================

    # -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # booking of an appointment, in a transaction:
    #   1. no appointment in the past;
    #   2. the row of the patient is LOCKED (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE): if the
    #      same patient books two slots at the same moment (two tabs,
    #      double click...), the second transaction waits for the end of the
    #      first one - and then sees the appointment it has just created;
    #   3. a single upcoming appointment per patient;
    #   4. finally the insertion. If the slot has just been taken by ANOTHER
    #      patient, it is the SQL constraint unq1_appointments (day, slot_id) that
    #      refuses the insertion - translated into BusinessException by _transaction.
    # -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    def add_appointment(self, day: date, slot: Slot, client: Client) -> Appointment:
        def work(session: Session) -> Appointment:
            today = dates.today()
            if day < today:
                raise BusinessException("ERRORS.PAST_DATE")
            patient_id = self._clients.lock(session, client.id)
            if patient_id is None:
                raise BusinessException("ERRORS.PATIENT_NOT_FOUND")
            if self._appointments.count_client_upcoming(session, patient_id, today) > 0:
                raise BusinessException("ERRORS.PATIENT_HAS_UPCOMING_APPOINTMENT")
            # knowing the ids of the slot and of the patient is enough to write
            # the foreign keys: no need to read these objects again in the session
            return self._appointments.add(session, Appointment(day=day, slot_id=slot.id,
                                                               client_id=patient_id))

        return self._transaction(work)

    def delete_appointment(self, appointment: Appointment) -> None:
        self._transaction(lambda session: self._appointments.remove(session, appointment.id))

    # =======================================================================
    # doctors and clients - the public methods delegate to the common
    # private methods, with the right descriptor
    # =======================================================================

    def add_doctor(self, data: PersonData) -> Doctor:
        return self._add_person(self._doctor, data)

    def edit_doctor(self, id: int, data: PersonData) -> Doctor:
        return self._edit_person(self._doctor, id, data)

    def delete_doctor(self, id: int) -> None:
        self._delete_person(self._doctor, id)

    def add_client(self, data: PersonData) -> Client:
        return self._add_person(self._client, data)

    def edit_client(self, id: int, data: PersonData) -> Client:
        return self._edit_person(self._client, id, data)

    # the client, their account AND all their appointments (ADMIN, or the patient
    # themselves from "Manage my account": same method, same rule)
    def delete_client(self, id: int) -> None:
        self._delete_person(self._client, id)

    # -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # creation: the user account AND the person, in ONE transaction.
    # -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    def _add_person(self, d: Descriptor, data: PersonData):
        last_name = data.last_name.strip().upper()
        first_name = data.first_name.strip()
        # the rules of the dbrdvmedecins2 database: login = last name in lower case,
        # password = login - unless the ADMIN has typed other ones
        login = (data.login or last_name).lower()
        password = data.password or login

        def work(session: Session):
            self._check_person_unique(session, d, first_name, last_name, None)
            self._check_login_free(session, login)
            user = User(login=login, password=hash_password(password), name=f"{first_name} {last_name}", role=d.role)
            person = d.factory(title=data.title, last_name=last_name, first_name=first_name, user=user)
            # the person references their account: SQLAlchemy first inserts the
            # account (to know its id), then the person
            d.dao.add(session, person)
            # flush: the INSERTs leave right away (and not at COMMIT); a
            # violated constraint therefore raises its error HERE
            session.flush()
            return person

        return self._transaction(work)

    # -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # edit: the person AND their account (the displayed name "first name LAST NAME"
    # must follow; the login and the password only change if they have been
    # typed).
    # -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    def _edit_person(self, d: Descriptor, id: int, data: PersonData):
        def work(session: Session):
            person = d.dao.read(session, id)
            if person is None:
                raise BusinessException(d.not_found_key)

            # optimistic lock: if the version in the database is no longer that of the
            # form, someone has edited this record in the meantime - we refuse
            # rather than silently overwrite their changes.
            # (If the concurrent edit happens AFTER this read, it is
            # the "WHERE version = ..." clause of the UPDATE that detects it.)
            if data.version is not None and data.version != person.version:
                raise BusinessException("ERRORS.CONCURRENT_UPDATE")

            last_name = data.last_name.strip().upper()
            first_name = data.first_name.strip()
            self._check_person_unique(session, d, first_name, last_name, id)

            # we merely modify the objects: they are "tracked" by the
            # session, which will itself send the necessary UPDATEs
            person.title = data.title
            person.last_name = last_name
            person.first_name = first_name

            user = person.user
            user.name = f"{first_name} {last_name}"
            if data.login and data.login.lower() != user.login:
                login = data.login.lower()
                self._check_login_free(session, login)
                user.login = login
            if data.password:
                user.password = hash_password(data.password)
            session.flush()
            return person

        return self._transaction(work)

    # -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # deletion, in ONE transaction, in the order imposed by the foreign
    # keys:
    #   1. possible refusal if appointments remain (doctor);
    #   2. what references the person (slots of a doctor, appointments
    #      of a client);
    #   3. the person (it references its account);
    #   4. its account.
    # -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    def _delete_person(self, d: Descriptor, id: int) -> None:
        def work(session: Session):
            person = d.dao.read(session, id)
            if person is None:
                raise BusinessException(d.not_found_key)
            if d.count_appointments is not None and d.count_appointments(session, id) > 0:
                raise BusinessException(d.has_appointments_key)
            if d.before_delete is not None:
                d.before_delete(session, id)
            d.dao.remove(session, id)
            self._users.remove(session, person.user_id)

        self._transaction(work)

    # refuses first and last names already used by ANOTHER person of the same type
    # (current_id: the person being edited, who obviously has the
    # right to keep their own first and last names; None for a creation)
    @staticmethod
    def _check_person_unique(session: Session, d: Descriptor, first_name: str, last_name: str,
                             current_id: int | None):
        namesake = d.dao.namesake(session, first_name, last_name)
        if namesake is not None and namesake.id != current_id:
            raise BusinessException(d.already_exists_key)

    def _check_login_free(self, session: Session, login: str):
        if self._users.read_by_login(session, login) is not None:
            raise BusinessException("ERRORS.LOGIN_TAKEN")

    # -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # runs [work] in a transaction:
    #   sessions.begin() -> a session and its transaction (START TRANSACTION);
    #   on leaving the with block: COMMIT if all went well; if an
    #   exception leaves it (BusinessException included), ROLLBACK: nothing is written.
    #
    # The "free login" and "unique first + last names" checks are made BEFORE
    # the write, to give a clear message. But two ADMINs could
    # save the same login (or the same doctor) at the same moment: in this
    # rare case, it is an SQL uniqueness constraint that refuses the second
    # write. The database errors are therefore intercepted AROUND the
    # transaction, to translate them into the same BusinessException:
    #   - StaleDataError: the UPDATE "WHERE id = ... AND version = ..." has
    #     modified no row (optimistic lock);
    #   - IntegrityError: a constraint of the database has refused the write.
    # Any other error is a real anomaly: it is let through.
    # -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    def _transaction[R](self, work: Callable[[Session], R]) -> R:
        try:
            with self._sessions.begin() as session:
                return work(session)
        except StaleDataError:
            raise BusinessException("ERRORS.CONCURRENT_UPDATE")
        except IntegrityError as e:
            match = CONSTRAINT.search(str(e.orig))
            if match and match.group(1) in CONSTRAINT_MESSAGES:
                raise BusinessException(CONSTRAINT_MESSAGES[match.group(1)])
            raise

docs.title: 11.12.5.1. The descriptors
docs.text:
Doctors and clients follow exactly the same business rules, with a few minor differences: a different DAO, a different role for their account, different error messages, and a different deletion rule. Rather than writing each method twice, the common code is written once (the methods [_add_person], [_edit_person], [_delete_person]) and configured by a descriptor that specifies which type of person is being handled:

  • lines 59–71: the descriptor is an immutable [dataclass]. Three of its fields are functions: [Callable[[Session, int], int]] is the type of a function that takes a session and an integer, and returns an integer. [count_appointments] counts a person’s appointments (to prevent the deletion of a doctor who has any); [before_delete] deletes references to the person (a doctor’s time slots, a client’s appointments);
  • lines 109–118: the doctors’ descriptor. [appointments.count_by_doctor] is a method associated with the object [appointments] (Example 22): a function that will receive the session and the ID;
  • lines 120–128: the one for clients: no deletion denial ([count_appointments=None]), but the prior deletion of all their appointments.

docs.title: 11.12.5.2. Read operations and the calendar
docs.text:
• lines 135–137: the reads are handled by a small generic method: [R] is the result type, which is the same as that of the function [work]. The session is opened by [self._sessions()] (without [begin]) while the function is executing, then closed by the block [with]. [SQLAlchemy] still starts a transaction on the first request ([BEGIN (implicit)] in the console); since nothing was written, closing the session cancels it ([ROLLBACK]): these are the lines the console displays when the application starts;
  • lines 139–167: each read instructs [_read] to call the method DAO. When the DAO method has parameters other than the session, an anonymous function ([lambda s: ...]) provides them;
  • Lines 171–180: A doctor’s schedule for a single day. The day’s appointments are stored in a dictionary ([{key: value for ...}]) that associates each time slot number with its corresponding appointment; Each time slot is then associated with its appointment, or with [None] ([bookings.get(slot.id)]). Three reads, across three sessions: any inconsistency between them (an appointment scheduled between two reads) would be inconsequential, since the schedule is merely a display.

docs.title: 11.12.5.3. Scheduling an appointment
docs.text:
• Lines 198–213: The method defines an internal function, [work], which contains the operations to be performed in the transaction, and passes it to the method [_transaction] (see below). The rules, in order: - No appointments in the past ([day < today]: the dates in [Python] are compared using the usual operators); - the patient’s record is locked ([lock], see [ClientRepository]): if the same patient books two time slots at the same time (two tabs, a double-click), the second transaction waits for the first one to complete and then sees the appointment it created; - only one upcoming appointment per patient; - finally, the insertion. The appointment is created using the slot ID and the patient ID: it is sufficient to know the values of the foreign keys; there is no need to re-read the objects. The named parameters of the constructor ([Appointment(day=..., slot_id=...)]) are provided by [SQLAlchemy] to any entity that does not have its own constructor.
  • There is one remaining scenario: the time slot has just been taken by another patient between the time the calendar is displayed and the time the reservation is made. In this case, the database constraint [unq1_appointments] prevents the insertion during the [COMMIT] operation. The [_transaction] method translates this error into [BusinessException];
  • lines 215–216: canceling an appointment. Permission checks (a patient can only cancel their own appointments) are performed by the web layer, which knows the user.

docs.title: 11.12.5.4. Management of doctors and clients
docs.text:
• lines 223–241: public methods delegate to common methods, using the correct descriptor;
  • lines 246–267: creation. The last name is capitalized, and spaces are removed from the first name; the default username is the last name in lowercase, and the password is the username (the rule for demo accounts in the SQL script). In the transaction: validations (no homonyms, free login), followed by the creation of the account and the person. The person receives their account through their relationship ([user=user]): [SQLAlchemy] knows it must first insert the account to obtain its ID, then the person. [session.flush()] sends [INSERT] immediately: a violated constraint triggers an error in the transaction, and the returned person has its ID;
  • Lines 274–309: the update. The form version is compared to the database version (optimistic lock, example 28); then we simply update the retrieved objects: they are tracked by the session, which will itself send the necessary [UPDATE] records. The displayed account name follows the first name and last name; the login and password change only if they have been entered;
  • lines 320–332: deletion, in the order dictated by the foreign keys: possible rejection (a doctor who has appointments), deletion of the references to the person, the person themselves, and then their account. In the reverse order, the database would reject each [DELETE]. All of this occurs in a single transaction: if any one step fails, none of the steps are executed;
  • lines 337–342: a homonym is rejected, unless it is the person currently being edited, who has the right to keep their own first and last names;
  • lines 344–346: A username can belong to only one account.

docs.title: 11.12.5.5. Transactions and uniqueness constraints
docs.text:
• lines 365–375: All updates go through this method. [sessions.begin()] opens a session and its transaction; Upon exiting the [with] block, the transaction is committed ([COMMIT]) if everything went well, or rolled back ([ROLLBACK]) if an exception occurs, including [BusinessException];
  • Lines 369–370: The optimistic lock detected a concurrent modification (example 28);
  • lines 371–374: a database constraint rejected the write. The checks performed before the write (unique username, no homonyms) provide a clear message in the vast majority of cases; however, two administrators could register the same username at the same time, or two patients could book the same time slot. The uniqueness constraint then rejects the second write, and [SQLAlchemy] releases a [IntegrityError]. Its original message ([e.orig], the error for [PyMySQL]) cites the name of the constraint (here with [MariaDB], for the second time slot booked twice on the same day):
(1062, "Duplicate entry '2026-09-26-2' for key 'unq1_appointments'")
  • The regular expression [CONSTRAINT] (line 91) extracts this name. [MySQL] 8 adds the prefix with the table name (['appointments.unq1_appointments']), [MariaDB] does not: the part [(?:[^'.]*\.)?] accepts this optional prefix ([(?:...)] is a non-capturing group, [?] makes it optional). The dictionary [CONSTRAINT_MESSAGES] (lines 84–88) associates each known constraint with the key of its message. This is why the script SQL names all of its constraints;
  • line 375: any other error is a true anomaly: [raise], with no parameters, rethrows the current exception, which will result in a 500 error page.

Note the structure of all write methods: an internal function [work], which contains the operations, is passed to [_transaction], which executes it within a transaction and translates the errors. This is equivalent to the annotation ***[@Transactional]*** of *[Spring]*, written in just a few lines: a function is an object like any other, which can be passed as a parameter.

docs.title: 11.13. Authentication
docs.text: The [auth] folder incorporates the mechanisms from Examples 25 through 27, with three differences: the access rule is reversed (everything is prohibited except what is declared public), users are retrieved from the database, and the creation of a customer account is protected by a “pass.”

docs.title: 11.13.1. auth/passwords.py
docs.text:
# =========================================================================
# auth/passwords.py
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Password hashing: bcrypt, 10 rounds, version $2b$ - like the
# hashes of the SQL script.
#
# bcrypt only takes into account the first 72 BYTES of a password (an
# accented character takes two of them, in UTF-8); the bcrypt library
# even refuses a longer password. We therefore only pass it these
# 72 bytes, on creation as on verification.
# =========================================================================
import bcrypt


def _bytes(password: str) -> bytes:
    return password.encode("utf-8")[:72]


# the hash to store in the database: "$2b$10$" + the salt + the result
def hash_password(password: str) -> str:
    return bcrypt.hashpw(_bytes(password), bcrypt.gensalt(rounds=10)).decode("ascii")


# checkpw hashes the typed password with the "salt" contained in the stored
# hash, then compares the two results
def verify(password: str, hashed: str) -> bool:
    return bcrypt.checkpw(_bytes(password), hashed.encode("ascii"))
  • Lines 15–16: [bcrypt] considers only the first 72 bytes of a password, and version 5 of the library rejects longer passwords (Example 25). Therefore, only these 72 bytes are passed to it, both during creation and verification: a longer password is accepted, but characters beyond the 72nd byte are ignored. An accented character occupies two bytes in [UTF-8];
  • lines 20–21: the hash is stored in text form: [decode("ascii")] converts the bytes returned by [bcrypt] into a string;
  • lines 26–27: verification (example 25). This module is used by authentication and by the business layer (account creation, password change).

docs.title: 11.13.2. auth/connected_user.py
docs.text:
# =========================================================================
# auth/connected_user.py
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# What the JWT token contains, and how to read it back.
#
# The claims of our tokens (see AuthService.set_token):
#   sub   : the id of the user account (JWT convention: "subject"), as text
#   login : the login
#   name  : the displayed name ("Marie PELISSIER"), for the navigation bar
#   role  : ADMIN, DOCTOR or USER
#   iat, exp : creation and expiration dates of the token
# =========================================================================
from dataclasses import dataclass

from rdvmedecins.entities import Role


# the connected user, in a typed form
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ConnectedUser:
    user_id: int
    login: str
    name: str
    role: Role

    # the user described by the claims of an already verified token; None if
    # a claim is missing or does not have the expected form
    @staticmethod
    def of(claims: dict) -> "ConnectedUser | None":
        try:
            return ConnectedUser(int(claims["sub"]), claims["login"], claims["name"],
                                 Role(claims["role"]))
        except (KeyError, ValueError, TypeError):
            return None

    @property
    def is_admin(self) -> bool:
        return self.role == Role.ADMIN

    @property
    def is_patient(self) -> bool:
        return self.role == Role.USER
  • lines 20–24: the logged-in user, in a typed form: Example 25 stored the token’s assertion dictionary in [g.user]; the application stores this object, whose attributes are known to the editor ([g.user.role]), and whose role is a value from the enumeration [Role];
  • Lines 29–34: Construction based on the assertions of an already verified token. The result type is written in quotation marks (["ConnectedUser | None"]): when [Python] reads the method definition, the class [ConnectedUser] is not yet fully defined, and its name cannot be used directly. A token with a missing assertion ([KeyError]) or an unexpected value ([ValueError]: an unknown role, a [sub] that is not a number) results in [None]: the user is not authenticated;
  • lines 36–42: two properties: the [@property] decorator transforms a method into a computed property, which is used without parentheses: [g.user.is_admin].

The token contains the account ID ([sub], in text form, as required by the JWT standard), the login, the display name, and the role: everything the navigation bar and access rules need, without having to query the database for every request.

docs.title: 11.13.3. auth/auth_service.py
docs.text:
# =========================================================================
# auth/auth_service.py
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The authentication logic:
#   - validate_user() : checks a login / password pair;
#   - set_token()     : builds the JWT token of a validated user
#                       and puts it in a cookie of the response;
#   - clear_token()   : deletes this cookie;
#   - current_user()  : the user described by the cookie of the request.
#
# Where does the JWT token travel?
# With a JavaScript client, it was the client code that kept the token
# and added it itself to each request ("Authorization: Bearer
# ..." header). A browser that displays ordinary HTML pages cannot
# do that: for it to present the token by itself on each request, it
# must be stored in a COOKIE. The options of this cookie matter for
# security:
#   - HttpOnly: the JavaScript of the page cannot read the cookie (an
#     injected script could therefore not steal the token);
#   - SameSite=Lax: the browser does NOT send the cookie with a POST coming
#     from another site (first protection against the so-called CSRF attack; the
#     second is the anti-CSRF token of the forms, see rdvmedecins/__init__.py);
#   - Secure: in production (HTTPS), the cookie never travels in clear;
#   - Max-Age: the cookie disappears at the same time as the token expires.
# =========================================================================
from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone

import jwt
from flask import Request, Response

from rdvmedecins.auth.passwords import verify
from rdvmedecins.auth.connected_user import ConnectedUser
from rdvmedecins.entities import User
from rdvmedecins.repositories.user_repository import UserRepository

# the name of the cookie that carries the token
JWT_COOKIE = "rdvmedecins_jwt"


class AuthService:

    def __init__(self, sessions, users: UserRepository, secret: str, duration_seconds: int,
                 cookie_secure: bool):
        # HMAC-SHA256 requires a key of at least 256 bits: we say so
        # clearly at startup rather than at the first login
        if len(secret.encode("utf-8")) < 32:
            raise RuntimeError("JWT_SECRET must be at least 32 characters long (see config.py).")
        self._sessions = sessions
        self._users = users
        self._secret = secret
        self._duration = timedelta(seconds=duration_seconds)
        self._cookie_secure = cookie_secure

    # None if the login does not exist or if the password is wrong
    def validate_user(self, login: str, password: str) -> User | None:
        with self._sessions() as session:
            user = self._users.read_by_login(session, login)
        if user is None or not verify(password, user.password):
            return None
        return user

    # -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # builds the JWT token of [user] and puts it in a cookie.
    # The token is SIGNED (HMAC-SHA256) with the secret key: the browser
    # can read it (it is not encrypted), but not modify it - any
    # modification would make the signature invalid.
    # -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    def set_token(self, response: Response, user: User):
        now = datetime.now(timezone.utc)
        claims = {
            "sub": str(user.id),
            "login": user.login,
            "name": user.name,
            "role": user.role.value,
            "iat": now,
            "exp": now + self._duration,
        }
        token = jwt.encode(claims, self._secret, algorithm="HS256")
        response.set_cookie(JWT_COOKIE, token, max_age=self._duration, path="/", httponly=True,
                            samesite="Lax", secure=self._cookie_secure)

    # clears the cookie: it is set again, empty, with a zero lifetime
    @staticmethod
    def clear_token(response: Response):
        response.delete_cookie(JWT_COOKIE, path="/")

    # the token present in the request, whether valid or not
    @staticmethod
    def token_of(request: Request) -> str | None:
        return request.cookies.get(JWT_COOKIE)

    # -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # the user described by the cookie of the request; None if there is no
    # token, or if the token is expired, forged or malformed.
    # jwt.decode checks the signature AND the expiration date (exp claim).
    # -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    def current_user(self, request: Request) -> ConnectedUser | None:
        token = self.token_of(request)
        if not token:
            return None
        try:
            claims = jwt.decode(token, self._secret, algorithms=["HS256"])
        except jwt.InvalidTokenError:
            return None
        return ConnectedUser.of(claims)
  • lines 46–47: a signature key that is too short is flagged when the application starts, rather than on the first login: [create_app] creates the service, and the exception terminates the application with this message;
  • Lines 55–60: Verification of a username and password. The service reads the user via DAO, in a session that remains open only for the duration of this read; password verification ([bcrypt], which is slow) occurs after the session is closed, to avoid maintaining an unnecessary connection to the database;
  • Lines 68–80: the token (example 25) and its cookie, [rdvmedecins_jwt]. [user.role.value]: the enumeration value, the string ["USER"]. The cookie is assigned the attribute [Secure] in production ([COOKIE_SECURE]);
  • lines 84–85: deleting the cookie. This is a static method: it does not require an object and is called on the class ([AuthService.clear_token(response)]);
  • lines 97–105: the user identified by the request cookie, or [None].

docs.title: 11.13.4. auth/security.py
docs.text:
The core of security: authentication of each request and the access rule.

# =========================================================================
# auth/security.py
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Who can access what, and how the user is recognized on each
# request (see examples 25 and 26).
#
# For each request, the authenticate function (a before_request of
# the application):
#   1. reads the token of the cookie, checks its signature and its expiration date,
#      and stores the user in g.user (None if there is none);
#   2. applies the access rule: ALL the actions require an authenticated
#      user, except those marked @public (login,
#      account creation, choice of language) and the static files.
#      It is the rule "everything is forbidden except what is allowed": an action
#      added later, that one would have forgotten to protect, is protected by default.
# Only then does Flask call the action, whose decorator
# @roles_required(...) checks the role.
#
# Two failure cases, two responses suited to an HTML application:
#   - no authenticated user (no token, expired or forged token)
#     -> redirect to the login page;
#   - insufficient role -> response 403, which web/errors.py turns into a page.
# =========================================================================
from functools import wraps

from flask import abort, current_app, g, redirect, request, url_for

from rdvmedecins.auth.auth_service import AuthService
from rdvmedecins.entities import Role
from rdvmedecins.web.flash import flash_error


# the token is valid, but the account it designates no longer exists: it has been
# deleted since the login (by the patient themselves in another
# tab, or by the ADMIN). This case is handled like an expired session:
# web/errors.py clears the cookie and sends back to the login page.
class InvalidSession(Exception):
    pass


# a decorator that MARKS an action as public (see example 24)
def public(action):
    action.public = True
    return action


def register(app, auth_service: AuthService):

    @app.before_request
    def authenticate():
        g.user = auth_service.current_user(request)
        # no route matches (the 404 page will follow), or a static file
        if request.endpoint is None or request.endpoint == "static":
            return None
        action = current_app.view_functions[request.endpoint]
        if getattr(action, "public", False) or g.user is not None:
            return None
        # a response returned by a before_request stops the processing:
        # the action is not called
        return to_login()


# -----------------------------------------------------------------------
# no authenticated user -> login page. If a cookie was
# present, its token is no longer valid: the session has expired.
# The cookie is then cleared, and the user is warned by a flash message.
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------
def to_login():
    response = redirect(url_for("auth.show_login"))
    if AuthService.token_of(request):
        AuthService.clear_token(response)
        flash_error("ERRORS.SESSION_EXPIRED")
    return response


# -----------------------------------------------------------------------
# the role of the user must be one of [roles]; otherwise, response 403.
# require_roles is called from a blueprint before_request (all the
# actions of the blueprint, see controllers/persons.py); roles_required is
# the decorator of an action (see example 26).
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------
def require_roles(*roles: Role):
    if g.user is None:
        raise InvalidSession()
    if g.user.role not in roles:
        abort(403)


def roles_required(*roles: Role):
    def decorator(action):
        @wraps(action)
        def protected_action(*args, **kwargs):
            require_roles(*roles)
            return action(*args, **kwargs)

        return protected_action

    return decorator
  • lines 37–38: an exception for a special case: the token is valid, but the account it refers to no longer exists (the patient deleted it in another tab, or the administrator deleted it). Actions that require the account raise this exception; the error handler treats it as an expired session (see [web/errors.py]);
  • lines 42–44: the decorator that marks an action as public (example 24);
  • lines 50–60: the application’s [before_request] function. First, the user is authenticated for all requests, including public requests: the login page must know whether the user is already logged in. Next, the access rule: a request that does not match any route ([request.endpoint is None]: the 404 page will follow) or that requests a static file is allowed; an action marked as public is allowed; an authenticated user is allowed. Otherwise, the function returns a response (redirecting to the login page), which stops processing: the action is not called.

This is the “everything is prohibited unless explicitly permitted” rule: an action added later—even if you forgot to secure it—is automatically secured. Forgetting to include [@public] on a public action is immediately obvious (the page redirects to the login page); failing to protect a private action is not immediately apparent: the default rule must be the safest. This is also the rule for version [Spring MVC] ([anyRequest().authenticated()]);

  • lines 68–73: the redirect to the login page. If the request contained a token cookie, it means that token is no longer valid (expired or tampered with): the cookie is deleted, and a pop-up message explains to the user that their session has expired (the screenshot of the end-of-session message, shown above);
  • lines 82–86: authorization. The parameter [*roles] accepts any number of roles in a tuple: [require_roles(Role.ADMIN, Role.DOCTOR)]. A role missing from the list results in a 403 error. The [g.user is None] test should never be true (the access rule has already filtered out anonymous visitors), unless [require_roles] were called from a public action: this provides an additional layer of security;
  • lines 89–98: the parameter decorator from Example 26, which calls [require_roles]. [require_roles] can also be used on its own, within the [before_request] of a blueprint, to protect all of its actions at once (see [controllers/persons.py]).

docs.title: 11.13.5. auth/captcha_drawing.py
docs.text: The image rendering is the same as in Example 27, reproduced exactly as shown. Its header comment highlights an important point: each character is drawn using lines ([<path>] elements), and never written as text (a [<text>] element); otherwise, a bot would simply have to read the image’s source code.

docs.title: 11.13.6. auth/captcha.py
docs.text:
# =========================================================================
# auth/captcha.py
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# A CAPTCHA ("test to tell a human from a robot") made by the
# server itself, without any external service: a few distorted characters,
# scrambled by lines, in an SVG image (see captcha_drawing.py). A
# human reads them easily; a robot that merely sends
# forms in a loop cannot do it.
#
# How it works:
#   1. generate() draws a random text, makes an image of it, and stores the
#      right answer IN THE SERVER'S MEMORY, under a random identifier;
#   2. the page displays the image and puts the identifier in a hidden field of the
#      form (the answer itself never leaves the server);
#   3. verify(id, typed) compares the input with the expected answer, then
#      FORGETS this captcha: each image is used only once, a robot cannot
#      replay an answer already found.
#
# A single CaptchaService object for the whole server, used by several
# requests IN PARALLEL (the server processes them on several threads): a
# lock (Lock) guarantees that only one thread at a time reads or modifies the
# dictionary of pending captchas.
#
# Accepted limit: the memory of a single process. With several processes
# or several servers, a shared storage would be needed.
# =========================================================================
import secrets
from dataclasses import dataclass
from datetime import datetime, timedelta
from threading import Lock

from rdvmedecins.auth import captcha_drawing

# validity duration of an image: one has 10 minutes to fill in the form
LIFETIME = timedelta(minutes=10)

# memory safeguard: beyond this, all the pending captchas are forgotten
MAX_CAPTCHAS = 10_000


# a captcha: id, to put in the hidden field "captchaId" of the form;
# svg, the image, to insert as is into the page
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Captcha:
    id: str
    svg: str


class CaptchaService:

    def __init__(self):
        # id -> (expected answer, expiration date)
        self._pending: dict[str, tuple[str, datetime]] = {}
        self._lock = Lock()

    def generate(self) -> Captcha:
        text = captcha_drawing.random_text(5)  # 5 characters
        id = secrets.token_urlsafe(16)  # a random identifier, impossible to guess
        with self._lock:
            self._purge()
            self._pending[id] = (text, datetime.now() + LIFETIME)
        return Captcha(id, captcha_drawing.svg(text))

    # true if [typed] is the right answer to captcha [id] (regardless of
    # case). The captcha is consumed in all cases: if two
    # requests present the same captcha at the same moment, only one
    # removes it (pop, under the lock) - the other fails.
    def verify(self, id: str | None, typed: str | None) -> bool:
        with self._lock:
            expected = self._pending.pop(id, None) if id else None
        if expected is None or typed is None:
            return False
        text, expires = expected
        return expires > datetime.now() and text.lower() == typed.strip().lower()

    # (called under the lock)
    def _purge(self):
        now = datetime.now()
        for id in [id for id, (_, expires) in self._pending.items() if expires <= now]:
            del self._pending[id]
        if len(self._pending) >= MAX_CAPTCHAS:
            self._pending.clear()

The service from Example 27, with an addition: the [_purge] method (lines 77–82), called each time a CAPTCHA is created, discards expired CAPTCHAs. Without it, captchas that are displayed but never used (such as when a login page is opened and then abandoned) would accumulate in memory. [MAX_CAPTCHAS] acts as a safeguard: a bot requesting millions of login pages would not be able to exhaust the server’s memory. The number [10_000] is written with an underscore, which separates the thousands for readability ([Python] ignores this). The list of identifiers to be deleted is constructed before the deletion loop: you cannot delete keys from a dictionary while iterating through it.

docs.title: 11.13.7. auth/limiter.py
docs.text:
# =========================================================================
# auth/limiter.py
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Second line of defense against robots (the first is the captcha): we COUNT
# the attempts, and beyond a threshold we BLOCK for a while.
#
#   - login: after LOGIN_MAX_FAILURES failures (wrong captcha or wrong
#     password) for the same login from the same IP address, this pair
#     is blocked LOGIN_BLOCK_MINUTES minutes. The same IP address is also
#     blocked if it accumulates 5 times more failures, all logins together (a
#     robot that tries thousands of different logins);
#   - account creation: at most REGISTRATION_MAX_PER_HOUR accounts created
#     per hour from the same IP address.
#
# Beware in a classroom: all the computers often go out on the Internet
# through the SAME IP address. This is why the login block applies
# first to the (IP, login) pair - a student who mistypes their
# password does not block their neighbors - and why the thresholds can be set
# in config.py.
#
# A single object for the whole server, called by parallel requests:
# all the public methods take the lock - only one thread at a
# time reads AND modifies the counters.
# =========================================================================
import math
from datetime import datetime, timedelta
from threading import Lock

ONE_HOUR = timedelta(hours=1)


class Counter:
    def __init__(self, start: datetime):
        self.number = 0  # attempts counted in the current window
        self.start = start  # start of the counting window
        self.blocked_until = datetime.min  # datetime.min if not blocked


class AttemptLimiter:

    def __init__(self, login_max_failures: int, login_block_minutes: int,
                 registration_max_per_hour: int):
        self._counters: dict[str, Counter] = {}
        self._lock = Lock()
        self._max_login_failures = login_max_failures
        self._login_block_duration = timedelta(minutes=login_block_minutes)
        self._max_registrations = registration_max_per_hour

    # ---------------------------------------------------------------- login

    # number of remaining block minutes (0 = the attempt is allowed)
    def login_block_minutes(self, ip: str, login: str) -> int:
        with self._lock:
            return max(self._remaining_minutes(self._login_key(ip, login)),
                       self._remaining_minutes(self._ip_key(ip)))

    def login_failure(self, ip: str, login: str):
        with self._lock:
            self._count(self._login_key(ip, login), self._max_login_failures,
                        self._login_block_duration, self._login_block_duration)
            self._count(self._ip_key(ip), self._max_login_failures * 5,
                        self._login_block_duration, self._login_block_duration)

    # a successful login resets the counter of THIS login
    def login_success(self, ip: str, login: str):
        with self._lock:
            self._counters.pop(self._login_key(ip, login), None)

    # ---------------------------------------------------------------- registration

    def registration_block_minutes(self, ip: str) -> int:
        with self._lock:
            return self._remaining_minutes(f"registration|{ip}")

    # one-hour window; once the quota is reached, blocked until the end of the hour
    def registration_success(self, ip: str):
        with self._lock:
            self._count(f"registration|{ip}", self._max_registrations, ONE_HOUR, ONE_HOUR)

    # ---------------------------------------------------------------- common mechanics
    # (the private methods are always called under the lock)

    def _remaining_minutes(self, key: str) -> int:
        counter = self._counters.get(key)
        if counter is None:
            return 0
        remaining = (counter.blocked_until - datetime.now()).total_seconds()
        # rounded UP to the minute: 30 s of remaining block -> "1 minute"
        return max(0, math.ceil(remaining / 60))

    # counts an attempt; if the threshold is reached within the window, blocks
    def _count(self, key: str, maximum: int, window: timedelta, block: timedelta):
        now = datetime.now()
        self._purge(now)
        counter = self._counters.get(key)
        if counter is None or now - counter.start > window:
            counter = Counter(now)
            self._counters[key] = counter
        counter.number += 1
        if counter.number >= maximum:
            counter.blocked_until = now + block
            counter.number = 0  # after the block, we start again from zero
            counter.start = counter.blocked_until

    # we forget the counters that are no longer useful (neither blocked, nor recent)
    def _purge(self, now: datetime):
        if len(self._counters) < 1000:
            return
        for key in [key for key, c in self._counters.items()
                    if c.blocked_until < now and now - c.start > ONE_HOUR]:
            del self._counters[key]

    @staticmethod
    def _login_key(ip: str, login: str) -> str:
        return f"login|{ip}|{login.strip().lower()}"

    @staticmethod
    def _ip_key(ip: str) -> str:
        return f"ip|{ip}"

A more complete version of the limiter from Example 27:

  • The connection block first targets the pair (address IP, login): in a classroom, all computers often access the Internet through the same address, IP, and a student who enters the wrong password should not block their neighbors. However, an address is also blocked if it accumulates five times as many failed attempts, across all logins: this is the case for a bot that tries thousands of different logins (lines 57–61);
  • account creation is limited to a certain number of accounts per hour per IP address (lines 71–78);
  • The counters are stored in a single dictionary, under keys prefixed by their usage ([login|...], [ip|...], [registration|...]);
  • lines 92–103: A counter tracks attempts within a time window; an attempt that occurs after the window ends triggers a new one. When the threshold is reached, the key is locked, and the counter resets to zero;
  • lines 106–111: Once the counter exceeds 1,000 entries, those that are no longer in use (neither blocked nor recent) are discarded.

Like the CAPTCHA, the limiter stores its data in the process’s memory: this is acceptable for an application served by a single process (the development server, [Waitress]), but not for multiple processes or multiple servers, which would not share their counters (shared storage would then be required, such as [Redis]).

docs.title: 11.13.8. auth/registration_pass.py
docs.text:
# =========================================================================
# auth/registration_pass.py
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The "pass" of account creation.
#
# To open the page "Create a patient account", one must first have
# typed the captcha of the authentication page (see
# controllers/registration.py, POST /register/access). The server then issues
# a pass:
#   - a random identifier, stored in an HttpOnly cookie;
#   - valid 15 minutes (the time to fill in the form, even when trying
#     several times after input errors);
#   - consumed as soon as an account is created: ONE captcha solved = ONE account at
#     most. A robot cannot create accounts in series.
#
# Without a valid pass, GET and POST /register send back to the
# authentication page: typing the URL /register directly does not make it
# possible to bypass the captcha.
#
# Like the captchas, the passes live in the memory of the process.
# =========================================================================
import secrets
from datetime import datetime, timedelta
from threading import Lock

from flask import Response

COOKIE = "rdvmedecins_registration"

LIFETIME = timedelta(minutes=15)
MAX_PASSES = 10_000


class RegistrationPass:

    def __init__(self):
        # id -> expiration date
        self._passes: dict[str, datetime] = {}
        self._lock = Lock()

    # issues a new pass; returns its identifier
    def issue(self) -> str:
        id = secrets.token_urlsafe(16)
        with self._lock:
            self._purge()
            self._passes[id] = datetime.now() + LIFETIME
        return id

    # true if [id] is an existing, non-expired pass
    def is_valid(self, id: str | None) -> bool:
        with self._lock:
            expires = self._passes.get(id) if id else None
        return expires is not None and expires > datetime.now()

    # the pass has been used: it is forgotten
    def consume(self, id: str | None):
        with self._lock:
            self._passes.pop(id, None)

    # (called under the lock)
    def _purge(self):
        now = datetime.now()
        for id in [id for id, expires in self._passes.items() if expires <= now]:
            del self._passes[id]
        if len(self._passes) >= MAX_PASSES:
            self._passes.clear()


# the cookie is sent by the browser only to the /register addresses...
def set_cookie(response: Response, id: str, secure: bool):
    response.set_cookie(COOKIE, id, max_age=LIFETIME, path="/register", httponly=True,
                        samesite="Lax", secure=secure)


# ... and it is cleared by setting it again empty, with a zero lifetime
def clear_cookie(response: Response):
    response.delete_cookie(COOKIE, path="/register")

Creating a patient account is a public page: a bot could create accounts in bulk. It is therefore protected by the login page’s CAPTCHA: the “Create a patient account” button sends this CAPTCHA to the server, which, if it is correct, issues a token:

  • lines 42–47: a random identifier, valid for 15 minutes, stored in memory like the CAPTCHAs;
  • lines 50–53: The registration page verifies the pass for each request—GET is treated the same as POST;
  • lines 56–58: Creating an account consumes the pass: one solved CAPTCHA equals one account at most;
  • lines 70–72: The pass is stored in a cookie. Its attribute, [path="/register"], limits the requests to which the browser attaches it: only addresses beginning with [/register];
  • lines 76–77: To delete a cookie, you must specify the same path as when it was set.

docs.title: 11.13.9. controllers/auth.py
docs.text:
The connection controller, which uses all of these services.

# =========================================================================
# controllers/auth.py
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The PUBLIC routes of the login:
#   GET  /        redirects to the home page of the role (or to /login)
#   GET  /login   displays the login form (with its captcha)
#   POST /login   checks attempt limit, captcha, login / password
#   POST /logout  the logout
#
# Protection against robots, in this order:
#   1. too many recent failures for this login from this IP address?
#      -> immediate refusal, without even looking at the password;
#   2. wrong answer to the captcha? -> refusal (counted as a failure);
#   3. only then, verification of the password.
# The password of an attempt refused at steps 1 or 2 is NEVER
# checked: a robot can therefore learn nothing by insisting.
# =========================================================================
from flask import Blueprint, g, redirect, render_template, request, url_for

from rdvmedecins.auth.auth_service import AuthService
from rdvmedecins.auth.security import public
from rdvmedecins.entities import Role
from rdvmedecins.models.view_models import LoginModel, Message
from rdvmedecins.web.services import auth_service, captchas, limiter

auth = Blueprint("auth", __name__)


# the home page of each role, right after the login
def home_page(role: Role) -> str:
    return url_for("area.patient_area") if role == Role.USER else url_for("schedule.show")


# the IP address of the visitor. Behind a reverse proxy (nginx...), it would be
# that of the proxy: the application would then have to be wrapped in the
# ProxyFix middleware of Werkzeug, which reads the X-Forwarded-For header.
def ip_address() -> str:
    return request.remote_addr or ""


# -----------------------------------------------------------------------
# GET /
# The route is public: the user has been established, if there is one, by
# auth/security.py (g.user), but nothing is required.
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------
@auth.get("/")
@public
def home():
    return redirect(home_page(g.user.role) if g.user else url_for("auth.show_login"))


# -----------------------------------------------------------------------
# GET /login[?login=xxx]: the optional parameter pre-fills the login
# field (used right after the creation of an account, see controllers/registration.py)
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------
@auth.get("/login")
@public
def show_login():
    # already logged in (token still valid): straight to the home page
    if g.user:
        return redirect(home_page(g.user.role))
    return form(request.args.get("login", "")[:30], None)


# -----------------------------------------------------------------------
# POST /login
# request.form.get: a missing field gives None (and not a 400 error) -
# it is the code that decides what to do with it.
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------
@auth.post("/login")
@public
def log_in():
    login = (request.form.get("login") or "").strip()
    password = request.form.get("password") or ""
    ip = ip_address()

    # 1. too many recent failures?
    minutes = limiter().login_block_minutes(ip, login)
    if minutes > 0:
        return form(login, Message("ERRORS.TOO_MANY_ATTEMPTS", {"minutes": str(minutes)}))

    # 2. the captcha
    if not captchas().verify(request.form.get("captchaId"), request.form.get("captcha")):
        limiter().login_failure(ip, login)
        return form(login, Message("ERRORS.WRONG_CAPTCHA"))

    # 3. the password
    user = auth_service().validate_user(login, password) if login and password else None
    if user is None:
        limiter().login_failure(ip, login)
        return form(login, Message("LOGIN.ERROR"))

    limiter().login_success(ip, login)
    response = redirect(home_page(user.role))
    auth_service().set_token(response, user)
    return response


# -----------------------------------------------------------------------
# POST /logout: clear the cookie of the token, then go to the login
# page. POST only: a simple link (GET), placed on another site,
# cannot log the user out without their knowledge.
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------
@auth.post("/logout")
@public
def log_out():
    response = redirect(url_for("auth.show_login"))
    AuthService.clear_token(response)
    return response


# the form, always with a NEW captcha (each image is used only
# once); the typed login is displayed again, never the password
def form(login: str, error: Message | None):
    model = LoginModel("LOGIN.TITLE", error, login, captchas().generate())
    return render_template("login.html", model=model)
  • line 24: Shared services are obtained through small functions in the [web/services.py] module (discussed later), which retrieve them from [app.extensions];
  • lines 30–31: Each role has its own home page: a patient portal for patients, and the calendar for others;
  • lines 37–38: the visitor’s address IP. Behind a reverse proxy ([nginx], [Apache]), this would be the proxy’s address, which is the same for all visitors: the application would then need to be wrapped in the [ProxyFix] middleware from [Werkzeug] (see the chapter on the lifecycle), which reads the original address from the [X-Forwarded-For] header added by the proxy;
  • lines 46–49: the public root of the site: it redirects to the user’s home page or to the login page;
  • lines 56–62: the login page. A user who is already logged in (whose token is still valid) is sent directly to their home page. The optional parameter [login] pre-fills the field (after an account is created); [[:30]] limits its length to that of a username;
  • Lines 70–96: the login process, in three steps, in this order: potential blocking, the CAPTCHA, and then only the password. An attempt rejected in the first two steps never checks the password: a bot cannot learn anything by persisting. [request.form.get(...) or ""]: an empty field returns an empty string. The error message is an object [Message]: a translation key and its parameters (discussed later);
  • lines 104–109: logout, in POST (example 25). It is public: a user whose session has expired must be able to click “Log out” without first being redirected;
  • lines 114–116: the login page, still with a new CAPTCHA. Its template is a [LoginModel] object (see [models/view_models.py]).

Note that the login form does not use [WTForms]: its three fields have no validation rules (an empty username simply results in a failed login), and the form is protected against CSRF attacks by [CSRFProtect], like all forms in the application.

docs.title: 11.14. The Web Layer: Shared Services
docs.text: The [web] folder contains what the controllers have in common. Each module in it answers a question that all controllers ask themselves: how to obtain a service, translate a text, display a message after a redirect, redisplay a rejected form, or convert an error into a page.

docs.title: 11.14.1. web/services.py
docs.text:
# =========================================================================
# web/services.py
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The shared objects of the application (see example 06): they are created ONCE,
# by the application factory (rdvmedecins/__init__.py), and
# stored in the app.extensions dictionary. These small functions find
# them there, for the application that processes the current request
# (current_app); they also give their TYPE to the analysis tools.
# =========================================================================
from flask import current_app

from rdvmedecins.auth.auth_service import AuthService
from rdvmedecins.auth.captcha import CaptchaService
from rdvmedecins.auth.limiter import AttemptLimiter
from rdvmedecins.auth.registration_pass import RegistrationPass
from rdvmedecins.web.application_model import ApplicationModel


def application() -> ApplicationModel:
    return current_app.extensions["rdvmedecins.application"]


def auth_service() -> AuthService:
    return current_app.extensions["rdvmedecins.auth"]


def captchas() -> CaptchaService:
    return current_app.extensions["rdvmedecins.captchas"]


def limiter() -> AttemptLimiter:
    return current_app.extensions["rdvmedecins.limiter"]


def passes() -> RegistrationPass:
    return current_app.extensions["rdvmedecins.passes"]

The shared objects, created by the factory and stored in [app.extensions], are retrieved by these small functions (example 06). They eliminate the need to repeat the dictionary key in each controller and provide their type to analysis tools: in a controller, the editor knows that [application()] is a [ApplicationModel] and offers its methods.

docs.title: 11.14.2. web/translator.py
docs.text:
# =========================================================================
# web/translator.py
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# French / English translation of the interface (see example 22).
#
# The dictionaries are the SAME files as those of the NestJS,
# ASP.NET Core and Spring MVC versions of the application (i18n/fr.json, i18n/en.json),
# read only once at startup.
#
# In the views, the t function (see web/common_model.py):
#   {{ t("LOGIN.TITLE") }}                            without parameter;
#   {{ t("AREA.HELLO", name=model.patient) }}         named parameters;
#   {{ t(message.key, message.params) }}              a dictionary of parameters.
#
# THE CURRENT LANGUAGE: g.language, set on each request from a cookie
# (see rdvmedecins/__init__.py, set_language function).
# =========================================================================
import json
import re
from pathlib import Path

from flask import g

LANGUAGES = ("fr", "en")
DEFAULT_LANGUAGE = "en"

# the cookie that remembers the chosen language (see controllers/language.py)
LANGUAGE_COOKIE = "rdvmedecins_language"

# {name}: a parameter in a text
PARAMETER = re.compile(r"\{(\w+)\}")


# the supported language that matches [code]: "fr" -> "fr"; "de" or None -> "en"
def language(code: str | None) -> str:
    return code if code in LANGUAGES else DEFAULT_LANGUAGE


class Translator:

    def __init__(self, folder: Path):
        # language -> (full key "LOGIN.TITLE" -> text)
        self._dictionaries: dict[str, dict[str, str]] = {}
        for code in LANGUAGES:
            with open(folder / f"{code}.json", encoding="utf-8") as file:
                self._dictionaries[code] = self._flatten(json.load(file))

    # -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # translate("DOCTORS.ADDED", {"name": "Marie PELISSIER"})
    #   -> looks for "DOCTORS.ADDED" in the dictionary of the language, and
    #      replaces {name} by its value. A key missing from the requested language
    #      is looked for in English; missing everywhere, the key itself
    #      is displayed (an omission is thus spotted immediately).
    # The parameters: a dictionary, and/or named parameters.
    # -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    def translate(self, key: str | None, params: dict | None = None, **others) -> str:
        if not key:
            return ""
        text = self._dictionaries[language(g.get("language"))].get(key)
        if text is None:
            text = self._dictionaries[DEFAULT_LANGUAGE].get(key, key)
        values = {**(params or {}), **others}
        if not values:
            return text
        return PARAMETER.sub(lambda m: str(values.get(m.group(1), m.group(0))), text)

    # { "LOGIN": { "TITLE": "Login" } } -> { "LOGIN.TITLE": "Login" }
    @classmethod
    def _flatten(cls, node: dict, prefix: str = "") -> dict[str, str]:
        result = {}
        for key, value in node.items():
            full_key = f"{prefix}.{key}" if prefix else key
            if isinstance(value, dict):
                result.update(cls._flatten(value, full_key))
            else:
                result[full_key] = value
        return result

The translator from Example 22, with three additions:

  • Lines 56–65: A text’s parameters can be provided by a dictionary (the second parameter, [params]), by named parameters ([**others]), or both. Application messages (the [Message] class, discussed later) carry their parameters in a dictionary; views, on the other hand, prefer named parameters. [{**a, **b}] creates a dictionary that combines those from [a] and [b];
  • line 61: a key missing from the requested language is looked up in English before being displayed as-is;
  • line 59: [g.get("language")] returns [None] if [g] lacks the [language] attribute, rather than throwing an exception: the translator works even if an error occurs before the [before_request] function, which sets the language.

The name of the language cookie is prefixed with the application name ([rdvmedecins_language]), just like the token and pass: cookies are associated with a domain name ([localhost]), not a port. The examples, which are also served by [localhost], could otherwise read the application’s cookies.

docs.title: 11.14.3. web/common_model.py
docs.text:
# =========================================================================
# web/common_model.py
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# What ALL the views need, whatever the page (see example
# 15): a "context processor", run before each view is
# built, adds its variables to the model of all the views:
#   - user     : the connected user (or None), for the navigation bar;
#   - language : "fr" or "en";
#   - path     : the requested URL (active menu of the navigation bar,
#                "Another image" link of the captcha);
#   - t        : the translation function (see web/translator.py).
# The flash messages are read by the layout (get_flashed_messages).
# =========================================================================
from flask import g, request

from rdvmedecins.web.translator import Translator


def register(app, translator: Translator):

    @app.context_processor
    def common_model():
        return {
            "user": g.get("user"),
            "language": g.get("language", "en"),
            "path": request.path,
            "t": translator.translate,
        }

The context processor from Example 15: four variables available in all views, without actions having to provide them: the logged-in user (for the navigation bar), the language (for the page’s [lang] attribute and the FR / EN buttons), the path of the requested URL (for the active menu and the “Another image” link in the CAPTCHA), and the translation function [t]. [g.get("user")] returns [None] if the attribute does not exist (for example, a fabricated error page before authentication).
