docs.title: 11.19.2. static/js/app.js
docs.text:
// =========================================================================
// static/js/app.js - the ONLY JavaScript of the application.
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// The whole application works without JavaScript. This script adds a
// convenience: before sending a form that carries the attribute
// data-confirmation="...", a modal dialog asks "Are you sure?"
// (the dialog itself is in the page: templates/fragments/confirmation.html).
// If JavaScript is disabled, the form is simply sent without
// confirmation - nothing breaks ("progressive enhancement" principle).
//
// Why not window.confirm()? Its box cannot be styled, and its
// buttons stay in the language of the browser, not in that of the page.
// =========================================================================

(() => {
  const modal = document.getElementById('confirmation-modal');
  if (!modal) {
    return;
  }
  const message = document.getElementById('confirmation-modal-message');
  const noButton = modal.querySelector('.modal-footer [data-action="no"]');

  let pendingForm = null; // the form to send if the user confirms
  let previousFocus = null; // the element to give the focus back to on closing

  function open(form) {
    pendingForm = form;
    previousFocus = document.activeElement;
    // textContent (and not innerHTML): the message is displayed as TEXT,
    // never interpreted as HTML
    message.textContent = form.dataset.confirmation;
    modal.classList.remove('d-none');
    // the focus goes on "No": an absent-minded press on Enter deletes nothing
    noButton.focus();
  }

  function close() {
    modal.classList.add('d-none');
    pendingForm = null;
    if (previousFocus) {
      previousFocus.focus();
    }
  }

  // 1. we intercept the sending of the forms to confirm
  document.querySelectorAll('form[data-confirmation]').forEach((form) => {
    form.addEventListener('submit', (event) => {
      event.preventDefault();
      open(form);
    });
  });

  // 2. the buttons of the dialog (Yes / No / close cross)
  modal.addEventListener('click', (event) => {
    const action = event.target.closest('[data-action]')?.dataset.action;
    if (action === 'yes') {
      const form = pendingForm;
      close();
      // form.submit() sends the form WITHOUT triggering the
      // 'submit' event again: no new confirmation request
      form.submit();
    } else if (action === 'no') {
      close();
    } else if (event.target.classList.contains('modal')) {
      close(); // click on the grey background, outside the dialog
    }
  });

  // 3. keyboard: Escape closes the dialog; Tab stays INSIDE the dialog
  //    (otherwise the focus would go to the greyed-out page, behind)
  modal.addEventListener('keydown', (event) => {
    if (event.key === 'Escape') {
      close();
    } else if (event.key === 'Tab') {
      const buttons = [...modal.querySelectorAll('button')];
      const first = buttons[0];
      const last = buttons[buttons.length - 1];
      if (event.shiftKey && document.activeElement === first) {
        event.preventDefault();
        last.focus();
      } else if (!event.shiftKey && document.activeElement === last) {
        event.preventDefault();
        first.focus();
      }
    }
  });
})();

The script from Example 21, completed:

  • lines 16–18: the script does nothing if the page does not have a confirmation window;
  • lines 26–34: upon opening, the message is placed using [textContent], not [innerHTML]: it is displayed as text and is never interpreted as HTML. The focus moves to the “No” button: accidentally pressing Enter does not delete anything;
  • lines 37–41: Upon closing, the focus returns to the element that had it previously (the “Delete” button), which is important for keyboard navigation;
  • lines 54–65: clicks within the window. [closest('[data-action]')] searches for the element with the attribute [data-action], starting from the clicked element and moving up through its parent elements: a click on an icon inside a button is thus attributed to the button. The operator [?.] returns [undefined] instead of raising an error if no element is found. A click on the grayed-out background closes the window;
  • lines 71–83: keyboard behavior: Esc closes the window; Tab and Shift-Tab cycle the focus among the buttons in the window, without moving to the grayed-out page behind it.

docs.title: 12. Conclusion
docs.text:
This document has presented the development of a MVC web application using the [Flask] framework: an application whose HTML pages are generated by the server, using [Jinja2] views, without a browser-side [JavaScript] framework. He followed the [Spring MVC] course step by step, which itself builds on the [ASP.NET Core MVC] and [NestJS] courses: actions and routing to views, forms, internationalization, security, and data access, followed by a comprehensive case study.

The same 28 examples and the same application were thus written using four frameworks: [TypeScript], [C#], [Java], and [Python]. The concepts are the same; only the names and mechanisms differ. The correspondences between [Spring MVC] and [Flask]:

Spring MVCFlaskclass [@SpringBootApplication], classes [@Configuration], methods [@Bean]factory [create_app], objects stored in [app.extensions]file [pom.xml], starters [Maven]file [requirements.txt], virtual environment, [pip][application.properties], profiles, [@ConfigurationProperties][config.py], [config_<profile>.py], variables [FLASK_...] ([app.config])Dependency injection: singleton beans, [@Service], [@Component]objects created manually by the factory, retrieved by [current_app][@Controller], [@GetMapping], [@PostMapping], view name, or [redirect:...]blueprints, [@bp.get], [@bp.post], [render_template], [redirect]model link, [@RequestParam], converters[request.args], [request.form], [Werkzeug] converters ([<int:id>])[Bean Validation]: [@NotBlank], [@Min], [@Max]..., [@Valid], [BindingResult][Pydantic] (parameters, JSON); [WTForms]: validators, [form.validate()], [form.errors]views [Thymeleaf] ([.html]), [th:text], [th:each], [th:if]views [Jinja2], [{{ }}], [{% for %}], [{% if %}]template and fragments ([th:replace], [th:fragment])[{% extends %}] and blocks, [{% include %}], macros[@ControllerAdvice] and [@ModelAttribute]context processor ([@app.context_processor])flash attributes ([RedirectAttributes])flash messages ([flash], [get_flashed_messages]), in the session cookieservlet filters, interceptorsWSGI, [before_request], [after_request], [teardown_request] middleware[@ControllerAdvice] / [@ExceptionHandler], [ErrorController][@app.errorhandler][Spring Security]: [SecurityFilterChain], resource server, [@PreAuthorize][before_request] and hand-written decorators ([PyJWT], [bcrypt])CSRF protection of [Spring Security][CSRFProtect] from [Flask-WTF]JSON dictionaries read by a [MessageSource], [#{...}], or [LocaleResolver]JSON dictionaries, [t(...)] view function, [g.language] set by a [before_request][Spring Data JPA] and [Hibernate], [JpaRepository], derived queries, [JPQL][SQLAlchemy]: mapped entities, [select(...)], sessions, handwritten DAO classes[@Transactional], [TransactionTemplate][with sessions.begin() as session:][@Version], managed by [Hibernate][version_id_col], managed by [SQLAlchemy][mvnw spring-boot:run], [Spring Boot DevTools][python app.py] in debug mode (automatic reload)executable archive ([java -jar]), with [Tomcat] includedWSGI server: [Waitress], [Gunicorn]

Compared to [Spring MVC], the key points to note are:

  • [Flask] is a micro-framework: it provides routing, requests and responses, the [Jinja2] views, and session management—and that’s it. Everything else (validation, forms, security, data access, translation) is handled by libraries chosen by the developer or written by the developer. This means more code to write, but the code is transparent: nothing happens “by magic,” and you can track every object from its creation (in [create_app]) to its use;
  • there is no dependency injection container: shared objects are created by the factory, stored in [app.extensions], and retrieved by [current_app]. For an application of this size, it’s simple and sufficient;
  • The objects [request], [g], [session], and [current_app] are proxies that, during a request, refer to the objects of that request. They eliminate the need to pass the query from one function to another, but can only be used while processing a query (or within a manually created application context);
  • the decorators of [Python] serve the same purpose as the annotations of [Java]: routes, tags ([@public]), and access controls ([@roles_required]). But a decorator is simply a function that you can write yourself in just a few lines;
  • [Python] is a dynamically typed language: type annotations ([list[Doctor]], [Protocol], generic classes) document the code and guide the editor, but are not checked at runtime. Tools such as [Pylance] (in [Visual Studio Code]) or [mypy] check them before execution;
  • [SQLAlchemy] requires writing the DAO layer (a few lines per request), but its requests—constructed using [Python] objects—remain close to the SQL they produce, and displaying the SQL ([SQL_ECHO]) commands allows you to verify what is being sent to the database. Loading relations is explicitly controlled, query by query;
  • The [Jinja2] views mix HTML and [{{ }}] / [{% %}] tags: they are not valid HTML pages like those of [Thymeleaf], but their language, similar to [Python], is powerful (filters, macros, template inheritance), and automatic escaping protects against HTML injection.

The case study shows that a classic HTML application, without the essential [JavaScript], remains a simple and robust solution: each page is a URL, the browser’s “Back” button works, and the server controls everything. The limited use of [JavaScript] (confirmation windows) enhances the user experience without being necessary for the application to function.

For more information, you can consult the documentation for [Flask] (flask.palletsprojects.com), [Jinja2] (jinja.palletsprojects.com), [Werkzeug] (werkzeug.palletsprojects.com), [WTForms] (wtforms.readthedocs.io), and [Flask-WTF] (flask-wtf.readthedocs.io), from [SQLAlchemy] (docs.sqlalchemy.org), from [Pydantic] (docs.pydantic.dev), and compare this application with its counterparts [Spring MVC], [ASP.NET Core MVC], and [NestJS].

docs.title: 6. Data Scopes
docs.text:
A web application serves many users at once, and each user makes numerous requests. Data can therefore be shared at several levels, known as its scope:

  • application scope: the data is shared by all users for the entire lifetime of the server (the list of doctors, for example);
  • request scope: the data exists only for the duration of a single request (a view’s model, the logged-in user as identified for that request);
  • client scope: the data is specific to a user and must persist from one request to the next (the selected language, the logged-in user).

Web applications have long used a server-maintained session for this last scope: a memory specific to each browser, identified via an identification cookie ([JSESSIONID] in [Java], [PHPSESSID] to [PHP]). The session for [Flask] is different: as we saw in Example 20, it is stored in a signed cookie on the client’s side. The server does not store anything between two requests from the same user: it is said to be stateless. This is what makes it possible, for example, to run multiple identical servers behind a load balancer: any one of them can handle any request. The trade-off is that a cookie is under the user’s control; the user can read it and attempt to modify it. Therefore, only non-sensitive data is stored there, and—if the data must be trusted—it is signed by the server, which then detects any modifications: this is the case for the session [Flask] and the authentication token (see the chapter on authentication).

In [Flask], each scope has its own container:

ScopeSupportLifetimeapplicationAn object created at startup, stored in [app.extensions] and retrieved by [current_app] (example 06)The entire server lifetime, shared by all requestsRequestThe object [g], and the object [request] itself (example 16)processing a requestsessionthe object [session], a dictionary stored in a signed cookieuntil the browser is closed (by default)clienta standard cookie set by [set_cookie] (example 22)the duration set by [max_age]

The objects [current_app], [g], [request], and [session] are imported from the package [flask]. These are proxies (example 05): during a request, each one identifies the object of that request (or of the application processing it).

docs.title: 6.1.1. The objects: services/counter.py
docs.text:
# services/counter.py: a shared counter, and the information of a request
from itertools import count
from threading import Lock


# APPLICATION scope: a single instance (see app.py)
class CounterService:

    def __init__(self):
        self._total = 0
        # several requests can run AT THE SAME TIME: the lock guarantees
        # that two simultaneous increments are not lost
        self._lock = Lock()

    def increment(self) -> int:
        with self._lock:
            self._total += 1
            return self._total


# REQUEST scope: one instance per request (see app.py, start function)
class RequestInfo:

    # a counter shared by all the instances (CLASS attribute);
    # next(...) is atomic: two threads never get the same number
    _instances = count(1)

    def __init__(self, start: str):
        self.number = next(RequestInfo._instances)
        self.start = start
  • Lines 7–18: a visit counter, with application scope: a single object, shared by all requests. As with the task list in Example 20, a lock protects the increment: the [self._total += 1] statement is not atomic (it reads the value, increments it, then writes it), and two threads executing it simultaneously could read the same value—resulting in a visit being lost;
  • lines 22–30: query-scope information: one object per query, containing a number and the time of the query. The number is derived from a counter shared by all instances: [count(1)], from the standard module [itertools], is an iterator that produces 1, 2, 3... each time [next] is called. This is a class attribute (declared at the class level, not in the constructor): it is shared by all instances.

docs.title: 6.1.2. The configuration: app.py
docs.text:
# app.py: the application of example 23
from datetime import datetime
from pathlib import Path

from flask import Blueprint, Flask, g

from controllers.scopes import scopes
from services.counter import CounterService, RequestInfo

BOOTSTRAP = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent / "common" / "bootstrap"


def create_app():
    app = Flask(__name__)
    app.jinja_env.trim_blocks = True
    app.jinja_env.lstrip_blocks = True
    # the key that signs the session cookie (SESSION scope)
    app.config["SECRET_KEY"] = "a-secret-key-for-example-23"
    # APPLICATION scope: a single object, created at startup, shared by ALL
    # the requests of ALL the users
    app.extensions["counter"] = CounterService()
    app.register_blueprint(Blueprint("bootstrap", __name__, static_folder=BOOTSTRAP,
                                     static_url_path="/bootstrap"))
    app.register_blueprint(scopes)

    # REQUEST scope: the g object is born and dies with each request. This
    # function, executed BEFORE the action, stores in it an object that the action and the
    # view will find again during THIS request
    @app.before_request
    def start():
        g.info = RequestInfo(datetime.now().strftime("%H:%M:%S.%f")[:-3])

    return app


if __name__ == "__main__":
    create_app().run(port=5000, debug=True)
  • line 18: the key that signs the session cookie;
  • line 21: the application-scope object;
  • lines 29–31: Before each request, a [RequestInfo] object is stored in [g]. The action and the view will retrieve it, but only during this request. [strftime("%H:%M:%S.%f")] formats the time with its microseconds ([%f], six digits); [[:-3]] removes the last three characters from the string, leaving the milliseconds.

docs.title: 6.1.3. The controller: controllers/scopes.py
docs.text:
# controllers/scopes.py: the four scopes of data
from flask import Blueprint, current_app, g, make_response, render_template, request, session

scopes = Blueprint("scopes", __name__)


@scopes.get("/")
def display():
    # APPLICATION: the shared counter
    total = current_app.extensions["counter"].increment()
    # SESSION: a dictionary specific to THIS browser, which Flask stores in a
    # SIGNED cookie (session); it lasts until the browser is closed
    session["visits"] = session.get("visits", 0) + 1
    # CLIENT: a piece of data kept by the BROWSER in an ordinary cookie,
    # sent back to the server with each request
    my_visits = to_integer(request.cookies.get("myVisits")) + 1
    response = make_response(render_template(
        "scopes/scopes.html", total=total, instance=g.info.number,
        session_visits=session["visits"], my_visits=my_visits))
    response.set_cookie("myVisits", str(my_visits), httponly=True, samesite="Lax")
    return response


# "41" -> 41; None or "abc" -> 0
def to_integer(text: str | None) -> int:
    try:
        return int(text)
    except (TypeError, ValueError):
        return 0
  • line 10: the application scope. [current_app] refers to the application processing the current request;
  • line 13: the session scope. [session] is used as a dictionary: [session.get("visits", 0)] returns the value of the key, or 0 if it is absent. When the action modifies the session, [Flask] sends, along with the response, a new cookie, [session], which contains the signed dictionary;
  • line 16: the client scope, with a regular cookie, [myVisits], read from [request.cookies]. Its value is a string provided by the browser and may therefore be missing or invalid; the function [to_integer] returns 0 in either case;
  • Lines 17–20: To set a cookie, you need the response object: [make_response] constructs it from the page generated by the view (example 05), then [set_cookie] adds the header [Set-Cookie] to it. Without [max_age], the cookie lasts until the browser is closed (it is a “session” cookie, as defined by browsers);
  • line 18: the request scope: the object stored in [g] by the function [start].

docs.title: 6.1.5. Execution
docs.text:
After two visits in a browser:

Let's track the requests using [curl], which acts as an initial browser by storing its cookies in the file [a.txt]:

curl -i -c a.txt -b a.txt http://localhost:5000/

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 581
Set-Cookie: myVisits=1; HttpOnly; Path=/; SameSite=Lax
Set-Cookie: session=eyJ2aXNpdHMiOjF9.arfKwA.YK-2GACLdbCJ_NXM5dYJYlqEF-4; HttpOnly; Path=/
...
      <li>application: 1 visit(s) to the site, all browsers combined</li>
      <li>request: object no. 2 (no. 2 in the view),
        request received at 15:38:08.779</li>
      <li>session: 1 visit(s) from this browser (1 in the view)</li>
      <li>client: 1 visit(s) from this browser</li>
...

The response sets two cookies. The first, [myVisits], contains the value in plain text. The second, [session], contains the session dictionary: the portion before the first period is JSON [{"visits":1}], encoded in Base64 (uncompressed, as in Example 20, since it is short); followed by the date and the signature.

The request scope object has the number 2, even though this is the first visit to the page: this is because the [start] function runs before every request received by the application, including requests for which no action exists (in this case, a request for a nonexistent URL, made just before) and requests for static files. In the browser, each page thus triggers a second request for the stylesheet of [Bootstrap]: hence the odd numbers in the screenshot. A second visit, with the same cookies:

curl -i -c a.txt -b a.txt http://localhost:5000/

Set-Cookie: myVisits=2; HttpOnly; Path=/; SameSite=Lax
Set-Cookie: session=eyJ2aXNpdHMiOjJ9.arfKwA.l68wWEMYpKTfN3xPp_lysXPExO8; HttpOnly; Path=/
...
      <li>application: 2 visit(s) to the site, all browsers combined</li>
      <li>request: object no. 3 (no. 3 in the view),
        request received at 15:38:08.799</li>
      <li>session: 2 visit(s) from this browser (2 in the view)</li>
      <li>client: 2 visit(s) from this browser</li>

A second “browser,” with its own cookie file, initially empty:

curl -c b.txt -b b.txt http://localhost:5000/

      <li>application: 3 visit(s) to the site, all browsers combined</li>
      <li>request: object no. 4 (no. 4 in the view),
        request received at 15:38:08.813</li>
      <li>session: 1 visit(s) from this browser (1 in the view)</li>
      <li>client: 1 visit(s) from this browser</li>

The application counter has continued running; the session and cookie for the second browser start over at 1. Finally, a malicious user forges their own cookies: 1,000 visits in [myVisits], and a session that purports to contain [{"visits":999}] (Base64-encoded as [eyJ2aXNpdHMiOjk5OX0]), with the signature of another session:

curl -b "myVisits=1000;session=eyJ2aXNpdHMiOjk5OX0.arfKwA.YK-2GACLdbCJ_NXM5dYJYlqEF-4" http://localhost:5000/

      <li>application: 4 visit(s) to the site, all browsers combined</li>
      ...
      <li>session: 1 visit(s) from this browser (1 in the view)</li>
      <li>client: 1001 visit(s) from this browser</li>

The regular cookie was accepted as is: 1,001 visits. The forged session, however, was rejected: its signature does not match its content, and [Flask] ignored it, as if it were absent. That is the key difference between a regular cookie and a signed cookie. Let’s remember the rule: data coming from the client is only trustworthy if it is signed by the server; and even when signed, it remains readable: we don’t put anything secret in it.

docs.title: 5. Internationalization
docs.text:
An internationalized application displays its text in the user's language. The case study is in French and English. The principle is simple: the views no longer contain text, but rather keys ([MENU.HOME]), and a dictionary for each language associates a text with each key. The selected language is stored in a cookie.

The [Flask] ecosystem offers an extension for this purpose, [Flask-Babel], which relies on the standard translation system [gettext]: texts are extracted from the code by a tool, translated into [.po] files, and then compiled into [.mo] files. It is a powerful system, but it requires specific tools and a compilation step. Instead, we’ll write a small class that reads JSON dictionaries: These are the same files as the [ASP.NET Core MVC], [NestJS], and [Spring MVC] versions from the case study, and their format can be read and written without any special tools. The [Babel] library, on the other hand, is still used for formatting dates and amounts (Example 16).

docs.title: 5.1.1. Dictionaries
docs.text:
The [i18n/fr.json] file:

{
  "MENU": {
    "HOME": "Accueil",
    "PRODUCTS": "Produits"
  },
  "HOME": {
    "TITLE": "Bienvenue",
    "HELLO": "Bonjour {name} !",
    "DATE": "Nous sommes le {date}."
  },
  "PRODUCTS": {
    "TITLE": "Nos produits",
    "NAME": "Produit",
    "PRICE": "Prix",
    "COUNT": "{n} produit(s) au catalogue."
  }
}

The keys are grouped by theme within nested JSON objects: the menu text “Home” has the full key [MENU.HOME]. A text string may contain placeholders, written as [{name}], which are replaced during translation. The file [i18n/en.json] has exactly the same keys:

{
  "MENU": {
    "HOME": "Home",
    "PRODUCTS": "Products"
  },
  "HOME": {
    "TITLE": "Welcome",
    "HELLO": "Hello {name}!",
    "DATE": "Today is {date}."
  },
  "PRODUCTS": {
    "TITLE": "Our products",
    "NAME": "Product",
    "PRICE": "Price",
    "COUNT": "{n} product(s) in the catalogue."
  }
}

docs.title: 5.1.2. The translation service: translation/translator.py
docs.text:
# translation/translator.py: the translation service
import json
import re
from pathlib import Path

from flask import g


class Translator:

    LANGUAGES = ("fr", "en")
    DEFAULT_LANGUAGE = "en"

    # {name}: a parameter in a text
    PARAMETER = re.compile(r"\{(\w+)\}")

    def __init__(self, folder: Path):
        # language -> (full key "HOME.HELLO" -> text)
        self._dictionaries: dict[str, dict[str, str]] = {}
        for language in self.LANGUAGES:
            with open(folder / f"{language}.json", encoding="utf-8") as file:
                self._dictionaries[language] = self._flatten(json.load(file))

    # the supported language that matches [code]: "fr" -> "fr"; "de" or None -> "en"
    @classmethod
    def language(cls, code: str | None) -> str:
        return code if code in cls.LANGUAGES else cls.DEFAULT_LANGUAGE

    # translate("HOME.HELLO", name="Marie") -> "Hello Marie!", in the
    # language of the current request (g.language, see app.py)
    def translate(self, key: str, **parameters) -> str:
        # a missing key displays the key itself: an oversight is visible on screen
        text = self._dictionaries[g.language].get(key, key)
        # each {name} is replaced by the value of the parameter of the same name
        return self.PARAMETER.sub(
            lambda m: str(parameters.get(m.group(1), m.group(0))), text)

    # { "MENU": { "HOME": "Home" } } -> { "MENU.HOME": "Home" }
    @classmethod
    def _flatten(cls, node: dict, prefix: str = "") -> dict[str, str]:
        result = {}
        for key, value in node.items():
            full_key = f"{prefix}.{key}" if prefix else key
            if isinstance(value, dict):
                result.update(cls._flatten(value, full_key))
            else:
                result[full_key] = value
        return result
  • lines 11–12: supported languages and the default language—class attributes shared by all objects of the class and accessible without an object ([Translator.LANGUAGES]);
  • line 15: the regular expression for a parameter: a curly brace ([\{], preceded by a [\] because the curly brace has a specific meaning in regular expressions), one or more word characters ([\w+]), and a closing curly brace. The parentheses capture the parameter name. [re.compile] parses the expression once and for all;
  • lines 17–22: the constructor reads the dictionaries once, when the service is created. [json.load] converts the contents of a JSON file into [Python] objects (nested dictionaries). [with open(...) as file] opens the file and ensures it is closed at the end of the block; [encoding="utf-8"] is essential, because the default encoding depends on the system (under [Windows], it is not always [UTF-8]);
  • Lines 25–27: A class method ([@classmethod] decorator) takes the class ([cls]) instead of an object; it is called on the class: [Translator.language("en")]. It returns the supported language corresponding to a code, or the default language if the code is unknown or missing;
  • lines 31–36: the translation of a key, in the language of the current query, read from [g.language] (see Example 16). A key missing from the dictionary is displayed as-is: an omission is immediately visible on the screen. The parameters are received as named parameters ([**parameters]); the regular expression method [sub] replaces each parameter found in the text with the result of a function—in this case, an anonymous function ([lambda m: ...])—which receives the match found ([m]): [m.group(1)] is the captured name, [m.group(0)] is the full text [{name}], which is retained if the parameter was not provided;
  • Lines 40–48: The nested JSON objects are “flattened” into a single dictionary, whose keys are the full keys: [{"MENU": {"HOME": "Home"}}] becomes [{"MENU.HOME": "Home"}]. The method is recursive: it calls itself for each nested object, using the current key as a prefix.

docs.title: 5.1.3. Format in the query language: translation/formats.py
docs.text:
# translation/formats.py: dates and amounts, formatted in the language of the request (see example 16)
from datetime import date
from decimal import Decimal

from babel.dates import format_date
from babel.numbers import format_currency
from flask import g


# a date in full words
def long_date(day: date) -> str:
    return format_date(day, format="full", locale=g.language)


# an amount in euros
def money(amount: Decimal) -> str:
    return format_currency(amount, "EUR", locale=g.language)

The filters in Example 16, which this time use [g.language]. [Babel] accepts a single language ([fr], [en]) as well as a language and a country ([fr_FR]); for [en], it applies U.S. conventions.

docs.title: 5.1.4. Configuration: app.py
docs.text:
# app.py: the application of example 22
from pathlib import Path

from flask import Blueprint, Flask, g, request

from controllers.language import LANGUAGE_COOKIE, language
from controllers.pages import pages
from translation import formats
from translation.translator import Translator

# Bootstrap, shared by the examples (see example 15)
BOOTSTRAP = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent / "common" / "bootstrap"


def create_app():
    app = Flask(__name__)
    app.jinja_env.trim_blocks = True
    app.jinja_env.lstrip_blocks = True
    # the translation service: the dictionaries, read ONCE, at startup
    translator = Translator(Path(app.root_path) / "i18n")
    app.extensions["translator"] = translator
    app.register_blueprint(Blueprint("bootstrap", __name__, static_folder=BOOTSTRAP,
                                     static_url_path="/bootstrap"))
    app.register_blueprint(language)
    app.register_blueprint(pages)

    # the language of each request: that of the [language] cookie, English otherwise
    @app.before_request
    def set_language():
        g.language = Translator.language(request.cookies.get(LANGUAGE_COOKIE))

    # in the views: {{ t('KEY') }}, {{ day | long_date }}, {{ price | money }}
    app.add_template_global(translator.translate, "t")
    app.add_template_filter(formats.long_date)
    app.add_template_filter(formats.money)
    return app


if __name__ == "__main__":
    create_app().run(port=5000, debug=True)
  • lines 20–21: the service, created once at startup. [app.root_path] is the application folder (that of [app.py]);
  • Lines 28–30: Before each action, the request language is set to the language of the [language] cookie if one exists and is supported; otherwise, it defaults to English. [request.cookies] is the dictionary of cookies sent by the browser;
  • line 33: the service’s [translate] method is made available to views as a global function under a short name, [t] (the second parameter of [add_template_global]). An object method is used like a function: [translator.translate] is a method associated with the object [translator].

docs.title: 5.1.5. Language selection: controllers/language.py
docs.text:
# controllers/language.py: the choice of the language
from urllib.parse import urlsplit

from flask import Blueprint, abort, redirect, request

from translation.translator import Translator

language = Blueprint("language", __name__)

LANGUAGE_COOKIE = "language"


# GET /language/fr: stores the choice in a cookie, then goes back to the previous page
@language.get("/language/<code>")
def change(code):
    if code not in Translator.LANGUAGES:
        abort(404)
    response = redirect(origin_page())
    # the cookie: one year of life, unreadable by the JavaScript of the page (httponly),
    # never sent with a POST request coming from another site (samesite)
    response.set_cookie(LANGUAGE_COOKIE, code, max_age=365 * 24 * 3600, httponly=True,
                        samesite="Lax")
    return response


# the page we come from (Referer header), of which we keep only the path:
# redirecting to a complete address coming from the request would allow
# sending the user to another site ("open redirect" flaw)
def origin_page() -> str:
    url = urlsplit(request.headers.get("Referer", ""))
    path = url.path
    # "//site.com/..." would be understood by the browser as an address
    # on ANOTHER site: rejected too
    if not path.startswith("/") or path.startswith("//"):
        return "/"
    return f"{path}?{url.query}" if url.query else path
  • line 16: an unknown language code: 404;
  • line 18: the action responds with a redirect to the page the user came from: the user is returned to that page, in the new language;
  • Lines 21–22: The response includes a cookie, which the browser will send back with every request. [max_age] is its lifetime, in seconds: one year. [httponly=True] makes it invisible to the [JavaScript] on the page; [samesite="Lax"] prevents the browser from sending it with a POST request originating from another site. Unlike the session cookie (example 20), this cookie is not signed: it’s not a problem if the user modifies it, as the server only accepts supported languages;
  • lines 29–36: the original page is specified by the [Referer] header in the request (the misspelled version, with a single [r], is the one used in the HTTP standard), which the browser populates with the URL from the page that contained the link. But this header comes from the client, which can put anything in it. Blindly redirecting to this address would turn our application into an *open redirect*: a malicious link bearing our domain name could send the user to a malicious site. Therefore, we retain only the path and parameters of URL ([urlsplit] breaks it down into its components), and we reject any path that begins with [//], which the browser would interpret as the address of another site.

docs.title: 5.1.6. Actions: controllers/pages.py
docs.text:
# controllers/pages.py: the actions know nothing about the language: they
# provide data, the views translate and format them
from dataclasses import dataclass
from datetime import date
from decimal import Decimal

from flask import Blueprint, render_template

pages = Blueprint("pages", __name__)


@dataclass
class Product:
    name: str
    price: Decimal


@pages.get("/")
def home():
    return render_template("pages/home.html", name="Marie", today=date(2026, 9, 23))


@pages.get("/products")
def products():
    return render_template("pages/products.html", products=[
        Product("Keyboard", Decimal("25")),
        Product("Mouse", Decimal("12.5")),
        Product("Screen", Decimal("1149")),
    ])

Actions are language-agnostic: they provide raw data (a name, a date, amounts). Translation and formatting are handled by the views.

docs.title: 5.1.7. Translate in the views
docs.text:
<!doctype html>
{# g.language: the language of the request, "fr" or "en" #}
<html lang="{{ g.language }}">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  {# the title is a KEY, provided by the page (title_key variable), translated by the layout #}
  <title>{{ t(title_key) }}</title>
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="{{ url_for('bootstrap.static', filename='css/bootstrap.min.css') }}">
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="{{ url_for('static', filename='css/styles.css') }}">
</head>
<body>
  <div class="container py-3">
    {% include "fragments/navbar.html" %}
    <main>
      {% block content %}{% endblock %}
    </main>
  </div>
</body>
</html>
  • Line 3: The page’s [lang] attribute indicates its language to browsers, search engines, and screen readers;
  • line 7: The page title is different for each page, but it is translated by the template. Each page provides the key for its title in a variable, [title_key].
<nav class="navbar navbar-expand bg-light rounded mb-3 px-3">
  <div class="navbar-nav me-auto">
    {# t('KEY'): the translation of a key, in the language of the request #}
    <a class="nav-link" href="/">{{ t("MENU.HOME") }}</a>
    <a class="nav-link" href="/products">{{ t("MENU.PRODUCTS") }}</a>
  </div>
  {# the current language is highlighted #}
  <div class="btn-group btn-group-sm">
    {% for code in ["fr", "en"] %}
    <a class="btn {{ 'btn-primary' if g.language == code else 'btn-outline-primary' }}"
       href="/language/{{ code }}">{{ code | upper }}</a>
    {% endfor %}
  </div>
</nav>
  • lines 4–5: the menu texts, translated;
  • lines 9–12: one button per language, which leads to the action [/language/<code>]. The current language is highlighted ([btn-primary], solid button).
{% extends "layout.html" %}
{# a variable defined OUTSIDE the blocks is visible to the layout #}
{% set title_key = "HOME.TITLE" %}

{% block content %}
  <h1>{{ t("HOME.TITLE") }}</h1>
  {# a parameter: a keyword parameter of the t function #}
  <p>{{ t("HOME.HELLO", name=name) }}</p>
  {# the date, formatted first, then passed as the [date] parameter #}
  <p>{{ t("HOME.DATE", date=today | long_date) }}</p>
{% endblock %}
  • line 3: a variable defined outside the blocks of a page that extends a template is visible to the template: this is how the page passes its title key to the template. (A variable defined within a block, on the other hand, would remain local to that block.);
  • line 8: a text parameter is a named parameter of the function [t];
  • Line 10: The date, formatted in the language of the request, then passed as a parameter.
{% extends "layout.html" %}
{% set title_key = "PRODUCTS.TITLE" %}

{% block content %}
  <h1>{{ t("PRODUCTS.TITLE") }}</h1>
  <table class="table table-sm w-auto">
    <thead><tr><th>{{ t("PRODUCTS.NAME") }}</th><th class="text-end">{{ t("PRODUCTS.PRICE") }}</th></tr></thead>
    <tbody>
      {% for product in products %}
      <tr>
        <td>{{ product.name }}</td>
        <td class="text-end">{{ product.price | money }}</td>
      </tr>
      {% endfor %}
    </tbody>
  </table>
  <p>{{ t("PRODUCTS.COUNT", n=products | length) }}</p>
{% endblock %}
  • Line 17: a calculated parameter. The product names, however, are not translated: they are data that, in a real application, would come from a database.

The home page, in English (the default language), then in French after clicking the “FR” button:

The products page, in both languages. The amounts follow the conventions of each language:

The language switch, as seen with [curl]. The option [-H] provides the header [Referer] that the browser would send:

curl -i -H "Referer: http://localhost:5000/products" http://localhost:5000/language/en

The redirect takes you back to the original page, and the cookie is set for one year. A [Referer] that points to another site does not redirect you there: only its path is retained.

curl -i -H "Referer: https://pirate.example/trap" http://localhost:5000/language/en

Location: /trap

...

The page [/trap] does not exist on our site: the user will receive a 404 error but will remain on our site. Finally, the home page, requested with the cookie [language=en] (option [-b] of [curl]):

curl -b "language=en" http://localhost:5000/

Another way to select the language would have been to read the browser’s [Accept-Language] header (Example 12). The two are often combined: the browser’s language on the first visit, followed by the language the user has selected. This case study focuses on the cookie, with English as the default.

docs.title: 1. Introduction
docs.text:
The document’s PDF is |HERE|.

The document’s codes are |HERE|.

This document is a product of Anthropic’s IA Claude. It follows the document “Step-by-Step Introduction to the [Spring MVC] Web Framework” (2026), which itself followed the documents “Step-by-Step Introduction to the [ASP.NET Core MVC] Web Framework” and “Step-by-Step Introduction to the [NestJS] Web Framework” (2026). This document adapts the [Spring MVC] course to the [Python] environment:

  • the [Spring MVC] framework and the [Java] language are replaced by the [Flask] 3.1 framework and the [Python] language (version 3.12 or later);
  • the [Thymeleaf] views are replaced by [Jinja2] views, the view engine from [Flask];
  • the [Bean Validation] validation is replaced by the [Pydantic] library (action parameters) and by the [WTForms] library (HTML forms);
  • [Spring Security] is replaced by a few dozen lines of [Python] written for this purpose, which rely on the libraries [PyJWT] (the JWT tokens) and [bcrypt] (password hashing);
  • ORM, [Hibernate], and [Spring Data JPA] are replaced by ORM and [SQLAlchemy], still based on [MySQL].

The document closely follows the structure of the [Spring MVC] course: first, numerous small projects, each focused on a specific concept, followed by a comprehensive case study—a web application for scheduling appointments at a medical practice—with all files fully commented. The examples have the same numbers and cover the same topics as in courses [Spring MVC] and [ASP.NET Core MVC]: a reader familiar with one of these courses can compare the frameworks example by example. However, this is not necessary: this document stands on its own and assumes no prior knowledge of [Spring] or [ASP.NET]. The only prerequisites are a basic understanding of web programming (the HTTP protocol, the HTML language) and the [Python] language (functions, classes, dictionaries, modules). A previous course by the author of this one, Introduction to the Python Language and the Flask Web Framework Through Examples (2020), introduces the [Python] language itself, for those who need to learn it first.

docs.title: 1.1. Flask’s Role in a Web Application
docs.text:
A web application is often built in layers, with each layer communicating only with its neighboring layers:

  • the web layer receives HTTP requests from the browser and returns HTML pages to it. This is the layer that [Flask] helps us write;
  • the business layer contains the application’s business rules (e.g., “a patient can have only one upcoming appointment”). It knows nothing about the web: it could just as easily serve a command-line application;
  • the data access layer (layer [DAO], for [Data Access Object]) reads from and writes to the database. We will use [SQLAlchemy], a ORM ([Object Relational Mapper]) that maps the rows of the tables to the [Python] objects.

The web layer itself follows the [MVC] ([Model – View – Controller]) model:

  • the controller (C) is a set of functions [Python], called actions, each of which processes a type of request (for example, [GET /schedule]). An action reads the request parameters, invokes the business layer, and then selects the view to display;
  • the model (M) is the set of data that the action passes to the view;
  • the view (V) is a [Jinja2] file (extension [.html]): a HTML page that contains [{{ ... }}] expressions and [{% ... %}] instructions ([{% if %}], [{% for %}]...), which the [Jinja2] engine replaces with data from the template.

A note on terminology, to avoid confusion: the [Flask] documentation refers to the function that processes a request as a “view function” and to the [Jinja2] file as a “template.” This document uses the terminology from the [MVC] model, as well as that from the [Spring MVC] and [ASP.NET Core MVC] courses: the function that processes a request is an action, the [Jinja2] file that generates the page is a view, and the term “template” refers to the common view from which other pages inherit (Chapter 4).

The processing of a request follows the numbered steps in the diagram:

  • 1: The browser sends a request, such as HTTP or [GET /schedule?doctorId=1&day=2026-09-26];
  • 2: The web server receives the request and passes it to the [Flask] application. During development, this server is [Werkzeug], the library on which [Flask] is built; in production, it will be a server such as [Waitress] or [Gunicorn]. [Werkzeug] compares the requested path to the application’s routes and selects the action responsible for handling this request: this is routing. Before reaching the action, the request may still pass through functions executed for all requests ([before_request]), which we will explore in subsequent chapters;
  • 3: The action requests the data it needs from the business layer; if necessary, the business layer contacts the [DAO] layer, which queries the database [MySQL] via SQL;
  • 4: The action constructs the view’s model M and instructs the [Jinja2] engine to generate the page (function [render_template]);
  • 5: The page HTML generated by the view is the action’s response, which [Flask] returns to the browser.

[Flask] is one of the two most widely used web frameworks in the [Python] world, along with [Django]. Free and open-source, it works anywhere that [Python] works ([Windows], [Linux], [macOS]). It is a micro-framework: its core is intentionally small (routing, requests and responses, sessions, [Jinja2] views), and everything else (form validation, database access, authentication, etc.) is handled by libraries chosen by the developer. Whereas [Spring Boot] configures a coherent set of components on its own, [Flask] lets the developer assemble their own: the application is more transparent, and you can see everything that’s going on inside it. This is, in fact, what makes it a good tool for learning: almost nothing is hidden. [Flask] can create servers that return JSON to a [JavaScript] client ([Angular], [React], [Flutter]...) as it does traditional web applications, where the server generates the HTML pages and the browser simply displays them. This document examines this second use case. Two concepts—[Python]—recur on every page: decorators ([@app.get("/")], [@app.before_request]...), which associate a function with a role, and the explicit passing of the objects each function needs, whereas [Spring] injects them automatically.

docs.title: 1.2. Tools Used
docs.text:
The examples were written and tested using the following tools (their installation is described in the appendix):

  • [Python] 3.13 (any version 3.12 or later is suitable). The [Python] installer also provides the [pip] tool, which downloads and installs the libraries, and the [venv] module, which creates virtual environments (we’ll discuss what these are later);
  • the [Visual Studio Code] editor, along with the [Python] extension from Microsoft (which also installs the [Pylance] extension, which analyzes the code);
  • a recent browser ([Chrome], [Firefox], [Edge]);
  • the command-line tool [curl], which displays the raw HTTP responses (it is included with [Windows] 10 and 11);
  • the DBMS [MySQL] (or [MariaDB]), for example, the one for [Laragon] under [Windows], starting from the chapter on data access, and for the case study.

Unlike [JDK], which does not contain [Spring], [Python] comes with a very comprehensive standard library; but [Flask] and the other libraries in the document are not included: [pip] downloads them from the [PyPI] repository ([Python Package Index]) during installation (so you must be connected to the Internet on that day). Each project describes its libraries in a [requirements.txt] file. The following table lists them, along with the versions used:

LibraryRoleVersion[Flask]the web framework: routing, requests, responses, sessions, views; It includes [Werkzeug] (requests HTTP, development server), [Jinja2] (views), and [itsdangerous] (signatures)3.1.3[asgiref]asynchronous actions ([async def]), installed by [Flask[async]] (example 03)3.12.1[Pydantic]Binding and validating action parameters (Chapter 3)2.13.5[email-validator]Validation of email addresses, for [Pydantic] and [WTForms]2.3.0[Flask-WTF]the HTML ([WTForms]) forms and anti-CSRF protection (Chapter 4)1.3.0[Babel]Language-specific formatting of dates and amounts (Chapters 3 and 4)2.18.0[PyJWT]Tokens JWT (Chapter 8)2.15.0[bcrypt]Password hashes (Chapter 8)5.0.0[SQLAlchemy]ORM, Database Access (Chapter 9)2.1.1[PyMySQL]The [MySQL] driver, written in [Python] (Chapter 9)1.2.3[Waitress]A production web server (case study)3.0.2

docs.title: 1.3. Run the case study
docs.text:
Reviewer’s note: I advise the reader to run the case study immediately as described below. Once you fully understand the role of this appointment application, ask your favorite IA to modify the application as follows: from now on, each doctor will be able to:

  • set their own appointment slots between two dates. This will allow them to adjust their schedule as needed;
  • remove certain time slots from the calendar for a given day—for example, if they are unavailable for personal reasons;

The modification is not straightforward because it involves a change to the database structure. Ask IA to provide you with the new application code and the SQL script to create the new database. To do this, you’ll need to provide him with the ZIP file containing the complete project as well as the SQL script for the old database.

Also, I haven’t reviewed the course created by Claude. He had already produced the perfect courses [NestJS], [ASP.NET Core MVC], and [Spring MVC]. I assumed the same was true for this one. If you run into a problem understanding something, the solution is always the same: ask your favorite IA to explain what you don’t understand. Claude, for example, is very good at this. You may need to “upload” the example you don’t understand to him.

End of note.

The case study at the end of this document is a complete application. Readers will likely want to see it in action before delving into the details of the framework: here’s how to run it. It’s located in the [rdvmedecins2-flask] folder, next to the [examples] folder:

flask-sept-2026/
├── examples/
└── rdvmedecins2-flask/

You must have installed [Python] (version 3.12 or later), [Visual Studio Code], and [MySQL] (see appendices). Then:

  • Create the [dbrdvmedecins2] database by running the [rdvmedecins2-flask/database/dbrdvmedecins2.sql] script. With [Laragon], open the [HeidiSQL] tool (Database button), then run the script via the File / Run SQL menu. At the command line, from the [rdvmedecins2-flask] folder:
mysql -u root < database/dbrdvmedecins2.sql
  • Open the [rdvmedecins2-flask] folder in [Visual Studio Code] (File menu / Open Folder), then open a terminal (Terminal menu / New Terminal);
  • create the application’s virtual environment and activate it. A virtual environment is a folder (here, [.venv]) that contains a copy of the [Python] interpreter and the libraries for a specific project—and only those libraries: Each project has its own, in the versions that suit it, without interfering with other projects on the computer. In [Windows] (command prompt or terminal of [Visual Studio Code]):
python -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\activate

and under [Linux] and [macOS]:

python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
  • Once the environment is activated, the terminal prompt begins with [(.venv)], and the commands [python] and [pip] are those of the environment. Under [Windows], the [PowerShell] terminal sometimes refuses to run the activation script (message: “Script execution is disabled on this system”): The command [Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope CurrentUser RemoteSigned], entered once and for all, enables it. [Visual Studio Code] detects the environment and offers to use it for the project: you must accept (you can also select it using the Python command: Select Interpreter, Ctrl-Shift-P); terminals opened afterward activate it automatically;
  • Install the application’s libraries in the virtual environment:
pip install -r requirements.txt
  • Verify the connection to the database. The application connects to [MySQL] on [localhost], port 3306, using the user [root] without a password (the default settings for [Laragon]). If your [root] account has a password, enter it in the application’s [config.py] file, on the [DB_PASSWORD = ""] line (for example, [DB_PASSWORD = "myPassword"]). To avoid writing a password to a project file, you can also specify it in the environment variable [FLASK_DB_PASSWORD], which takes precedence over the file: [set FLASK_DB_PASSWORD=myPassword] over [Windows] (command prompt), [$env:FLASK_DB_PASSWORD="myPassword"] takes precedence over [PowerShell], [export FLASK_DB_PASSWORD=myPassword] takes precedence over [Linux], and [macOS];
  • launch the application (under [Linux] and [macOS], [python3] if [python] does not exist):
python app.py
  • The application reads the database, then starts the [Flask] development server. The console displays the SQL commands sent to the database (we’ve included only the main ones here), followed by the server messages:
... INFO sqlalchemy.engine.Engine BEGIN (implicit)
... INFO sqlalchemy.engine.Engine SELECT doctors.title, doctors.last_name, doctors.first_name, ... FROM doctors LEFT OUTER JOIN users AS users_1 ON users_1.id = doctors.user ORDER BY doctors.last_name, doctors.first_name
... INFO sqlalchemy.engine.Engine ROLLBACK
... INFO sqlalchemy.engine.Engine BEGIN (implicit)
... INFO sqlalchemy.engine.Engine SELECT clients.title, clients.last_name, clients.first_name, ... FROM clients LEFT OUTER JOIN users AS users_1 ON users_1.id = clients.user ORDER BY clients.last_name, clients.first_name
... INFO sqlalchemy.engine.Engine ROLLBACK
 * Serving Flask app 'rdvmedecins'
 * Debug mode: on
WARNING: This is a development server. Do not use it in a production deployment. Use a production WSGI server instead.
 * Running on http://127.0.0.1:8081
Press CTRL+C to quit
 * Restarting with stat
 ... (the same SQL commands)
 * Debugger is active!
 * Debugger PIN: 332-612-699

Each line of [SQLAlchemy] begins with the date and time (replaced here by [...]). It shows that the application has read the list of doctors and clients (the two requests SQL), that the server is listening on port 8081 at the address [127.0.0.1] (i.e., [localhost]), and that it is running in debug mode: the application restarts automatically whenever a [Python] file is modified ([Restarting with stat]: the process monitoring the files restarts the application, which re-reads the database), and an unexpected error displays a debug page (the “PIN” hides this page from the console). The warning reminds you that this server is intended for development, not for production (the case study explains how to use a production server);

  • Open the URL [http://localhost:8081] in a browser:

  • Log in with one of the demo accounts, each of which uses the username as the password: [admin] (administrator), [pelissier], [tatou], [dupont] (doctors), [martin], [durand], [bistrou], [german] (patients). You must also enter the characters from the image, in uppercase or lowercase.

Upon startup, the application reads the database: if [MySQL] is inaccessible, it stops immediately, and the console displays the reason at the end of a long error message (before the line “Background on this error”). If the message is [Can't connect to MySQL server on 'localhost' ([Errno 111] Connection refused)] (or [[WinError 10061]] under [Windows]), it means that [MySQL] has not started; with [Access denied for user 'root'@'localhost'], it means the password is incorrect; with [Unknown database 'dbrdvmedecins2'], that the script SQL has not been executed; with [ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'flask'], that the virtual environment is not enabled (or that the libraries have not been installed in it); with [Address already in use] (or [Port 8081 is in use by another program]), that port 8081 is already in use (by version [Spring MVC] of the application, for example). The application’s [README.md] file describes other scenarios. Stop the application using [Ctrl-C] in the terminal.

The case study at the end of the document demonstrates how to use the application and then explains each of its files.

docs.title: 1.4. Examples
docs.text:
The examples are stored in the [examples] folder, with one subfolder per example:

examples/
├── 01-structure/
├── 02-routing/
├── ...
├── 28-layers/
├── common/
│   └── bootstrap/
└── requirements.txt

Each example is a small application ([Flask]) that runs on its own. All examples use the same libraries, described in the file [examples/requirements.txt]:

# the libraries of the examples: pip install -r requirements.txt
# (the versions with which the examples were written and tested)
Flask[async]==3.1.3
Flask-WTF==1.3.0
email-validator==2.3.0
pydantic==2.13.5
Babel==2.18.0
PyJWT==2.15.0
bcrypt==5.0.0
SQLAlchemy==2.1.1
PyMySQL[rsa]==1.2.3
  • line 3: [Flask], and what is needed to write asynchronous actions (the additional [[async]], which adds the [asgiref] library; see example 03);
  • lines 4–7: forms, validation, and language-specific formatting;
  • lines 8–9: authentication (Chapter 8);
  • lines 10–11: database access (Chapter 9). The [[rsa]] update to [PyMySQL] adds the [cryptography] library, which is required to connect to a [MySQL] 8 server using a password-protected account.

Each line is in the form [name==version]: the [==] operator requires exactly this version, the one with which the examples were tested. One could be less strict ([Flask>=3.1]: version 3.1 or later); however, a future version of a library may change its behavior, and a course must be reproducible exactly as written. Lines beginning with [#] are comments.

To run the examples, first create the virtual environment for the examples once and for all in the [examples] folder (see the case study for details):

python -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\activate
pip install -r requirements.txt

([source .venv/bin/activate] under [Linux] and [macOS]). The [common/bootstrap] folder contains the CSS and [Bootstrap] frameworks, shared by the examples that format their pages (starting with Example 15).

Almost all of the examples have the same structure. For example, the one in Example 13:

13-first-view/
├── controllers/
│   ├── __init__.py
│   └── views.py
├── models/
│   ├── __init__.py
│   └── page.py
├── templates/
│   └── views/
│       ├── index.html
│       └── unknown.html
└── app.py
  • [app.py]: the application’s startup file, which is executed; it builds the application and starts the server (see Example 01);
  • [controllers]: the controllers, i.e., the files containing the actions. This is a package [Python]: a folder containing modules ([.py] files), which can be imported ([from controllers.views import views]). The file [__init__.py], which is empty here, turns the folder into a package (it is executed when the package is first imported);
  • [models]: the classes that describe the models (actions and views);
  • [templates]: the views [Jinja2] (from Chapter 4). [Flask] looks for them in this folder, next to the application file;
  • [static] (starting with Example 15): files sent as-is to the browser (style sheets, images, scripts [JavaScript]).

To run an example, open a terminal in its folder (in [Visual Studio Code]: right-click the example folder, then select “Open in the built-in terminal”), and activate the example’s virtual environment if it isn’t already active ([..\.venv\Scripts\activate] under [Windows], [source ../.venv/bin/activate] under [Linux], and [macOS]: the environment is located in the [examples] folder, which is the parent of the example folder), and type:

python app.py

All examples listen on port 5000: only one can be run at a time. Stop the server by entering [Ctrl-C] in the terminal. With [macOS], port 5000 is sometimes already occupied by the system’s “AirPlay Receiver” (message [Address already in use]): You can disable it in System Settings / General / AirDrop and Handoff, or change the port in the [app.py] file from the example ([port=5001]).

When you open the [examples] folder in [Visual Studio Code], the [Python] extension suggests using the [.venv] environment: This allows you to benefit from syntax highlighting, code completion, and error reporting in each file. Each example is launched from its own folder; this is why the imports for an example ([from controllers.views import views]) start from that folder. [Pylance], which analyzes the code from the open folder ([examples]), can then highlight these imports by reporting them as missing: this has no effect on execution. For [Pylance] to find them, simply open the example’s folder itself (File menu / Open Folder). Finally, all examples run in debug mode (see Example 01): a running application restarts automatically, in about one second, as soon as one of its [Python] files is modified and saved.

Examples that use [Bootstrap] find it in the [common/bootstrap] folder, not in their own folder: this ensures that only one copy of the file exists. Each of these examples calls it using URL and [/bootstrap/...], via a few lines in its [app.py] file. For example, [15-layout/app.py]:

# app.py: the application of example 15
from datetime import date
from pathlib import Path

from flask import Blueprint, Flask, request

from controllers.pages import pages

# Bootstrap, shared by the examples: the examples/common/bootstrap folder,
# designated from the location of THIS file (and not from the current folder)
BOOTSTRAP = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent / "common" / "bootstrap"


def create_app():
    app = Flask(__name__)
    app.jinja_env.trim_blocks = True
    app.jinja_env.lstrip_blocks = True
    # a blueprint without routes, which only serves static files: the
    # BOOTSTRAP folder, under the /bootstrap/... URL
    app.register_blueprint(Blueprint("bootstrap", __name__, static_folder=BOOTSTRAP,
                                     static_url_path="/bootstrap"))
    app.register_blueprint(pages)
  • Line 11: the path to the folder [common/bootstrap]. [__file__] is the path to the currently running file ([app.py]); [Path(...).resolve()] makes it an absolute path; [.parent] refers to the folder containing it ([15-layout]), and [.parent.parent] refers to the parent folder ([examples]). The operator [/] of an object [Path] adds an element to the path, using the correct separator ([\] under [Windows], [/] elsewhere). The path therefore does not depend on the current folder: the example finds [Bootstrap] no matter where it is launched from;
  • lines 20–21: A blueprint is a group of routes stored in the application (see Example 02). This blueprint has no routes: it is used solely to publish the [common/bootstrap] folder (parameter [static_folder]) under URL [/bootstrap] (parameter [static_url_path]). A page can thus use the style sheet [/bootstrap/css/bootstrap.min.css].

The other lines in this file will be explained in Example 15.

docs.title: 1.5. Document Content
docs.text:
The document is structured as follows:

ChapterContentsExamplesActions, Routing, ResponsesFrom request to action: routes, blueprints, responses, redirects, shared services01 to 06The Action TemplateRequest parameters: binding, conversion, validation with [Pydantic], forms POST07 to 12The view and its template[Jinja2], template, macros, forms [WTForms], validation, PRG, anti-CSRF protection13 to 21InternationalizationAn application in French and English22Data Scopesapplication, query, session, client23The lifecycle of a requestWSGI middleware, [before_request], [after_request], [teardown_request], converters, error handlers24Authentication and authorizationJWT in a cookie, decorators, roles, CAPTCHA, attempt limits25–27Layered ArchitectureWeb / Business Logic / DAO with [SQLAlchemy] and [MySQL]28Case StudyThe RdvMedecins application, explained file by file-

Each example introduces only a few new concepts, and the chapters build on one another: it is best to read them in order. The case study, meanwhile, draws on all the concepts from the previous chapters: whenever relevant, its commentary refers to the example where the concept was introduced. The appendices describe how to install the tools: [Python], [Visual Studio Code] and its extension [Python], [MySQL] with [Laragon], and [curl].

docs.title: 9. Layered Architecture and Data Access
docs.text:
The previous examples kept their data in memory. A real application stores it in a database and is organized into layers (see the diagram in the introduction):

  • the web layer (controllers, views): read the request, call the business layer, select the view;
  • the business layer: business rules;
  • the DAO layer (*Data Access Object*): database queries.

Each layer is aware only of the layer below it, and as few of its details as possible: the web layer is unaware of SQL, and the business layer is unaware of HTML. This separation makes each layer easier to understand, test, and evolve. Example 28 applies this to managing a list of people: it is, on a smaller scale, the management of doctors and clients from the case study.

In [Python], database access is organized across several layers:

  • The DB-API standard (PEP 249) defines the common interface for database drivers: open a connection, execute a SQL command, and read rows. For [MySQL] (and [MariaDB]), we use [PyMySQL], a driver written entirely in [Python], which installs without a compiler;
  • [SQLAlchemy] is the most widely used data access library in [Python]. It has two levels. Its core (*Core*) manages connections (including a connection pool, which keeps a few connections open and lends them to queries, since opening a connection is costly) and constructs SQL statements from [Python] expressions, regardless of the DBMS. Its ORM (*Object-Relational Mapper*) maps [Python] classes (the entities) to database tables and transforms the read rows into objects.

This is equivalent to [JDBC], [JPA] and [Hibernate] to [Java], or [Entity Framework Core] to [C#]. The [Flask-SQLAlchemy] extension slightly simplifies the configuration of [SQLAlchemy] in a [Flask] application; we use [SQLAlchemy] directly, which demonstrates what is happening and keeps the business layers and DAO independent of [Flask].

The example requires a running [MySQL] (or [MariaDB]) server: the appendix explains how to install one using [Laragon].

docs.title: 9.1.1. The database
docs.text:
The database [dbpersons] is created by the script SQL. Using [Laragon], you can run it, for example, in the [HeidiSQL] tool (File menu / Run a SQL file), or from the command line, from the example folder:

mysql -u root < database/dbpersons.sql

The [database/dbpersons.sql] file:

-- database of example 28: a single table, [persons]
-- the script is written in UTF-8
SET NAMES utf8mb4;
DROP DATABASE IF EXISTS dbpersons;
CREATE DATABASE dbpersons CHARACTER SET utf8mb4 COLLATE utf8mb4_unicode_ci;
USE dbpersons;

CREATE TABLE persons (
  id INT NOT NULL AUTO_INCREMENT,
  -- the version of the row, increased by SQLAlchemy at each modification
  version INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  first_name VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL,
  last_name VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL,
  age INT NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (id),
  -- two persons cannot have the same first and last names
  CONSTRAINT unq_persons_first_name_last_name UNIQUE (first_name, last_name)
) ENGINE = InnoDB;

INSERT INTO persons (first_name, last_name, age) VALUES
  ('Marie', 'Pélissier', 42),
  ('Jacques', 'Bromard', 35),
  ('Philippe', 'Jandot', 58);
  • Line 3: The script is written in [UTF-8]; this is specified to the server so that accents in the data ([Pélissier]) remain intact;
  • line 5: the character set [utf8mb4] accepts all characters (accents, emojis, etc.). The [utf8mb4_unicode_ci] collation compares strings without distinguishing between uppercase and lowercase letters or accents: for [MySQL], [pelissier], and [Pélissier] are equal;
  • line 11: a version number, incremented each time the line is modified (see “optimistic lock,” below);
  • line 17: a named uniqueness constraint: the database does not allow two people with the same first and last names. The name will be used to identify the error.
