docs.text:
# config.py: the configuration of the application (see example 25)

# the secret key: it signs the session (flash messages) and the anti-CSRF tokens
SECRET_KEY = "a-secret-key-for-example-28"

# the error messages of WTForms are translated by WTForms itself (see example 19)
WTF_I18N_ENABLED = False

# the connection to the database: a SQLAlchemy URL.
#   mysql+pymysql: the MySQL DBMS, through the PyMySQL driver
#   root:        : the root user, without a password (those of Laragon);
#                  with a password: root:myPassword@...
#   localhost:3306/dbpersons: the server, its port, the database
#   charset=utf8mb4: the exchanges with the database are done in UTF-8
DATABASE_URL = "mysql+pymysql://root:@localhost:3306/dbpersons?charset=utf8mb4"

# True: the SQL statements sent to the database are displayed in the console
SQL_ECHO = False
  • Line 15: [SQLAlchemy] refers to a base identified by URL. [mysql+pymysql]: the dialect SQL ([MySQL]) and the driver ([PyMySQL]); then the user and their password (here, [root]; without a password, the configuration is [Laragon]), the server, its port, and the database; finally, the settings: [charset=utf8mb4] enables communication between the driver and the server at [UTF-8]. If your server has a password, modify this line, or set the environment variable [FLASK_DATABASE_URL] (example 25);
  • Line 18: At [True], [SQLAlchemy] displays in the console every SQL command sent to the database. This is very informative, and we’ll use it later on.
# app.py: the application of example 28; the assembly of the three layers
from pathlib import Path

from flask import Blueprint, Flask
from flask_wtf.csrf import CSRFProtect
from sqlalchemy import create_engine
from sqlalchemy.orm import sessionmaker

from controllers.persons import persons
from dao.persons_dao import PersonsDao
from business.persons_business import PersonsBusiness

BOOTSTRAP = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent / "common" / "bootstrap"


def create_app():
    app = Flask(__name__)
    app.jinja_env.trim_blocks = True
    app.jinja_env.lstrip_blocks = True
    app.config.from_pyfile("config.py")
    app.config.from_prefixed_env()

    # the access to the database: the SQLAlchemy "engine" manages a POOL of connections
    # (connections opened once, then reused from one request to the next).
    # pool_pre_ping: a connection is tested before being reused
    engine = create_engine(app.config["DATABASE_URL"], echo=app.config["SQL_ECHO"],
                           pool_pre_ping=True)
    # the session factory; expire_on_commit=False: the objects read remain
    # usable after the end of the transaction (by the view, in particular)
    sessions = sessionmaker(engine, expire_on_commit=False)

    # the assembly of the layers: DAO -> business; the web layer only knows the business layer
    app.extensions["business"] = PersonsBusiness(sessions, PersonsDao())

    app.register_blueprint(Blueprint("bootstrap", __name__, static_folder=BOOTSTRAP,
                                     static_url_path="/bootstrap"))
    app.register_blueprint(persons)
    CSRFProtect(app)
    return app


if __name__ == "__main__":
    create_app().run(port=5000, debug=True)
  • Lines 26–27: The *engine* of [SQLAlchemy] is the object that manages connections to a database and the connection pool. It is created once, at startup; the first connection is opened only upon the first request. [pool_pre_ping=True] checks a connection from the pool before reusing it: a [MySQL] server closes connections that have been inactive for too long, and the application would otherwise receive an error;
  • Line 30: A session of type ORM is the object used to read from and write to entities; it borrows a connection from the pool and tracks the entities it has read to detect changes to them. [sessionmaker] creates a session factory, each call to which will produce a session. By default, at the end of a transaction, the session “expires” the entities (it forgets their values, to read them again the next time they are used). [expire_on_commit=False] prevents this: the entities returned by the business layer remain usable after the transaction, by the view that displays them;
  • line 33: assembling the layers: the business layer receives the session factory and the DAO layer. The web layer will only be aware of the business layer;
  • line 38: Anti-CSRF protection for the entire application (Example 21).

docs.title: 9.1.3. The Person Entity
docs.text:
# entities/person.py: a row of the [persons] table
from sqlalchemy import String
from sqlalchemy.orm import DeclarativeBase, Mapped, mapped_column


# the parent class of all the entities: SQLAlchemy records in it the
# class <-> table mapping of each of its child classes
class Base(DeclarativeBase):
    pass


class Person(Base):
    # the name of the table
    __tablename__ = "persons"

    # the primary key, generated by the database (AUTO_INCREMENT); SQLAlchemy reads
    # its value back after each INSERT. Mapped[int]: the Python type of the column
    id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)
    # the optimistic lock: see __mapper_args__ below
    version: Mapped[int] = mapped_column()
    first_name: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(String(30))
    last_name: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(String(30))
    age: Mapped[int]

    # version_id_col: SQLAlchemy increases the version at each UPDATE, and adds
    # the condition "AND version = <value read>"
    __mapper_args__ = {"version_id_col": version}

    def __init__(self, first_name: str, last_name: str, age: int):
        self.first_name = first_name
        self.last_name = last_name
        self.age = age
  • lines 8–9: All entities in an application inherit from the same base class, derived from [DeclarativeBase]. [SQLAlchemy] stores the description of each entity (its table, its columns) in this class: this is the declarative model;
  • line 14: the table associated with the class;
  • line 18: a column is declared by an attribute annotated with [Mapped[type]]: the column’s type, [Python]. [mapped_column] specifies its characteristics: in this case, the primary key. By default, an integer primary key is generated by the database ([AUTO_INCREMENT]): [SQLAlchemy] re-reads its value after each [INSERT];
  • Lines 21–23: [String(30)] specifies the column length (useful if [SQLAlchemy] were to create the table itself). A column with no special characteristics can simply use the annotation ([age]). The type [Mapped[str]] makes the column required ([NOT NULL]); [Mapped[str | None]] would make it optional;
  • line 27: [version_id_col] designates the version column: [SQLAlchemy] increments it with each [UPDATE], and adds the condition [AND version = <value read>] to it. If another query has modified the row in the meantime, its version has changed; [UPDATE] does not modify any rows, and [SQLAlchemy] throws a [StaleDataError] exception. This is an optimistic lock: nothing is blocked, but concurrent modifications are detected;
  • Lines 29–32: a constructor to create a person in a single line.

docs.title: 9.1.4. The DAO layer
docs.text:
# dao/persons_dao.py: the DAO layer, queries, no business rule.
# Each method receives the SQLAlchemy SESSION, opened by the business
# layer: all the queries of a same operation thus share the same
# connection, and the same transaction
from sqlalchemy import delete, select
from sqlalchemy.orm import Session

from entities.person import Person


class PersonsDao:

    # SELECT ... FROM persons ORDER BY last_name, first_name
    def list(self, session: Session) -> list[Person]:
        return list(session.scalars(select(Person).order_by(Person.last_name, Person.first_name)))

    # SELECT ... WHERE id = ?; None if the person does not exist
    def read(self, session: Session, id: int) -> Person | None:
        return session.get(Person, id)

    # a person with the same first and last names, other than [except_id]:
    # SELECT ... WHERE first_name = ? AND last_name = ? AND id <> ? LIMIT 1
    def namesake(self, session: Session, first_name: str, last_name: str, except_id: int = 0) -> Person | None:
        query = select(Person).where(Person.first_name == first_name, Person.last_name == last_name,
                                     Person.id != except_id).limit(1)
        return session.scalars(query).first()

    # INSERT (new person): the person is added to the session, and
    # flush sends the SQL statement RIGHT AWAY (and not at COMMIT)
    def add(self, session: Session, person: Person) -> Person:
        session.add(person)
        session.flush()
        return person

    # DELETE FROM persons WHERE id = ?
    def delete(self, session: Session, id: int):
        session.execute(delete(Person).where(Person.id == id))

The DAO layer contains only queries, with no business rules. Each method receives the session opened by the business layer: all queries for a single business operation thus share the same connection and the same transaction.

  • Line 15: [select(Person)] constructs a query ([SELECT]) on the "persons" table; [order_by] sorts it. The columns are written as attributes of the class ([Person.last_name]): the editor can verify their names, and no SQL is written by hand. [session.scalars(...)] executes the query and returns the entities constructed from the read rows;
  • line 19: reading by primary key, or [None];
  • lines 23–26: [where] adds conditions, written using the operators from [Python] ([==], [!=]): [SQLAlchemy] translates them into SQL, with parameters (the values are never copied into the text of the SQL command, which makes SQL injection impossible). [first()] returns the first entity, or [None];
  • lines 30–33: [session.add] assigns a new entity to the session; [flush] immediately sends [INSERT] to the database (without [flush], it would go to [COMMIT]). The database then generates the ID, which [SQLAlchemy] stores in the entity;
  • line 37: a [DELETE], constructed in the same way.

docs.title: 9.1.5. The business layer
docs.text:
# business/data.py: the data of a person, as the web layer passes them on
from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class PersonData:
    first_name: str
    last_name: str
    age: int

A person’s data, as transmitted by the web layer to the business layer: a simple object, unrelated to [Flask], [WTForms], or [SQLAlchemy].

# business/exception.py: a business rule refuses the operation; the message
# is intended for the user
class BusinessException(Exception):
    pass

An exception class specific to the business layer: a business rule rejects the operation, and the exception message is intended for the user.

# business/persons_business.py: the BUSINESS layer, the business rules, and only them.
# Each method opens its TRANSACTION: committed (COMMIT) at the end of the with
# block, cancelled (ROLLBACK) if an exception comes out of it
from sqlalchemy.exc import IntegrityError
from sqlalchemy.orm import sessionmaker
from sqlalchemy.orm.exc import StaleDataError

from dao.persons_dao import PersonsDao
from entities.person import Person
from business.data import PersonData
from business.exception import BusinessException

NAMESAKE = "A person already has these first and last names."
MODIFIED = "This record has been modified meanwhile: reload it."
UNKNOWN = "This person does not exist (anymore)."


class PersonsBusiness:

    # sessions: the SQLAlchemy session "factory" (see app.py)
    def __init__(self, sessions: sessionmaker, dao: PersonsDao):
        self._sessions = sessions
        self._dao = dao

    def list(self) -> list[Person]:
        # sessions.begin(): a session AND its transaction; the with block closes them
        with self._sessions.begin() as session:
            return self._dao.list(session)

    def read(self, id: int) -> Person:
        with self._sessions.begin() as session:
            return self._read(session, id)

    def add(self, data: PersonData) -> Person:
        try:
            with self._sessions.begin() as session:
                # rule 1: no two persons with the same first and last names
                if self._dao.namesake(session, data.first_name, data.last_name):
                    raise BusinessException(NAMESAKE)
                return self._dao.add(session, Person(data.first_name, data.last_name, data.age))
        except IntegrityError as e:
            raise self._translate(e)

    def edit(self, id: int, version: int | None, data: PersonData) -> Person:
        try:
            with self._sessions.begin() as session:
                person = self._read(session, id)
                # rule 2: we do not modify a record modified meanwhile by someone else
                if person.version != version:
                    raise BusinessException(MODIFIED)
                if self._dao.namesake(session, data.first_name, data.last_name, id):
                    raise BusinessException(NAMESAKE)
                # the entity read is "tracked" by the session: it is enough to
                # modify it; flush sends the UPDATE right away
                person.first_name = data.first_name
                person.last_name = data.last_name
                person.age = data.age
                session.flush()
                return person
        except StaleDataError:
            # the UPDATE "WHERE id = ... AND version = ..." modified no row
            raise BusinessException(MODIFIED)
        except IntegrityError as e:
            raise self._translate(e)

    def delete(self, id: int) -> Person:
        with self._sessions.begin() as session:
            person = self._read(session, id)
            self._dao.delete(session, id)
            return person

    def _read(self, session, id: int) -> Person:
        person = self._dao.read(session, id)
        if person is None:
            raise BusinessException(UNKNOWN)
        return person

    # two simultaneous additions: the uniqueness constraint of the database rejected the
    # second one; e.orig: the original error, that of the PyMySQL driver
    @staticmethod
    def _translate(e: IntegrityError) -> Exception:
        if "unq_persons_first_name_last_name" in str(e.orig):
            return BusinessException(NAMESAKE)
        return e
  • Line 27: Each method opens its own session and transaction: [sessions.begin()] returns a session with a transaction that has been started. At the end of the [with] block, the transaction is committed ([COMMIT]) and the session is closed; if an exception occurs within the block, the transaction is rolled back ([ROLLBACK]): none of the changes made within the block are retained. The business layer thus determines the scope of transactions: one business operation equals one transaction;
  • lines 34–42: Rule No. 1: No two people may have the same first and last names. The business layer checks this rule before writing to the database and raises a [BusinessException] if it is not met. But this check is not sufficient: two simultaneous requests could both verify that there are no namesakes, and then both proceed to insert the data. The database’s uniqueness constraint then rejects the second [INSERT], and [SQLAlchemy] triggers a [IntegrityError], which the [_translate] method transforms into the same [BusinessException]. The database is the last line of defense;
  • lines 44–64: Rule No. 2: Do not modify a record that has been modified in the meantime by someone else. The update form carries the version of the record that was read (in a hidden field); if it differs from the current version, the record has changed since it was displayed. Here again, the database (via the optimistic lock) detects cases where a concurrent modification occurs between the read and the [UPDATE]: this is the [StaleDataError] exception. Note that the modification is performed simply by changing the attributes of the read entity: the session tracks this, and [flush] sends a [UPDATE] containing only the modified columns;
  • lines 66–70: Deleting a person results in the confirmation message;
  • lines 72–76: A nonexistent person is a business error;
  • lines 80–84: A static method does not accept either an object or a class; it is simply a function defined within the class. [e.orig] is the original exception, that of the driver [PyMySQL], whose message contains the name of the violated constraint. Another integrity error is reported as-is: this is not a business error, but a programming error.

docs.title: 9.1.6. The Web Layer
docs.text:
# models/person_form.py: the fields of the form and their constraints (see example 19)
from flask_wtf import FlaskForm
from wtforms import HiddenField, IntegerField, StringField
from wtforms.validators import DataRequired, InputRequired, Length, NumberRange, Optional


def clean(value):
    return value.strip() if isinstance(value, str) else value


# a version: an integer, or None if the field is empty (add form)
def integer_or_none(value):
    return int(value) if value not in (None, "") else None


class PersonForm(FlaskForm):

    class Meta:
        locales = ["en"]

    first_name = StringField("First name", filters=[clean], validators=[
        DataRequired("The first name is required."), Length(max=30, message="30 characters at most.")])
    last_name = StringField("Last name", filters=[clean], validators=[
        DataRequired("The last name is required."), Length(max=30, message="30 characters at most.")])
    age = IntegerField("Age", validators=[
        InputRequired("The age is required."),
        NumberRange(min=0, max=150, message="The age must be between 0 and 150.")])
    # the version of the record, carried by a hidden field (edit only)
    version = HiddenField(filters=[integer_or_none])

The form [WTForms] (Example 19). The hidden field [version] has a filter that converts it to an integer, or to [None] if it is empty (add form).

# controllers/persons.py: the WEB layer; it only knows the business layer
from flask import Blueprint, current_app, flash, redirect, render_template, url_for

from business.data import PersonData
from business.exception import BusinessException
from business.persons_business import PersonsBusiness
from models.person_form import PersonForm

persons = Blueprint("persons", __name__)


def business() -> PersonsBusiness:
    return current_app.extensions["business"]


@persons.get("/")
def home():
    return redirect(url_for("persons.list_persons"))


@persons.get("/persons")
def list_persons():
    return render_template("persons/list.html", persons=business().list())


@persons.get("/persons/add")
def add_form():
    return form_page("Add a person", url_for("persons.add"), PersonForm())


@persons.post("/persons/add")
def add():
    form = PersonForm()
    if not form.validate():
        return form_page("Add a person", url_for("persons.add"), form)
    try:
        p = business().add(PersonData(form.first_name.data, form.last_name.data, form.age.data))
    except BusinessException as e:
        # a business rule refuses: we display the form again, the message at the bottom of the page
        return form_page("Add a person", url_for("persons.add"), form, str(e))
    flash(f"{p.first_name} {p.last_name} has been added.", "success")
    return redirect(url_for("persons.list_persons"))


@persons.get("/persons/<int:id>/edit")
def edit_form(id):
    try:
        p = business().read(id)
    except BusinessException as e:
        flash(str(e), "error")
        return redirect(url_for("persons.list_persons"))
    # obj=p: the fields of the form are filled with the attributes of p of the same name
    return form_page("Edit a person", url_for("persons.edit", id=id),
                     PersonForm(obj=p))


@persons.post("/persons/<int:id>/edit")
def edit(id):
    action = url_for("persons.edit", id=id)
    form = PersonForm()
    if not form.validate():
        return form_page("Edit a person", action, form)
    try:
        data = PersonData(form.first_name.data, form.last_name.data, form.age.data)
        p = business().edit(id, form.version.data, data)
    except BusinessException as e:
        return form_page("Edit a person", action, form, str(e))
    flash(f"{p.first_name} {p.last_name} has been edited.", "success")
    return redirect(url_for("persons.list_persons"))


@persons.post("/persons/<int:id>/delete")
def delete(id):
    try:
        p = business().delete(id)
        flash(f"{p.first_name} {p.last_name} has been deleted.", "success")
    except BusinessException as e:
        # no form to display again: the error also travels as a flash message
        flash(str(e), "error")
    return redirect(url_for("persons.list_persons"))


# the page of the form: title, submission address, form, global error
def form_page(title: str, action: str, form: PersonForm, error: str | None = None):
    return render_template("persons/form.html", title=title, action=action,
                           form=form, error=error)
  • lines 12–13: the business layer, the only layer known to the controller;
  • lines 32–42: the add operation, in three steps: form validation (input errors), calling the business layer (business rules), then the PRG schema. A [BusinessException] re-displays the form, along with its footer message. [flash] receives a category as its second parameter (["success"]), which the template uses to select the message’s presentation;
  • lines 46–54: the edit form, pre-filled: the parameter [obj] fills the form fields with the object’s attributes of the same name, including the version. A nonexistent person redirects to the list, with a flashing error message;
  • lines 58–69: the edit, following the same pattern as the add operation;
  • lines 73–80: deletion. There is no form to redisplay: any error is also displayed in a pop-up message, of category ["error"].

The web layer contains neither SQL nor any business rules: it translates the request into a call to the business layer and the result into a page.

<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <title>Persons</title>
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="{{ url_for('bootstrap.static', filename='css/bootstrap.min.css') }}">
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="{{ url_for('static', filename='css/styles.css') }}">
</head>
<body>
  <div class="container py-3" style="max-width: 40rem">
    {# the success messages (flash messages of the "success" category): at the top #}
    {% for message in get_flashed_messages(category_filter=["success"]) %}
    <div class="alert alert-success" role="status">{{ message }}</div>
    {% endfor %}
    <main>
      {% block content %}{% endblock %}
    </main>
    {# the error: of the current request, or from before the redirect (flash message) #}
    {% for message in get_flashed_messages(category_filter=["error"]) + ([error] if error else []) %}
    <div class="error-area" role="alert">{{ message }}</div>
    {% endfor %}
  </div>
  {% include "fragments/confirmation.html" %}
  <script src="{{ url_for('static', filename='js/app.js') }}"></script>
</body>
</html>
  • lines 12–14: [category_filter] renders only the flash messages of the specified categories: success messages, at the top of the page;
  • lines 19–21: errors, at the bottom of the page: those occurring before a redirect (flash messages), followed by the error from the current request (variable [error]). The operator [+] concatenates two lists.

docs.title: 9.1.8. The commands SQL
docs.text:
Let’s restart the application with the environment variable [FLASK_SQL_ECHO=true] (under [Windows]: [$env:FLASK_SQL_ECHO="true"]), and monitor the SQL commands for a modification in the console. The display of the change form for person No. 1:

INFO sqlalchemy.engine.Engine BEGIN (implicit)
INFO sqlalchemy.engine.Engine SELECT persons.id, persons.version, persons.first_name, persons.last_name, persons.age
FROM persons
WHERE persons.id = %(pk_1)s
INFO sqlalchemy.engine.Engine [generated in 0.00017s] {'pk_1': 1}
INFO sqlalchemy.engine.Engine COMMIT

A transaction, [SELECT], per primary key, whose value is passed as a parameter ([%(pk_1)s]; see the parameter syntax for [PyMySQL]). Saving the master record with a new age:

INFO sqlalchemy.engine.Engine BEGIN (implicit)
INFO sqlalchemy.engine.Engine SELECT persons.id, persons.version, persons.first_name, persons.last_name, persons.age
FROM persons
WHERE persons.id = %(pk_1)s
INFO sqlalchemy.engine.Engine [cached since 0.05972s ago] {'pk_1': 1}
INFO sqlalchemy.engine.Engine SELECT persons.id, persons.version, persons.first_name, persons.last_name, persons.age
FROM persons
WHERE persons.first_name = %(first_name_1)s AND persons.last_name = %(last_name_1)s AND persons.id != %(id_1)s
 LIMIT %(param_1)s
INFO sqlalchemy.engine.Engine [generated in 0.00016s] {'first_name_1': 'Marie', 'last_name_1': 'Pélissier', 'id_1': 1, 'param_1': 1}
INFO sqlalchemy.engine.Engine UPDATE persons SET version=%(version)s, age=%(age)s WHERE persons.id = %(persons_id)s AND persons.version = %(persons_version)s
INFO sqlalchemy.engine.Engine [generated in 0.00015s] {'version': 1, 'age': 43, 'persons_id': 1, 'persons_version': 0}
INFO sqlalchemy.engine.Engine COMMIT

In a single transaction, we can see the following: reading the record, searching for a namesake, and then the [UPDATE]. This transaction modifies only the changed column ([age]), increments the version (from 0 to 1), and sets the optimistic lock condition ([AND persons.version = 0]). The entry [cached since] indicates that [SQLAlchemy] reused the translation in SQL from a previously constructed request. Now let’s submit the same form a second time, still with version 0:

INFO sqlalchemy.engine.Engine BEGIN (implicit)
INFO sqlalchemy.engine.Engine SELECT persons.id, persons.version, persons.first_name, persons.last_name, persons.age
FROM persons
WHERE persons.id = %(pk_1)s
INFO sqlalchemy.engine.Engine [cached since 0.09593s ago] {'pk_1': 1}
INFO sqlalchemy.engine.Engine ROLLBACK

The version being read (1) is not the same as the form’s version (0): the business layer raised a [BusinessException], which rolled back the transaction ([ROLLBACK]), and the page displays “This record has been modified meanwhile: reload it.” Similarly, the process of adding a namesake stops after the namesake search, without a [INSERT].

docs.title: 3. The Action Template
docs.text:
An action requires information sent by the browser: the parameters of the URL ([?name=martin&age=42]), form fields, the request body JSON, and sometimes a request header HTTP. The original course refers to all of this information as the action model. This chapter shows how an action retrieves this information, converts it to the correct type, and validates it. This process is called data binding.

[Flask] is much more minimalist here than other frameworks: it provides access to the request information in the form of character strings and stops there. Converting ["42"] to the integer 42, verifying that a name has at least two characters, and assembling the fields into an object—all of this is the responsibility of the application. We’ll first do this by hand (Example 07), then using the [Pydantic] library (Examples 08–12), which describes a model using a class in which each field specifies its type and constraints. In the next chapter, the HTML forms will be handled by another library, [WTForms], designed specifically for them; [Pydantic] remains the natural tool for the parameters of a URL and for the JSON bodies of the API.

Note on terminology: In the following chapter, the word “model” will primarily refer to the data that an action transmits to its view. The model of an action, as used in this chapter, is what it receives.

Examples 07 through 12 are run in the same way as those in the previous chapter: open a terminal to the example directory, with the virtual environment activated ([python app.py]); [Ctrl-C] stops the server. Their [app.py] files are all similar: a factory [create_app] that creates the application, configures the provider JSON (accents preserved, keys in their original order; see Example 03), and saves a blueprint. We’ll only comment on them when they introduce something new.

docs.title: 3.1. Example 07: The parameters of URL
docs.text:
The parameters for URL are the portion that follows [?]: [?name=martin&age=42]. This portion is called the query string (*query string*). Each parameter is a pair of [name=value]; the pairs are separated by [&]. The [controllers/parameters.py] file:

# controllers/parameters.py: the parameters of the URL (the "query string")
from flask import Blueprint, abort, request

parameters = Blueprint("parameters", __name__, url_prefix="/parameters")


# /parameters/action01?name=martin: request.args contains the parameters of
# the URL; get returns the value of the parameter, or None if it is missing
@parameters.get("/action01")
def action01():
    name = request.args.get("name")
    return f"name = [{name}], of type {type(name).__name__}"


# /parameters/action02?age=42: type=int CONVERTS the value (a string) into
# an integer; a missing parameter, or one that is not an integer, gives None
@parameters.get("/action02")
def action02():
    age = request.args.get("age", type=int)
    return f"age = [{age}], of type {type(age).__name__}"


# /parameters/action03?age=42: a REQUIRED parameter; its absence, or a
# value that is not an integer, stops the action with a 400 response (Bad Request)
@parameters.get("/action03")
def action03():
    text = request.args.get("age")
    if text is None:
        # abort raises an exception, which Flask turns into an error response
        abort(400, "the [age] parameter is required")
    # the conversion is up to us
    try:
        age = int(text)
    except ValueError:
        abort(400, f"[{text}] is not an integer")
    return f"age = [{age}], of type {type(age).__name__}"


# /parameters/action04?page=2: a default value if the parameter is missing
@parameters.get("/action04")
def action04():
    page = request.args.get("page", default=1, type=int)
    return f"page = [{page}]"


# /parameters/action05?q=flask: the name of the URL parameter is not necessarily
# that of the Python variable
@parameters.get("/action05")
def action05():
    search = request.args.get("q")
    return f"search = [{search}]"


# /parameters/action06?name=martin&age=42: all the parameters at once, as a dictionary
@parameters.get("/action06")
def action06():
    return request.args.to_dict()
  • line 11: [request.args] contains the parameters of URL, which have already been decoded by [Werkzeug]. This is a special dictionary, a [MultiDict], which, as we’ll see in Example 10, accepts multiple values per key. Its method [get] returns the value of a parameter, or [None] if it is absent. Unlike [request.args["name"]], which would throw an exception for a missing parameter, [get] never causes an error;
  • line 12: the action displays the value and its type: [type(x)] is the class of [x], and [__name__] is the name of that class. A value retrieved from URL is always a string ([str]);
  • line 19: the parameter [type] of [get] specifies a conversion function applied to the string: in this case, [int], the class of integers, whose call to [int("42")] returns 42. If the conversion fails ([int("abc")] raises a [ValueError]), [get] returns [None], just as it would for a missing parameter: the action cannot distinguish between the two cases, and the input error goes unnoticed;
  • Lines 26–35: a required parameter and a manual conversion that distinguishes between the two possible errors. [abort(400, message)] terminates the action with a 400 response (*Bad Request*—the request is invalid), accompanied by the message (see Example 03). The statement [try] / [except ValueError] catches the exception thrown by [int];
  • line 42: a default value, used if the parameter is missing (or if its conversion fails). This is a typical case for a page number in a list;
  • line 50: there is no requirement to name the variable [Python] the same as the parameter of URL. Search engines often use a short parameter, [q] (*query*);
  • line 57: [to_dict()] converts [MultiDict] into a standard [Python] dictionary (by retaining only the first value of each parameter), which the action returns as: [Flask] transforms it into JSON (see Example 03).

Let’s test each action with [curl]. A parameter is present, then absent:

curl -i "http://localhost:5000/parameters/action01?name=martin"
curl http://localhost:5000/parameters/action01

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 28

name = [martin], of type str
name = [None], of type NoneType

The quotation marks around URL are necessary in a terminal: without them, the shell would interpret [&] (which runs a command in the background under [Linux]) and [?]. A value containing spaces or special characters must be encoded in the URL: a space becomes [%20], and [&] becomes [%26] (otherwise, it would separate two parameters). The browser handles this automatically; with [curl], you have to write it out. [Werkzeug] decodes the value before storing it in [request.args]:

curl "http://localhost:5000/parameters/action01?name=jean%20dupont%20%26%20sons"

name = [jean dupont & sons], of type str

The conversion using [type=int], which was successful at first but then failed:

curl "http://localhost:5000/parameters/action02?age=42"
curl "http://localhost:5000/parameters/action02?age=abc"

age = [42], of type int
age = [None], of type NoneType

The required parameter for action 03, missing and then invalid:

curl -i http://localhost:5000/parameters/action03
curl "http://localhost:5000/parameters/action03?age=abc"

HTTP/1.1 400 BAD REQUEST
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 122

<!doctype html>
<html lang=en>
<title>400 Bad Request</title>
<h1>Bad Request</h1>
<p>the [age] parameter is required</p>
<!doctype html>
<html lang=en>
<title>400 Bad Request</title>
<h1>Bad Request</h1>
<p>[abc] is not an integer</p>

The default value and the renamed parameter:

curl http://localhost:5000/parameters/action04
curl "http://localhost:5000/parameters/action04?page=3"
curl "http://localhost:5000/parameters/action05?q=flask"

page = [1]
page = [3]
search = [flask]

Finally, all parameters at once. The parameter [name] appears twice: [to_dict()] retains only the first value.

curl "http://localhost:5000/parameters/action06?name=martin&age=42&name=durand"

{
  "name": "martin",
  "age": "42"
}

The age remained a string (["42"], enclosed in quotes in JSON): no conversion was requested. In a browser (here [Chromium]), JSON appears on a single line: [Flask] only indents JSON in debug mode, and the screenshot was taken without it; the “Pretty-print” checkbox would display it indented. Incidentally, the address bar shows the encoding of accented characters in URL ([é] becomes [%C3%A9], with its two bytes in [UTF-8]):

This first example illustrates the limitations of the manual approach: for each parameter, you must write the reading, conversion, and handling of missing values and errors. With ten parameters, the action’s code would be overwhelmed by these checks. It is better to describe what is expected and let a library handle the verification. That is the purpose of the following example.

docs.title: 3.2. Example 08: An action model described by a class
docs.text: [Pydantic] is the most widely used data validation library in [Python] (it is at the core of the [FastAPI] framework). It describes the data expected by a class: each attribute has a type and, optionally, constraints. [Pydantic] is responsible for converting the received data into these types and for validating the constraints. It is installed in the example’s virtual environment (file [requirements.txt]).

docs.title: 3.2.1. The model: models/person.py
docs.text:
# models/person.py: the model of the action, a Pydantic class in which each
# field carries its type and its constraints
from typing import Annotated, Literal

from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict, EmailStr, Field


class PersonModel(BaseModel):
    # the received strings are stripped of the spaces that surround them
    model_config = ConfigDict(str_strip_whitespace=True)

    # required (no default value), from 2 to 20 characters
    name: Annotated[str, Field(min_length=2, max_length=20)]
    # an integer ("42" is converted to 42), between 0 and 150
    age: Annotated[int, Field(ge=0, le=150)]
    # one of these three values only
    title: Literal["Mr", "Mme", "Melle"]
    # optional (None by default); if present, a valid email address
    email: EmailStr | None = None
  • Line 8: A [Pydantic] model is a class that inherits from [BaseModel]. Its attributes are declared at the class level, along with their types, as in a [dataclass] (Example 06);
  • Line 10: The model’s configuration. [str_strip_whitespace=True] removes the spaces surrounding the received strings: a name entered as [" martin "] becomes ["martin"] before being validated. The attribute [model_config] is not a field in the template: [Pydantic] recognizes this reserved name;
  • Line 13: the field [name]. [Annotated[str, Field(...)]] reads “the type [str], annotated by [Field(...)].” [Annotated], from the standard module [typing], allows additional information to be attached to a type—information that [Python] ignores but that the libraries read: here, the constraints of [Pydantic], a length of 2 to 20 characters ([min_length], [max_length]). The field has no default value: it is required;
  • line 15: the type [int]: [Pydantic] converts the string ["42"] to the integer 42, and rejects ["abc"]. The constraints [ge] (*greater or equal*) and [le] (*less or equal*) limit the value. There are also [gt] and [lt] for strict inequalities;
  • line 17: [Literal["Mr", "Mme", "Melle"]] is the type of the three values listed, and only those;
  • line 19: [EmailStr] is the type of an email address; [Pydantic] validates its syntax using the [email-validator] library (which is also installed by [requirements.txt]). [EmailStr | None]: an address, or [None]. The default value [= None] makes the field optional.

This template describes the expected data; it contains no validation instructions. This is known as a declarative style.

docs.title: 3.2.2. The action: controllers/persons.py
docs.text:
# controllers/persons.py: an action whose model is a Pydantic class
from flask import Blueprint, request

from models.person import PersonModel

persons = Blueprint("persons", __name__, url_prefix="/persons")


# /persons/action01?name=martin&age=42&title=Mr
# model_validate: Pydantic creates the object from the dictionary of parameters
# (BINDING: conversion of the strings into the type of each field), then checks
# the constraints (VALIDATION). An invalid model raises a ValidationError,
# turned into a 400 response by app.py: the action stops there
@persons.get("/action01")
def action01():
    person = PersonModel.model_validate(request.args.to_dict())
    return {
        # model_dump: the object as a dictionary (serializable to JSON)
        "person": person.model_dump(),
        "ageType": type(person.age).__name__,
    }
  • Line 16: The [model_validate] class method creates a [PersonModel] object from a dictionary—in this case, the one containing the parameters of URL. It performs two actions, in this order: - binding: each value in the dictionary is assigned to the field of the same name, after being converted to the field’s type (["42"] → 42); - validation: the constraints for each field are checked (length, bounds, allowed values, etc.).
  • If either step fails, [model_validate] throws a [ValidationError] exception, which contains a list of all errors (not just the first one). The action does not handle it: it stops; we’ll see who takes care of it;
  • line 19: [model_dump()] returns the object as a dictionary, which [Flask] can convert to JSON;
  • line 20: the age type, to show that the conversion took place.

docs.title: 3.2.3. Error handling: app.py
docs.text:
# app.py: the application of example 08
from flask import Flask
from pydantic import ValidationError

from controllers.persons import persons


def create_app():
    app = Flask(__name__)
    # JSON: accents kept, keys in their original order (see example 03)
    app.json.ensure_ascii = False
    app.json.sort_keys = False
    app.register_blueprint(persons)

    # an invalid model: Pydantic's ValidationError exception becomes,
    # for the WHOLE application, a 400 response that details the errors
    @app.errorhandler(ValidationError)
    def invalid_model(e: ValidationError):
        errors = [{"field": ".".join(str(x) for x in err["loc"]), "message": err["msg"]}
                  for err in e.errors()]
        return {"status": 400, "errors": errors}, 400

    return app


if __name__ == "__main__":
    create_app().run(port=5000, debug=True)
  • Lines 17–21: The decorator [@app.errorhandler(ValidationError)] registers an exception handler: when an action throws a [ValidationError] (or an exception of a derived class), [Flask] calls this function, passing the exception as a parameter, and returns its return value as the response. Declared at the application level, the handler applies to all of its actions: every action that validates a model benefits from it, without having to write a single line of error-handling code;
  • Line 19: [e.errors()] returns the list of errors. Each error is a dictionary; We retain two pieces of information: [loc] (*location*), the affected field, in the form of a tuple ([("name",)]; see Example 10 for a longer tuple), and [msg], the message. The expression [[... for err in e.errors()]] is a list comprehension: it constructs a list by applying the expression on the left to each element;
  • line 21: a tuple [(body, code)] (see Example 03): a dictionary, converted to JSON, and the code 400.

docs.title: 3.2.4. Execution
docs.text:
A valid template:

curl -i "http://localhost:5000/persons/action01?name=martin&age=42&title=Mr"

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json
Content-Length: 116

{
  "person": {
    "name": "martin",
    "age": 42,
    "title": "Mr",
    "email": null
  },
  "ageType": "int"
