The age has indeed become an integer (without quotation marks in JSON), and the missing address is [None] ([null] in JSON). A name surrounded by spaces ([%20]) and a present address:

curl "http://localhost:5000/persons/action01?name=%20%20martin%20&age=42&title=Mme&email=martin@example.com"

{
  "person": {
    "name": "martin",
    "age": 42,
    "title": "Mme",
    "email": "martin@example.com"
  },
  "ageType": "int"
}

No parameters: the three required fields are missing.

curl -i http://localhost:5000/persons/action01

HTTP/1.1 400 BAD REQUEST
Content-Type: application/json
Content-Length: 248

{
  "status": 400,
  "errors": [
    {
      "field": "name",
      "message": "Field required"
    },
    {
      "field": "age",
      "message": "Field required"
    },
    {
      "field": "title",
      "message": "Field required"
    }
  ]
}

Four invalid fields at once:

curl "http://localhost:5000/persons/action01?name=m&age=abc&title=Mlle&email=xx"

{
  "status": 400,
  "errors": [
    {
      "field": "name",
      "message": "String should have at least 2 characters"
    },
    {
      "field": "age",
      "message": "Input should be a valid integer, unable to parse string as an integer"
    },
    {
      "field": "title",
      "message": "Input should be 'Mr', 'Mme' or 'Melle'"
    },
    {
      "field": "email",
      "message": "value is not a valid email address: An email address must have an @-sign."
    }
  ]
}

All errors are reported at once, allowing the user to correct everything in one go. The messages are in English: [Pydantic] is not translated. The following example replaces them with its own messages.

docs.title: 3.3. Example 09: Validation Performed by the Action
docs.text: In Example 08, an invalid form interrupts the action, and the application handler responds. This is convenient for a API, whose clients are programs that expect a standardized error response. However, a web page often prefers to redisplay the form with the error messages: in this case, the action must decide how to handle an invalid model. The [models/person.py] model is the one from Example 08.

docs.title: 3.3.1. Custom messages: models/messages.py
docs.text:
# models/messages.py: the messages of the validation errors, in English.
# Each Pydantic error is a dictionary: its TYPE ("missing",
# "string_too_short"...), the field concerned (loc), a message in English (msg),
# and the context (ctx): the values of the constraints ({"min_length": 2}...)
MESSAGES = {
    "missing": "the field is required",
    "string_too_short": "{min_length} character(s) at least",
    "string_too_long": "{max_length} character(s) at most",
    "int_parsing": "an integer is expected",
    "greater_than_equal": "the value must be greater than or equal to {ge}",
    "less_than_equal": "the value must be less than or equal to {le}",
    "literal_error": "unknown value",
    "value_error": "invalid value",
    "too_short": "{min_length} item(s) at least",
}


# the name of the field: loc is a tuple, ("name",) or ("color", 1) for the 2nd
# item of a list
def field(error: dict) -> str:
    return ".".join(str(x) for x in error["loc"])


# our own message; an unknown error type keeps Pydantic's message
def message_en(error: dict) -> str:
    template = MESSAGES.get(error["type"])
    if template is None:
        return error["msg"]
    # format replaces {min_length}... with the values of the context
    return template.format(**error.get("ctx", {}))
  • Lines 5–14: Each error in [Pydantic] has a type and a unique identifier (["missing"] for a missing field, ["string_too_short"] for a string that is too short, etc.), independent of the English message. The [MESSAGES] dictionary associates its own message with each type. Some contain tags such as [{min_length}], [{ge}]...: the documentation for [Pydantic] provides, for each error type, the values of its context;
  • lines 20–21: the name of the field causing the error, taken from the tuple [loc]. [".".join(...)] assembles the elements of the tuple—converted to strings—separating them with periods;
  • lines 25–30: our own error message. [MESSAGES.get(...)] returns [None] for an error type not found in the dictionary; in that case, the English message from [Pydantic] is used. Otherwise, [format] replaces each occurrence of [{name}] in the message with the value of the same name from the context: ["{min_length} character(s) at least".format(min_length=2)] yields ["2 character(s) at least"]. The notation [**dictionary] passes the dictionary entries as named parameters; [error.get("ctx", {})] returns an empty dictionary for an error without context.

This technique (translating based on the error type) is the one used in the case study: messages there are identified by keys, which are translated into the user’s language.

docs.title: 3.3.2. The action: controllers/persons.py
docs.text:
# controllers/persons.py: it is the action that decides what to do with an invalid model
from flask import Blueprint, request
from markupsafe import escape
from pydantic import ValidationError

from models.messages import field, message_en
from models.person import PersonModel

persons = Blueprint("persons", __name__, url_prefix="/persons")


@persons.get("/action01")
def action01():
    try:
        person = PersonModel.model_validate(request.args.to_dict())
    except ValidationError as e:
        # the errors, field by field: e.errors() gives their list
        items = "".join(f"<li>{field(error)}: {message_en(error)}</li>" for error in e.errors())
        return f"<p>The form contains errors:</p><ul>{items}</ul>"
    # escape: the entered name is inserted into HTML; its characters < > & " '
    # are replaced by < >... (otherwise, an input could inject HTML)
    return f"<p>Welcome {person.title} {escape(person.name)} ({person.age} years old)</p>"
  • Lines 14–19: The action itself intercepts the [ValidationError] within a [try] / [except] block. If an error occurs, it constructs a HTML list of errors ([<ul>], one [<li>] tag per error);
  • line 22: if successful, a welcome message. The name is passed through the [escape] function in the [markupsafe] library (installed with [Flask]). [escape] replaces characters that have meaning in HTML ([<], [>], [&], ["], [']) with their entities ([<], [>]...): they will be displayed as-is instead of being interpreted. Without this precaution, a user could enter a “name” containing HTML, or even [JavaScript], which would execute in the browser of anyone viewing the page. This is the most common security vulnerability on the web: script injection (*XSS*, *cross-site scripting*). The title and age do not require this protection: their values have been validated by the template (one of three allowed values, an integer). In the next chapter, the [Jinja2] view engine will perform this escaping automatically for any value inserted into a page.

A valid entry, followed by an entry containing four errors:

The raw response to the second query, and the response for a name containing HTML:

curl "http://localhost:5000/persons/action01?name=m&age=abc&title=Mx&email=xx"
curl "http://localhost:5000/persons/action01?name=%3Cb%3Emartin%3C/b%3E&age=42&title=Mr"

<p>The form contains errors:</p><ul><li>name: 2 character(s) at least</li><li>age: an integer is expected</li><li>title: unknown value</li><li>email: invalid value</li></ul>
<p>Welcome Mr <b>martin</b> (42 years old)</p>

The name [<b>martin</b>] (encoded as [%3Cb%3E...] in URL) is displayed as-is, without being bolded: its tags have been neutralized. Note that the response this time is a 200 status code: this is because the action chose to return a normal page containing the errors.

docs.title: 3.4. Example 10: Multiple Parameters
docs.text:
The same parameter may appear multiple times in a URL: [?color=red&color=green]. This is what a browser sends for a group of checkboxes with the same name, or a multiple-select list (see the next chapter). The [controllers/arrays.py] file:

# controllers/arrays.py: a parameter that appears several times in the URL
from flask import Blueprint, request
from pydantic import ValidationError

from models.choice import ChoiceModel
from models.messages import field, message_en

arrays = Blueprint("arrays", __name__, url_prefix="/arrays")


# /arrays/action01?color=red&color=green: get returns only the FIRST value
@arrays.get("/action01")
def action01():
    return {"color": request.args.get("color")}


# /arrays/action02?color=red&color=green: getlist returns ALL the
# values, in a list (empty if the parameter is missing)
@arrays.get("/action02")
def action02():
    colors = request.args.getlist("color")
    return {"color": colors, "count": len(colors)}


# /arrays/action03?color=red: a list, validated by ChoiceModel
@arrays.get("/action03")
def action03():
    colors = request.args.getlist("color")
    try:
        ChoiceModel(color=colors)
        errors = []
    except ValidationError as e:
        errors = [f"{field(error)}: {message_en(error)}" for error in e.errors()]
    return {"colors": colors, "valid": not errors, "errors": errors}
  • line 14: [get] returns only the first value of the parameter;
  • line 21: [getlist] returns all its values in a list, which is empty if the parameter is missing. This is the distinctive feature of [MultiDict]: it retains the list of values for each key;
  • lines 27–34: the list is validated using a [Pydantic] template. This time, the model is constructed by a standard call, [ChoiceModel(color=colors)], with the fields passed as named parameters: this is equivalent to [model_validate] on a dictionary. The object created serves no purpose other than validation: it is not retained. The expression [not errors] is equivalent to [True] for an empty list.

The template [models/choice.py]:

# models/choice.py: a list, and a constraint on EACH item of the list
from typing import Annotated, Literal

from pydantic import BaseModel, Field


class ChoiceModel(BaseModel):
    # list[Literal[...]]: each item must be "red", "green" or "blue";
    # min_length=1: the list must contain at least one item
    color: Annotated[list[Literal["red", "green", "blue"]], Field(min_length=1)]
  • Line 10: The type [list[Literal["red", "green", "blue"]]] is that of a list in which each element is one of three colors. The constraint [min_length=1], applied to a list, pertains to the number of elements: there must be at least one.

The file [models/messages.py] is the one from Example 09. The results:

curl "http://localhost:5000/arrays/action01?color=red&color=green"
curl "http://localhost:5000/arrays/action02?color=red&color=green"
curl http://localhost:5000/arrays/action02

{
  "color": "red"
}
{
  "color": [
    "red",
    "green"
  ],
  "count": 2
}
{
  "color": [],
  "count": 0
}

Validation was successful at first, then failed due to an unknown color, and then due to an empty list:

curl "http://localhost:5000/arrays/action03?color=red&color=blue"
curl "http://localhost:5000/arrays/action03?color=red&color=yellow"
curl http://localhost:5000/arrays/action03

{
  "colors": [
    "red",
    "blue"
  ],
  "valid": true,
  "errors": []
}
{
  "colors": [
    "red",
    "yellow"
  ],
  "valid": false,
  "errors": [
    "color.1: unknown value"
  ]
}
{
  "colors": [],
  "valid": false,
  "errors": [
    "color: 1 item(s) at least"
  ]
}

The "unknown value" error refers to [color.1]: the error tuple [loc] is [("color", 1)]; the field and index of the problematic element in the list (the second one, with indices starting at 0).

docs.title: 3.5. Example 11: The parameters of a POST query
docs.text:
The previous examples used GET requests, whose parameters are contained in URL. A POST request carries its data in its body, in two main forms:

  • fields from a HTML form: the body has the same syntax as a query string ([name=martin&age=42]), and its type (header [Content-Type]) is [application/x-www-form-urlencoded];
  • a JSON document, sent by a program ([JavaScript] on a page, client of a API...): the type is [application/json].

The file [controllers/post.py]:

# controllers/post.py: the parameters of a POST request
from flask import Blueprint, request
from pydantic import ValidationError

from models.messages import field, message_en
from models.person import PersonModel

post = Blueprint("post", __name__, url_prefix="/post")


# the fields of an HTML form (application/x-www-form-urlencoded body):
# request.form, a "multi" dictionary (MultiDict), like request.args
@post.post("/action01")
def action01():
    return {
        "receivedType": request.content_type,
        # flat=False: each field -> the list of its values
        "fields": request.form.to_dict(flat=False),
    }


# a JSON body: get_json deserializes it (dictionary, list...); a body
# that is not JSON -> error 415 (unsupported type) or 400 (malformed JSON)
@post.post("/action02")
def action02():
    return {"receivedType": request.content_type, "body": request.get_json()}


# a single field of the form
@post.post("/action03")
def action03():
    name = request.form.get("name")
    return f"name = [{name}]"


# the fields of the form, bound and validated by the PersonModel class
@post.post("/action04")
def action04():
    try:
        person = PersonModel.model_validate(request.form.to_dict()).model_dump()
        errors = []
    except ValidationError as e:
        person = None
        errors = sorted(f"{field(error)}: {message_en(error)}" for error in e.errors())
    return {"person": person, "valid": not errors, "errors": errors}
  • line 13: [post.post(...)]: the first [post] is the blueprint, the second is the method that declares a route for the method HTTP POST (see example 02);
  • line 16: [request.content_type] is the [Content-Type] header of the request;
  • line 18: [request.form] contains the fields of a form sent in POST. Like [request.args], this is a [MultiDict]. [to_dict(flat=False)] actually creates a dictionary where each value is the list of values for the field;
  • line 26: [request.get_json()] deserializes a JSON body: the text JSON becomes a [Python] object (a dictionary for a JSON object, a list for a JSON array...). If the body is not declared as JSON, [get_json] causes a 415 error (*Unsupported Media Type*); if it is, but the text is malformed, a 400 error occurs;
  • line 32: a field, interpreted as a parameter of URL;
  • lines 38–45: the [PersonModel] template from Example 08, this time linked to the form fields. The code is the same as with the parameters of URL: only the dictionary source changes. [sorted] sorts the messages to ensure a consistent response.

With [curl], the [-d] (*data*) option sends a body; the request then becomes a POST request, of type [application/x-www-form-urlencoded], unless the [-H] (*header*) option specifies a different type. The option [-X POST] explicitly sets the method (it is optional here). The fields of a form, including a repeated field:

curl -i -X POST -d "name=martin&age=42&hobby=tennis&hobby=piano" http://localhost:5000/post/action01

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json
Content-Length: 195

{
  "receivedType": "application/x-www-form-urlencoded",
  "fields": {
    "name": [
      "martin"
    ],
    "age": [
      "42"
    ],
    "hobby": [
      "tennis",
      "piano"
    ]
  }
}

A JSON body, which contains an integer and an array:

curl -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d "{\"name\": \"martin\", \"age\": 42, \"children\": [\"léa\", \"tom\"]}" http://localhost:5000/post/action02

{
  "receivedType": "application/json",
  "body": {
    "name": "martin",
    "age": 42,
    "children": [
      "léa",
      "tom"
    ]
  }
}

The quotation marks in JSON are preceded by a [\] to prevent the command string from ending; Under [Linux] and [macOS], you can also enclose JSON in apostrophes: [-d '{"name": "martin"}']. Unlike form fields, the JSON carries data types: age is already an integer. A body that is not JSON, followed by a malformed JSON:

curl -i -d "name=martin" http://localhost:5000/post/action02
curl -i -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d "{\"name\": " http://localhost:5000/post/action02

HTTP/1.1 415 UNSUPPORTED MEDIA TYPE
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 215

<!doctype html>
<html lang=en>
<title>415 Unsupported Media Type</title>
<h1>Unsupported Media Type</h1>
<p>Did not attempt to load JSON data because the request Content-Type was not 'application/json'.</p>
HTTP/1.1 400 BAD REQUEST
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 163

<!doctype html>
<html lang=en>
<title>400 Bad Request</title>
<h1>Bad Request</h1>
<p>Failed to decode JSON object: Expecting value: line 1 column 10 (char 9)</p>

A single field, then the same URL requested as GET:

curl -d "name=jean%20dupont" http://localhost:5000/post/action03
curl -i "http://localhost:5000/post/action03?name=martin"

name = [jean dupont]
HTTP/1.1 405 METHOD NOT ALLOWED
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
Allow: POST, OPTIONS
Content-Length: 153

<!doctype html>
<html lang=en>
<title>405 Method Not Allowed</title>
<h1>Method Not Allowed</h1>
<p>The method is not allowed for the requested URL.</p>

URL exists, but not for the GET method: [Flask] returns a 405 (*Method Not Allowed*), and its header [Allow] lists the accepted methods ([OPTIONS] is automatically handled by [Flask] for any route). Finally, the template linked to the form fields, first valid then invalid:

curl -d "name=martin&age=42&title=Mr" http://localhost:5000/post/action04
curl -d "name=m&age=200" http://localhost:5000/post/action04

{
  "person": {
    "name": "martin",
    "age": 42,
    "title": "Mr",
    "email": null
  },
  "valid": true,
  "errors": []
}
{
  "person": null,
  "valid": false,
  "errors": [
    "age: the value must be less than or equal to 150",
    "name: 2 character(s) at least",
    "title: the field is required"
  ]
}

docs.title: 3.6. Example 12: Custom Binding and Validation
docs.text:
Standard types aren’t always sufficient. This example shows three ways to extend binding and validation:

  • a path converter: a date in French format, [23-09-2026], in the path of URL;
  • a decorator that provides the action with a parameter that does not come from the URL, but from a HTTP header;
  • "custom" types for [Pydantic]: a constraint (no spaces) and a conversion (a [dd/mm/yyyy] date).
12-custom-binding/
├── app.py
├── binding/
│   ├── date_fr.py
│   ├── language.py
│   └── types.py
└── controllers/
    └── examples.py

docs.title: 3.6.1. A path converter: binding/date_fr.py
docs.text:
In Example 02, we encountered the [Werkzeug] converters: [<int:id>] accepts only an integer and converts it. You can write new ones.

# binding/date_fr.py: a French date "23-09-2026" in the path of the URL
from datetime import date, datetime

from werkzeug.routing import BaseConverter, ValidationError


# a Werkzeug CONVERTER (the library on which Flask is built):
# it decides whether a piece of the path is suitable, and turns it into a Python object
class DateFrConverter(BaseConverter):
    # the regular expression of the piece of path: dd-mm-yyyy
    regex = r"\d{2}-\d{2}-\d{4}"

    # text of the path -> date object
    def to_python(self, value: str) -> date:
        try:
            # strptime checks that the date exists: "31-02-2026" is rejected
            return datetime.strptime(value, "%d-%m-%Y").date()
        except ValueError:
            # the route does not match: Flask looks for another route, then answers 404
            raise ValidationError()

    # date object -> text of the path (used by url_for)
    def to_url(self, value: date) -> str:
        return value.strftime("%d-%m-%Y")
  • line 9: a converter is a class that inherits from [BaseConverter];
  • line 11: the attribute [regex] is a regular expression that describes the format of the accepted path segment: [\d] denotes a digit, [{2}] denotes the repetition of the preceding element—in this case, two digits. The prefix [r] in the string (*raw string*) prevents [Python] from interpreting [\]. Routing only attempts to use this converter on a path segment of this form;
  • lines 14–20: [to_python] transforms the path text into a [Python] object, in this case a [date]. [datetime.strptime] (*string parse time*) parses a string according to a specific format: [%d] for the day, [%m] for the month, and [%Y] for the four-digit year; [.date()] retains the date without the time. [strptime] verifies that the date exists: [31-02-2026] is in the correct format, but raises a [ValueError]. The converter then raises the [ValidationError] exception from [Werkzeug] (not to be confused with the one from [Pydantic]): for routing, the route does not match the URL, which will therefore result in a 404 error if no other route matches it;
  • Lines 23–24: the inverse operation, used by [url_for] to construct a URL from a date. [strftime] (*string format time*) formats a date.

The converter is stored in [app.py]:

# app.py: the application of example 12
from flask import Flask

from controllers.examples import examples
from binding.date_fr import DateFrConverter


def create_app():
    app = Flask(__name__)
    # a path variable converter, under the name [datefr]: the routes
    # can now write <datefr:day>, like <int:id>
    app.url_map.converters["datefr"] = DateFrConverter
    app.register_blueprint(examples)
    return app


if __name__ == "__main__":
    create_app().run(port=5000, debug=True)
  • Line 12: [app.url_map] is the application’s routing table; its dictionary, [converters], associates a name with each converter ([int], [path]...). We add ours to it, under the name [datefr]. The entry must precede those of the blueprints that use it.

docs.title: 3.6.2. A parameter provided by a decorator: binding/language.py
docs.text:
An action [Flask] receives the path variables as parameters, and nothing else. To provide it with additional information, we can decorate the action: the decorator replaces the action with a function that calculates the information, then calls the action by passing it that information.

# binding/language.py: a decorator that PROVIDES a parameter to the action
from functools import wraps

from flask import request


# @with_language, placed on an action, passes it the [language] parameter, read from
# the header "Accept-Language: fr-FR,fr;q=0.9,en;q=0.8" -> "fr"
def with_language(action):
    # wraps: the produced function keeps the name of the action (Flask uses it
    # to name the route)
    @wraps(action)
    def action_with_language(*args, **kwargs):
        # request.accept_languages: the header already parsed by Werkzeug;
        # best_match: the browser's preferred language among those offered
        kwargs["language"] = request.accept_languages.best_match(["fr", "en"], default="fr")
        return action(*args, **kwargs)

    return action_with_language
  • Line 9: A decorator is a function that takes a function (in this case, the action) and returns another function (see Example 01). Writing [@with_language] above [def hello(...)] is equivalent to writing, after the definition, [hello = with_language(hello)];
  • Line 13: The function that will replace the action. [*args] receives positional parameters in a tuple, and [**kwargs] (*keyword arguments*) receives named parameters in a dictionary. This is how [Flask] passes the path variables ([id=3]): the function receives them without needing to know them;
  • line 16: a named parameter, [language], is added. [request.accept_languages] is the request header [Accept-Language], which has already been parsed by [Werkzeug]. The browser specifies the user’s languages here, in order of preference: [fr-FR,fr;q=0.9,en;q=0.8] (the coefficient [q] measures the preference, on a scale from 0 to 1). [best_match] selects, from among the languages offered by the application, the one the user prefers, or the value [default] if none are suitable;
  • line 17: the call to the original action, with the received parameters and the new one. The notations [*args] and [**kwargs] unpack the tuple and the dictionary into parameters this time;
  • line 12: the function [action_with_language] retrieves the name ([__name__]) and documentation of the action. This is essential here: [Flask] names each route after the name of its function (the [hello] of [url_for("examples.hello")]), and would refuse to register two routes with the same name, [action_with_language], if two actions used the decorator.

We’ll see this approach throughout the course: the [@login_required] and [@role_required] decorators in the chapter on authentication are built the same way.

docs.title: 3.6.3. "Custom" types for Pydantic: binding/types.py
docs.text:
# binding/types.py: "home-made" types for the Pydantic models
from datetime import date, datetime
from typing import Annotated

from pydantic import AfterValidator, BeforeValidator


# a "home-made" constraint: the string must not contain a space.
# The function receives the value ALREADY converted to str; it returns it, or raises
# a ValueError whose message becomes that of the validation error
def no_space(value: str) -> str:
    if " " in value:
        raise ValueError("the field must not contain a space")
    return value


# Annotated: the str type, completed by a check executed AFTER the
# conversion. NoSpace is then used like an ordinary type
NoSpace = Annotated[str, AfterValidator(no_space)]


# a "home-made" conversion: "23/09/2026" -> date(2026, 9, 23), executed BEFORE
# the validation of the date type
def date_fr(value):
    if isinstance(value, str):
        try:
            return datetime.strptime(value, "%d/%m/%Y").date()
        except ValueError:
            raise ValueError(f"[{value}] is not a valid dd/mm/yyyy date")
    return value


DateFr = Annotated[date, BeforeValidator(date_fr)]
  • Lines 11–14: a validation function: it takes the field’s value as input, returns it if it is valid, and raises a [ValueError] otherwise. The exception message becomes the validation error message;
  • line 19: the type [NoSpace] is the type [str], annotated by [AfterValidator(no_space)]: [Pydantic] will call the function after verifying (and, if necessary, converting) the value to [str]. This allows us to define, once, a type that can be reused in all models, just like an ordinary type;
  • Lines 24–30: a conversion function. The type ***[date] of *[Pydantic] accepts strings in the international format, ***[2026-09-23]; we want the French format, ***[23/09/2026]. The function receives the raw value: if it is a string, it converts it to [date]. Any other value (a pre-constructed [date]**, for example) is returned as-is;
  • line 33: [BeforeValidator]: the function is called before the validation of type [date], which therefore receives a pre-constructed [date].

docs.title: 3.6.4. The controller: controllers/examples.py
docs.text:
# controllers/examples.py: custom binding and validation
from datetime import date

from flask import Blueprint, request, url_for
from pydantic import BaseModel, ValidationError

from binding.language import with_language
from binding.types import DateFr, NoSpace

examples = Blueprint("examples", __name__, url_prefix="/examples")


# /examples/schedule/23-09-2026: a custom path converter (see app.py)
@examples.get("/schedule/<datefr:day>")
def schedule(day: date):
    # url_for uses the to_url method of the converter: date -> "23-09-2026"
    return f"schedule for the day [{day}], of type {type(day).__name__}, " \
           f"URL: {url_for('examples.schedule', day=day)}"


# /examples/hello: a parameter that does not come from the URL, but from a header,
# provided by the @with_language decorator
@examples.get("/hello")
@with_language
def hello(language: str):
    return "Hello!" if language == "en" else "Bonjour !"


# the model of the search: two "home-made" types
class SearchModel(BaseModel):
    keyword: NoSpace | None = None
    since: DateFr | None = None


# /examples/search?keyword=flask&since=01/09/2026
@examples.get("/search")
def search():
    model = SearchModel.model_validate(request.args.to_dict())
    return f"search for [{model.keyword}] since [{model.since}]"


# --------------------------------------------------------------- errors
# errorhandler of a BLUEPRINT: turns an exception raised by one of ITS
# actions into a response (the same decorator on the application applies to all)
@examples.errorhandler(ValidationError)
def validation(e: ValidationError):
    # the message of the first error, without Pydantic's "Value error, " prefix
    message = e.errors()[0]["msg"].removeprefix("Value error, ")
    return message, 400, {"Content-Type": "text/plain; charset=utf-8"}
  • Lines 14–18: The path variable [day] uses the converter [datefr]: The action receives a [date]. [url_for] constructs the URL for this same action based on the date, using the converter’s [to_url] method. The [\] separator at the end of the line continues the instruction on the next line; two consecutive literal strings are concatenated;
  • Lines 23–25: The order of the decorators matters. They are applied from bottom to top: [@with_language] first transforms the action, then [@examples.get] saves the transformed function to the blueprint. In the reverse order, the blueprint would save the original action, and the parameter [language] would never be provided;
  • lines 30–32: a model that uses the two “custom” types as if they were ordinary types. Both fields are optional;
  • lines 45–49: an exception handler, this time declared on the blueprint: it handles only exceptions thrown by the actions of this blueprint. [removeprefix] removes the prefix ["Value error, "] from the message, which [Pydantic] adds to messages from [ValueError]. The response is a tuple of three elements: the body, the code, and a dictionary of headers (see Example 03), in this case for a plaintext response.

docs.title: 3.6.5. Execution
docs.text:
The path converter:

curl "http://localhost:5000/examples/schedule/23-09-2026"
curl -i "http://localhost:5000/examples/schedule/31-02-2026"

schedule for the day [2026-09-23], of type date, URL: /examples/schedule/23-09-2026
HTTP/1.1 404 NOT FOUND
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 207
...

The date is displayed by [Python] in international format (this is the result of converting a [date] to a string), but the URL constructed by [url_for] has reverted to the French format. February 31 does not exist: 404. A date in international format, [2026-09-23], does not match the pattern described by the regular expression: 404 as well.

The decorator. The [-H] option of [curl] sets the header [Accept-Language]:

curl -H "Accept-Language: en-US,en;q=0.9,fr;q=0.8" http://localhost:5000/examples/hello
curl -H "Accept-Language: fr-FR,fr;q=0.9" http://localhost:5000/examples/hello
curl http://localhost:5000/examples/hello

Hello!
Bonjour !
Bonjour !

Without a header [Accept-Language] ([curl] does not send one), this is the default language. The chapter on internationalization will revisit this issue, with the user selecting the language.

"Custom" types:

curl "http://localhost:5000/examples/search?keyword=flask&since=01/09/2026"
curl "http://localhost:5000/examples/search"
curl -i "http://localhost:5000/examples/search?keyword=flask%20mvc"
curl "http://localhost:5000/examples/search?since=2026-09-01"
curl "http://localhost:5000/examples/search?since=31/02/2026"

search for [flask] since [2026-09-01]
search for [None] since [None]
HTTP/1.1 400 BAD REQUEST
Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 34

the field must not contain a space
[2026-09-01] is not a valid dd/mm/yyyy date
[31/02/2026] is not a valid dd/mm/yyyy date

docs.title: 3.6.6. Conclusion
docs.text:
Let’s summarize the methods available to an action for obtaining its template:

SourceMethodPath variablesthe action’s parameters, typed by the converters ([<int:id>], [<datefr:day>])Parameters of URL[request.args]: [get] (along with [type] and [default]), [getlist], [to_dict]Fields in a POST form[request.form], a [MultiDict], and a [request.args]Body JSON[request.get_json()]Headers[request.headers], and objects that have already been analyzed, such as [request.accept_languages]Conversion and validationa template [Pydantic]: [model_validate], [ValidationError], [e.errors()]Common errors[@app.errorhandler] (entire application) or [@blueprint.errorhandler] (a blueprint)Calculated parameterA decorator that adds a named parameter to the action

HTML forms, on the other hand, require more than just validation: they must be displayed, re-displayed with the user’s input and any errors, and protected against forged requests. This will be the role of [WTForms], covered in the next chapter once views have been introduced.

docs.title: 7. The Lifecycle of a Request
docs.text:
Between the arrival of a request and the dispatch of its response, [Flask] goes through several steps, and the application can intervene at each one. We’ve already encountered several of these: path variable converters (examples 02 and 12), the [before_request] functions (examples 16, 22, and 23), and error handlers (examples 08 and 12). This chapter combines them into a single example, which displays a message in the console at each step so you can observe the order:

  • 1 and 8. The WSGI middleware. [WSGI] (*Web Server Gateway Interface*) is the standard that connects a web server written in [Python] to an application. From the server’s perspective, a [Flask] application is simply a callable object that receives the request description and generates the response. Middleware is a similar type of object that wraps around the application: it intercepts the request before it reaches [Flask] and the response afterward. It is the equivalent of [Java] servlet filters;
  • 2. Routing. [Flask] searches for the route that corresponds to URL, and the route converters transform the path variables;
  • 3 and 4. The [before_request] functions, executed in the order in which they are registered. If any of them returns a response (or throws an exception), processing stops there: the action is not called. This is where we verify that a user is logged in (next chapter);
  • 5. The action, and the view it generates;
  • 6. The [after_request] functions, which receive the response, can modify it (add a header or a cookie), and must return it. They are executed in the reverse order of their registration;
  • 7. The [teardown_request] functions, which are always executed at the very end, even if an exception has interrupted processing. They can no longer modify the response; their purpose is to free up resources (such as closing a database connection);
  • x. Error handlers ([errorhandler]): An exception thrown by a [before_request] function, by an action, or by a view is handed off to the handler registered for its class, which generates an error response. This response then passes through the [after_request] functions, just like a regular response.

These are the equivalents of the [Spring MVC] interceptors and the [ASP.NET Core MVC] action filters. The functions [before_request], [after_request], and [teardown_request] are often referred to as hooks.

docs.title: 7.1. Example 24: The steps involved in processing a request
docs.text:
24-lifecycle/
├── app.py
├── controllers/
│   └── calc.py
├── filters/
│   ├── errors.py
│   ├── hooks.py
│   ├── integer.py
│   ├── logger.py
│   └── marks.py
└── templates/
    ├── calc/
    │   └── result.html
    ├── error.html
    └── layout.html

The application has only one action, which calculates the square of an integer: [/square/7]. Depending on URL, it either succeeds or fails in various ways.

docs.title: 7.1.1. The WSGI middleware: filters/logger.py
docs.text:
# filters/logger.py: a WSGI MIDDLEWARE. WSGI is the standard that connects a
# Python web server to an application: the application is a callable object
# app(environ, start_response). A middleware is such an object, which WRAPS
# the application: it sees each request go by BEFORE Flask, and the response AFTER
class LoggerMiddleware:

    def __init__(self, application):
        self.application = application  # the wrapped application (Flask)

    def __call__(self, environ, start_response):
        # environ: a dictionary that describes the request (method, path...)
        request = environ["REQUEST_METHOD"] + " " + environ["PATH_INFO"]
        if environ.get("QUERY_STRING"):
            request += "?" + environ["QUERY_STRING"]
        print()
        print("---", request)
        print("1. middleware (before)")
        status = []

        # start_response: the function through which Flask announces the code and the
        # headers of the response; we wrap it to note the code on the way
        def spy_start_response(status_line, headers, exc_info=None):
            status.append(status_line)
            return start_response(status_line, headers, exc_info)

        # all the rest: Flask, the action, the view
        response = self.application(environ, spy_start_response)
        print(f"8. middleware (after: code {status[0] if status else '?'})")
        return response
  • Line 7: The middleware receives the application it wraps;
  • line 10: the special method [__call__] makes the object callable: [middleware(environ, start_response)] executes this method. This is the signature imposed by [WSGI]: [environ] is a dictionary that describes the request (the method in [REQUEST_METHOD], the path in [PATH_INFO], the parameters in [QUERY_STRING], the headers, etc.) ; [start_response] is a function provided by the server, which the application calls to report the response code and headers;
  • lines 12–17: the middleware displays the request. This is message #1: nothing has happened yet in [Flask];
  • lines 22–24: To determine the response code, the middleware passes one of its own functions to the application—instead of [start_response]—which records the code as it passes through, then calls the actual function. This is an internal function (defined within another function): it has access to the variables of the function that contains it, in this case the list [status];
  • line 27: the call to the wrapped application: the rest of the processing takes place within this call;
  • line 28: message No. 8, when [Flask] has finished.

A middleware component operates at the level of [WSGI]: it is unaware of [request], [g], or the routes of [Flask]. It is used for processing that applies to all requests, regardless of the application: logging, compression, handling a proxy, etc. [Werkzeug] provides a few of these, such as [ProxyFix], which corrects the client’s address when the application is located behind a proxy server (the case study discusses this in relation to the clients’ IP address).

docs.title: 7.1.2. The converter: filters/integer.py
docs.text:
# filters/integer.py: the <integer:n> path variable, converted to an integer, or
# None if it is not an integer (it is then the action that decides)
from werkzeug.routing import BaseConverter


class IntegerConverter(BaseConverter):
    # any piece of path (without a slash)
    regex = r"[^/]+"

    def to_python(self, value: str) -> int | None:
        print(f'2. conversion of the parameter (received value: "{value}")')
        try:
            return int(value)
        except ValueError:
            return None

A converter (example 12) that accepts any portion of a path ([[^/]+]: one or more characters other than [/]) and converts it in its entirety, or to [None] if it is not a valid path. Unlike [<int:n>], which would return a 404 page for [/square/abc], here the action will determine the outcome. It displays message #2.

docs.title: 7.1.3. Marked actions: filters/marks.py
docs.text:
The [before_request] functions run before all actions. Often, a process applies only to certain actions. A simple way to specify them is to mark them:

# filters/marks.py: two decorators that MARK an action, without changing
# anything in its execution: they add an attribute to it, which the functions
# of filters/hooks.py look for


def block(action):
    action.block = True
    return action


def timing(action):
    action.timing = True
    return action

These two decorators do not change the action itself: they add an attribute to it (in [Python], a function is an object to which attributes can be added), and leave it unchanged. The [before_request] functions will search for these markers on the action targeted by the request.

docs.title: 7.1.4. Hooks: filters/hooks.py
docs.text:
# filters/hooks.py: functions executed BEFORE and AFTER each action
import time

from flask import abort, current_app, g, request


# the action that will handle the current request (None if no route matches).
# request.endpoint: the name of the action ("calc.square"); view_functions:
# the name -> function dictionary of the application
def targeted_action():
    return current_app.view_functions.get(request.endpoint)


# is the [name] mark (see marks.py) placed on the targeted action?
def marked(name: str) -> bool:
    return getattr(targeted_action(), name, False)


def register(app):

    # before_request: before the action. If the function returns a response (or raises
    # an exception), the processing stops there: the action is not called
    @app.before_request
    def block():
        if marked("block"):
            print(f"3. before_request Block (targeted action: {request.endpoint})")
            if "block" in request.args:
                abort(403)  # a 403 error response (access denied)

    @app.before_request
    def timing_start():
        if marked("timing"):
            print("4. before_request Timing (before)")
            # the start time, stored in g (request scope)
            g.start = time.perf_counter()

    # after_request: after the action (and the view it built), with the
    # response, which the function can modify; it must return it
    @app.after_request
    def timing_after(response):
        if marked("timing"):
            print(f"6. after_request Timing (code {response.status_code})")
        return response

    # teardown_request: at the very end, always called, with the possible
    # (unhandled) exception; it can no longer change the response
    @app.teardown_request
    def timing_end(exception):
        if "start" in g:
            ms = round((time.perf_counter() - g.start) * 1000)
            outcome = "" if exception is None else f", exception {type(exception).__name__}"
            print(f"7. teardown_request Timing (end, {ms} ms{outcome})")
  • Lines 10–11: the action that will handle the request. After routing, [request.endpoint] contains the name of the selected route ([calc.square]: the blueprint name, a period, the function name); [current_app.view_functions] is the dictionary that maps each name to its corresponding function. If no route matches, [request.endpoint] is set to [None], and the function returns [None];
  • lines 15–16: Is the flag set? [getattr(object, name, default)] returns the given name attribute, or the default value if it does not exist (or if the object is [None]);
  • line 19: The callbacks are registered by a function called by [app.py];
  • lines 24–28: the first hook, message #3: for an action marked [block], the parameter [?block] of URL causes a 403 error (*Forbidden*, access denied): [abort] throws an exception, which interrupts processing;
  • lines 31–35: the second hook, message no. 4: for an action marked [timing], the start time is stored in [g]. [time.perf_counter()] is a precise clock designed to measure durations;
  • lines 39–43: message #6. The function receives the response and must return it (possibly modified). [response.status_code] is the response code;
  • lines 47–52: message #7, containing the elapsed time since hook #4. The ["start" in g] test verifies that the measurement has started. The function receives the exception that interrupted processing, if there is one that has not been handled, and [None] otherwise.

docs.title: 7.1.5. Error handling: filters/errors.py
docs.text:
# filters/errors.py: the error handlers of the application
from flask import render_template
from werkzeug.exceptions import HTTPException


def register(app):

    # an "unexpected" exception of a given type: ValueError and its subclasses
    @app.errorhandler(ValueError)
    def value_error(e: ValueError):
        print(f"x. errorhandler ValueError ({e})")
        # instead of the default error page, our [error] view, with the 500 code
        return render_template("error.html", code=500), 500

    # the HTTP errors (abort(400), abort(403), unknown page -> 404...):
    # HTTPException is the parent class of all the HTTP exceptions of Werkzeug
    @app.errorhandler(HTTPException)
    def http_error(e: HTTPException):
        print(f"e. errorhandler HTTPException (code {e.code})")
        return render_template("error.html", code=e.code), e.code
  • Lines 9–13: an exception handler for the [ValueError] class (and its subclasses): an “unexpected” error, converted into a “custom” error page with status code 500 (*Internal Server Error*). The exception message is displayed in the console, but not on the page: it may contain internal details that are not relevant to the user;
  • Lines 17–20: a handler for all HTTP errors. [abort(400)], [abort(403)], a URL for a missing route (404), a forbidden method (405): all throw an exception of a subclass of [HTTPException] ([BadRequest], [Forbidden], [NotFound]...), which carries its code in the [code] attribute. This single handler therefore replaces all English error pages from [Werkzeug] with ours.

For an exception, [Flask] selects the handler registered for the class closest to its own. You can also register a handler for a specific code: [@app.errorhandler(404)]. An exception that has no handler becomes a 500 error: in debug mode, this is the debug page (example 03); without debug mode, it is the standard 500 error page or the page from the handler registered for code 500.

docs.title: 7.1.6. The controller and the error page
docs.text:
# controllers/calc.py: an action marked by two decorators
from flask import Blueprint, abort, render_template

from filters.marks import block, timing

calc = Blueprint("calc", __name__)


@calc.get("/square/<integer:n>")
@block
@timing
def square(n: int | None):
    print(f"5. action square({n})")
    if n is None:
        abort(400)  # a 400 error: see filters/errors.py
    if n == 13:
        raise ValueError("13 brings bad luck")  # an "unexpected" error
    return render_template("calc/result.html", n=n, square=n * n)
  • lines 9–11: the route uses the [integer] converter; the action bears both decorators. Order matters here as well (example 12): decorators are applied from bottom to top, and the route decorator must be the last one applied (the first one written) to register the decorated function;
  • line 15: a parameter that is not an integer: error 400;
  • line 17: the number 13 causes an “unexpected” error;
  • line 18: the normal case.
{% extends "layout.html" %}
{# the error page; its model: the error code #}

{% block content %}
  <div class="alert alert-danger">
    <h1 class="h4">Error {{ code }}</h1>
    <p class="mb-0">
      {% if code == 400 %}Bad request.
      {% elif code == 403 %}Access denied.
      {% elif code == 404 %}Page not found.
      {% else %}Internal server error.
      {% endif %}
    </p>
  </div>
{% endblock %}

The error page receives the error code and displays an appropriate message.

docs.title: 7.1.7. Configuration: app.py
docs.text:
# app.py: the application of example 24
from pathlib import Path

from flask import Blueprint, Flask

from controllers.calc import calc
from filters import hooks, errors
from filters.integer import IntegerConverter
from filters.logger import LoggerMiddleware

BOOTSTRAP = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent / "common" / "bootstrap"


def create_app():
    app = Flask(__name__)
    app.jinja_env.trim_blocks = True
    app.jinja_env.lstrip_blocks = True
    app.register_blueprint(Blueprint("bootstrap", __name__, static_folder=BOOTSTRAP,
                                     static_url_path="/bootstrap"))
    # the converter of the <integer:...> variables
    app.url_map.converters["integer"] = IntegerConverter
    app.register_blueprint(calc)
    # the functions executed before and after each action, in the order
    # in which they are registered
    hooks.register(app)
    # the error handlers
    errors.register(app)
    # the WSGI middleware: it WRAPS the whole Flask application
    app.wsgi_app = LoggerMiddleware(app.wsgi_app)
    return app


if __name__ == "__main__":
    create_app().run(port=5000, debug=True)
  • Line 21: the converter;
  • Lines 25–27: the callbacks and error handlers;
  • line 29: the middleware. [app.wsgi_app] is the method by which the server calls the [Flask] application; it is replaced by the middleware, which will call the old one. We wrap [app.wsgi_app] rather than [app] itself so that the variable [app] remains the object [Flask], with its methods ([run], [route]...).

docs.title: 7.1.8. Execution
docs.text:
The normal case, [/square/7]:

The server console displays the eight steps, in order:

--- GET /square/7
1. middleware (before)
2. conversion of the parameter (received value: "7")
3. before_request Block (targeted action: calc.square)
4. before_request Timing (before)
5. action square(7)
6. after_request Timing (code 200)
7. teardown_request Timing (end, 1 ms)
8. middleware (after: code 200 OK)
127.0.0.1 - - [26/Sep/2026 15:39:00] "GET /square/7 HTTP/1.1" 200 -

The last line is the development server log entry for [Werkzeug], written after the response was sent. A blocked access, [/square/7?block]:

--- GET /square/7?block
1. middleware (before)
2. conversion of the parameter (received value: "7")
3. before_request Block (targeted action: calc.square)
e. errorhandler HTTPException (code 403)
6. after_request Timing (code 403)
8. middleware (after: code 403 FORBIDDEN)

The first call raised an exception: the second call and the action were not executed. The error response, generated by the handler, passes through [after_request]; [teardown_request] was called but did not display anything, as the operation did not begin. A parameter that is not an integer, [/square/abc]:

--- GET /square/abc
1. middleware (before)
2. conversion of the parameter (received value: "abc")
3. before_request Block (targeted action: calc.square)
4. before_request Timing (before)
5. action square(None)
e. errorhandler HTTPException (code 400)
6. after_request Timing (code 400)
7. teardown_request Timing (end, 0 ms)
8. middleware (after: code 400 BAD REQUEST)

This time, the action was called—[None]—and it raised error 400. An “unexpected” error, [/square/13]:

--- GET /square/13
1. middleware (before)
2. conversion of the parameter (received value: "13")
3. before_request Block (targeted action: calc.square)
4. before_request Timing (before)
5. action square(13)
x. errorhandler ValueError (13 brings bad luck)
6. after_request Timing (code 500)
7. teardown_request Timing (end, 0 ms)
8. middleware (after: code 500 INTERNAL SERVER ERROR)

The exception was handled by its handler: the user sees the “custom” error page, not the debug page, even though debug mode is enabled. Finally, a URL that does not correspond to any route, [/unknown]:

--- GET /unknown
1. middleware (before)
e. errorhandler HTTPException (code 404)
8. middleware (after: code 404 NOT FOUND)

Routing failed: no route, no converter, no action. The callbacks were executed, but nothing was displayed because they could not find a target action. The 404 page is ours:

curl -i http://localhost:5000/unknown

HTTP/1.1 404 NOT FOUND
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 375
...
  <div class="alert alert-danger">
    <h1 class="h4">Error 404</h1>
    <p class="mb-0">
Page not found.
    </p>
  </div>
...

Let’s focus on the essentials. The [before_request] functions are the right place for checks common to many actions (Is the user logged in? Do they have permission to access this action?): the next chapter uses them for authentication. Error handlers ensure that the user never sees a technical page, regardless of the error: the case study includes one for each type of error.

docs.title: 4. The view and its model
docs.text:
Until now, actions generated their own responses: text, JSON, and a few HTML tags written in a string. In a MVC application, this is the role of a view: a file that describes the page HTML, with placeholders for the data passed to it by the action—the view model.

[Flask] comes with a view engine, [Jinja2], written by the same team (the *Pallets* project). Other engines can be used ([Mako], [Chameleon]...), but [Jinja2] is by far the most widely used in [Python]: it is found in [Django] (as an option), in [Ansible], in static site generators... This is the one used in this course.

A [Jinja2] view (the documentation refers to it as a *template*, a page template) is a text file—in this case, HTML—in which three types of tags are interpreted on the server:

  • [{{ expression }}]: the value of an expression, inserted into the page;
  • [{% instruction %}]: an instruction: condition ([if]), loop ([for]), template inheritance ([extends], [block]), inclusion ([include]), macro...;
  • [{# comment #}]: a comment that does not appear on the generated page.

Everything else is copied as-is. The syntax of the expressions is similar to that of [Python]. This differs from [Thymeleaf], the view engine for course [Spring MVC], whose views are valid HTML files enriched with [th:] attributes; Instead, it brings [Jinja2] closer to [Razor] ([ASP.NET Core MVC]), which mixes HTML and code. By default, [Flask] searches for views in the application’s [templates] folder.

docs.title: 4.1. Example 13: A First View
docs.text:
13-first-view/
├── app.py
├── controllers/
│   └── views.py
├── models/
│   └── page.py
└── templates/
    └── views/
        ├── index.html
        └── unknown.html

docs.title: 4.1.1. The view template: models/page.py
docs.text:
# models/page.py: the model of the view, the data that the action passes to the view
from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass
class PageModel:
    title: str
    message: str
    time: str

The view model is a simple [dataclass] (see Example 06): the three pieces of information that the view will display. There is no requirement to define a view’s model as a class: three separate variables could be passed to the view. However, a class documents what the view expects and allows the editor to verify the action’s code. This is the approach the case study will follow, where each view has its own model class.

docs.title: 4.1.2. The controller: controllers/views.py
docs.text:
# controllers/views.py: actions that return a VIEW
from datetime import datetime

from flask import Blueprint, render_template

from models.page import PageModel

views = Blueprint("views", __name__)


# render_template: the Jinja2 engine builds the page from the view
# templates/views/index.html and from the variables passed as keyword parameters
# (here a single one, [model]); the produced page is the response of the action
@views.get("/")
def index():
    model = PageModel(
        "My first view",
        "This page was built by Jinja2, on the server.",
        datetime.now().strftime("%H:%M:%S"))
    return render_template("views/index.html", model=model)


# the same view with another model; or another view, with the 404 code
@views.get("/hello/<name>")
def hello(name):
    if name == "unknown":
        # a tuple (page, code): the page, sent with the 404 code
        return render_template("views/unknown.html", name=name), 404
    model = PageModel(
        f"Hello {name}",
        "This time, the title of the page comes from the URL.",
        datetime.now().strftime("%H:%M:%S"))
    return render_template("views/index.html", model=model)
  • line 4: imports the function [render_template];
  • lines 16–19: the action builds the view model. [datetime.now().strftime("%H:%M:%S")]: the current time, formatted (see Example 12);
  • line 20: [render_template] instructs [Jinja2] to generate the page: the first parameter is the view path, relative to the [templates] folder; the named parameters that follow are the view’s variables; in this case, there is only one: [model]. [render_template] returns the text of the generated page, which becomes the action’s response (of type [text/html]);
  • line 28: another view, with a different variable ([name]). The tuple [(page, 404)] sends the page with a 404 status code (see Example 03): a custom error page;
  • Lines 29–33: the same view as the action [index], with a different template. This is the benefit of separating actions from views: a single view can be used by multiple actions.

docs.title: 4.1.3. The view: templates/views/index.html
docs.text:
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  {# {{ ... }}: the value of an expression, inserted into the page #}
  <title>{{ model.title }}</title>
</head>
<body>
  <h1>{{ model.title }}</h1>
  <p>{{ model.message }}</p>
  <p>Page built at {{ model.time }}.</p>
</body>
</html>
  • line 5: a comment [Jinja2];
  • Line 6: [{{ model.title }}] inserts the value of the [title] attribute from the [model] variable. The dot notation for [Jinja2] is more flexible than that for [Python]: [model.title] first looks for an attribute [title], and then, if that is not found, a key ["title"] (if [model] is a dictionary). The view code therefore does not need to know whether its model is an object or a dictionary.

Everything inserted by [{{ }}] is escaped: the characters [<], [>], [&], ["], and ['] are replaced by their entity codes HTML. This is the role that function [escape] played in Example 09, but this time it is automatic: [Flask] enables automatic escaping (*autoescape*) for views whose names end with [.html], [.htm], [.xml], [.xhtml], or [.svg]. This prevents a view from inadvertently inserting the HTML provided by a user into the page.

docs.title: 4.1.4. The view: templates/views/unknown.html
docs.text:
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <title>Unknown</title>
</head>
<body>
  <h1>Nobody is called [{{ name }}] here.</h1>
</body>
</html>

A view is not required to receive an object: the variable [name] is a string.

docs.title: 4.1.5. Execution
docs.text:
The raw response shows the work done by [Jinja2]: the [{{ }}] tags have been replaced with their values, and the comment has disappeared (an empty line remains in its place; we’ll see in the next example how to avoid this).

curl -i http://localhost:5000/

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 242

<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">

  <title>My first view</title>
</head>
<body>
  <h1>My first view</h1>
  <p>This page was built by Jinja2, on the server.</p>
  <p>Page built at 15:30:51.</p>
</body>
</html>

The “custom” error page, followed by a name containing HTML ([<b>martin], encoded in URL):

curl -i http://localhost:5000/hello/unknown
curl http://localhost:5000/hello/%3Cb%3Emartin

HTTP/1.1 404 NOT FOUND
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 164

<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <title>Unknown</title>
</head>
<body>
  <h1>Nobody is called [unknown] here.</h1>
</body>
</html>
...
  <title>Hello <b>martin</title>
...
  <h1>Hello <b>martin</h1>
...

The [<b>] tag was escaped without any action or view being involved.

docs.title: 4.2. Example 14: The Jinja2 Language
docs.text: This example combines the main constructs of [Jinja2] into a single view.

docs.title: 4.2.1. The template and the action
docs.text:
# models/basics.py: the model of the view of example 14
from dataclasses import dataclass
from decimal import Decimal


@dataclass
class Product:
    name: str
    price: Decimal
    in_stock: bool


@dataclass
class Address:
    street: str
    city: str


@dataclass
class BasicsModel:
    title: str
    name: str
    nickname: str | None
    html: str
    logged_in: bool
    currency: str
    products: list[Product]
    cart: list[Product]
    address: Address

The template contains values of various types: strings, [None], booleans, lists of objects, empty lists, and objects containing other objects. The [Decimal] type, from the standard module [decimal], exactly represents decimal numbers (unlike the type [float], for which [0.1 + 0.2] equals [0.30000000000000004]); this is the type to use for amounts.

# controllers/basics.py: a view that uses the main constructs of Jinja2
from decimal import Decimal

from flask import Blueprint, render_template

from models.basics import Address, BasicsModel, Product

basics = Blueprint("basics", __name__)


@basics.get("/")
def index():
    model = BasicsModel(
        title="Jinja2 basics",
        name="Martin",
        nickname=None,
        html="<b>this is HTML</b>",
        logged_in=True,
        currency="€",
        products=[
            Product("Keyboard", Decimal("25"), True),
            Product("Mouse", Decimal("12.5"), False),
            Product("Screen", Decimal("149"), True),
        ],
        cart=[],
        address=Address("12 rue des Lilas", "Angers"))
    return render_template("basics/index.html", model=model)

The action builds the model and passes it to the view. [Decimal("12.5")]: a decimal is constructed from a string to avoid using an inaccurate [float].

docs.title: 4.2.2. Configuration: app.py
docs.text:
# app.py: the application of example 14
from flask import Flask

from controllers.basics import basics


def create_app():
    app = Flask(__name__)
    # the {% ... %} tags leave no blank lines in the produced page:
    # trim_blocks removes the line break that follows a tag, lstrip_blocks the
    # spaces that precede it on its line
    app.jinja_env.trim_blocks = True
    app.jinja_env.lstrip_blocks = True
    app.register_blueprint(basics)
    return app


if __name__ == "__main__":
    create_app().run(port=5000, debug=True)
  • Lines 12–13: [app.jinja_env] is the application’s [Jinja2] environment—the object that loads and executes the views. By default, a [{% %}] tag standing alone on its line leaves the spaces preceding it and the line break following it in the generated page: a loop would produce numerous empty lines. [trim_blocks] removes the line break following a tag, while [lstrip_blocks] removes the spaces preceding it. These two settings do not affect the page’s display (the browser ignores these whitespace characters), but they make the generated HTML more readable. All of the following examples enable them.

docs.title: 4.2.3. The view: templates/basics/index.html
docs.text:
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <title>{{ model.title }}</title>
</head>
<body>
  {# {% set %}: a variable of the view; the filters (|) transform a value #}
  {% set total = model.products | sum(attribute="price") %}
  {% set count = model.products | length %}
  <h1>{{ model.title }}</h1>
  {# 1. display a value of the model; None is displayed... "None": the filter
        default(text, true) replaces an empty or None value. This Jinja2
        comment does not appear in the produced page #}
  <p>1. Name: {{ model.name }} - nickname: [{{ model.nickname }}] [{{ model.nickname | default("", true) }}]</p>
  {# 2. {{ }} escapes HTML; the safe filter inserts it as is #}
  <p>2a. {{ model.html }}</p>
  <p>2b. {{ model.html | safe }}</p>
  {# 3. a condition #}
  {% if model.logged_in %}
  <p>3. You are logged in.</p>
  {% else %}
  <p>3. You are not logged in.</p>
  {% endif %}
  {# 4. a loop: [loop] describes the state of the loop #}
  <p>4. Our products:</p>
  <ul>
    {% for product in model.products %}
    <li>no. {{ loop.index0 }}: {{ product.name }}, {{ product.price }} {{ model.currency }}
      {{ "(in stock)" if product.in_stock else "(sold out)" }}
      {% if loop.first %}- the first one{% endif %}
      {% if loop.last %}- the last one, seen by {{ model.name }}{% endif %}
    </li>
    {% endfor %}
  </ul>
  {# 5. the empty list: the else block of a for loop #}
  <p>5. Your cart:
    {% for p in model.cart %}<span>{{ p.name }}</span>{% else %}it is empty.{% endfor %}
  </p>
  {# 6. computed expressions, the set variables, and the format filter #}
  <p>6. {{ count }} products, for a total of {{ total }} {{ model.currency }};
    average price: {{ "%.2f" | format(total / count) }} {{ model.currency }}</p>
  {# 7. an object inside an object, and a Python method (upper) #}
  <p>7. Address: {{ model.address.street }}, {{ model.address.city.upper() }}</p>
  <p>8. An email address: contact@example.com</p>
</body>
</html>
  • Lines 9–10: [{% set %}] creates a view variable. Filters transform a value: [value | filter] or [value | filter(parameters)]. The filter [sum(attribute="price")] sums the [price] attributes of the elements in a list; the filter [length] returns the length of a list. [Jinja2] provides about fifty filters: [upper], [lower], [title], [trim], [join], [sort], [round], [default], [replace], [truncate]... ;
  • line 15: the value [None] is displayed... [None]. The filter [default(value, true)] replaces an “empty” value ([None], empty string, zero) with the specified value; without the second parameter [true], it would only replace an undefined variable;
  • lines 17–18: [{{ }}] escapes HTML (2a); the filter [safe], on the other hand, declares that the value is safe HTML, to be inserted as-is (2b). [safe] is reserved for HTML generated by the application itself, never for user input;
  • lines 20–24: a condition: [{% if %}], [{% elif %}], [{% else %}], [{% endif %}]. Unlike [Python], whose blocks are delimited by indentation, [Jinja2] closes each block with a [end...] tag;
  • lines 28–34: a loop [{% for %}] ... [{% endfor %}]. Within the loop, the special variable [loop] describes the loop’s state: [loop.index] (the iteration number, starting at 1), [loop.index0] (starting at 0), [loop.first], [loop.last] (true on the first and last iterations), [loop.length] (the number of elements). Variables outside the loop ([model.name]) remain accessible;
  • line 30: the conditional expression for [Python], [a if condition else b], is also that of [Jinja2];
  • Line 38: A [for] loop can contain a [{% else %}] block, which is executed if the list is empty. This is simpler than a [if] that would check the length of the list;
  • Lines 41–42: calculated expressions ([total / count]). The filter [format] applies a format similar to the [%] operator from [Python]: ["%.2f"] displays a number with two decimal places. In Example 16, we’ll see a much better way to format numbers and amounts;
  • line 44: dot notation traverses objects ([model.address.city]) and allows you to call their methods: [upper()] is a method of the strings [Python];
  • line 45: an email address, written as-is. The character [@], which has a specific meaning in other view engines ([Razor]), has no such meaning in [Jinja2]: only the tags [{{ }}], [{% %}], and [{# #}] are interpreted.

docs.title: 4.3. Example 15: Template, fragments, static files
docs.text:
The pages of a website usually share the same structure: a header, a navigation bar, a footer, and the same style sheets. Rather than repeating this structure in every view, it is written once in a template (*layout*), which the pages extend. This example also uses [Bootstrap], the most widely used CSS framework, for styling.

15-layout/
├── app.py
├── controllers/
│   └── pages.py
├── static/
│   └── css/
│       └── styles.css
└── templates/
    ├── fragments/
    │   ├── card.html
    │   └── navbar.html
    ├── layout.html
    └── pages/
        ├── home.html
        ├── raw.html
        └── team.html

docs.title: 4.3.1. Static Files
docs.text:
A HTML page references other files: style sheets, [JavaScript] scripts, and images. These files, which the server sends as-is, are called static files. [Flask] automatically serves the contents of the application’s [static] folder under the URL [/static/...] directory: the [static/css/styles.css] file is available at URL and [/static/css/styles.css].

/* a few settings in addition to Bootstrap */
body {
  background-color: #f5f7fa;
}

/* the footer of the layout */
.footer {
  margin-top: 2rem;
  font-size: 0.85rem;
  color: #6c757d;
}

/* the error messages, at the bottom of the page, on a light pink background */
.error-area {
  margin-top: 1.5rem;
  padding: 0.75rem 1rem;
  background-color: #fdecef;
  border: 1px solid #f5c2c7;
  border-radius: 0.375rem;
  color: #842029;
}

A few additional CSS rules in addition to [Bootstrap]: a light gray background, the footer style, and the style for an error area that will be used in the following examples.

[Bootstrap], on the other hand, is used by examples 15 through 28. Rather than placing a copy in each user’s [static] folder, the examples share it: it is located in the [examples/common/bootstrap] folder. You must therefore instruct [Flask] to also use this folder. This is the purpose of the following lines in [app.py]:

# app.py: the application of example 15
from datetime import date
from pathlib import Path

from flask import Blueprint, Flask, request

from controllers.pages import pages

# Bootstrap, shared by the examples: the examples/common/bootstrap folder,
# designated from the location of THIS file (and not from the current folder)
BOOTSTRAP = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent / "common" / "bootstrap"


def create_app():
    app = Flask(__name__)
    app.jinja_env.trim_blocks = True
    app.jinja_env.lstrip_blocks = True
    # a blueprint without routes, which only serves static files: the
    # BOOTSTRAP folder, under the /bootstrap/... URL
    app.register_blueprint(Blueprint("bootstrap", __name__, static_folder=BOOTSTRAP,
                                     static_url_path="/bootstrap"))
    app.register_blueprint(pages)

    # a "context processor": executed before building EACH view,
    # it adds its variables to the model of all the views
    @app.context_processor
    def common_model():
        return {"path": request.path, "year": date.today().year}

    return app


if __name__ == "__main__":
    create_app().run(port=5000, debug=True)
  • Line 11: The path to the [common/bootstrap] folder. [Path], from the standard module [pathlib], represents a file path. [Path(__file__)] is the path to the file [app.py] itself ([__file__] is a variable that [Python] defines in each module); [resolve()] makes it absolute; [parent] refers to the folder containing it ([15-layout]), [parent.parent] refers to the folder above it ([examples]); the operator [/] adds an element to the path. Specifying the folder based on the file’s location—rather than the current folder—allows the application to be launched from any folder;
  • lines 20–21: A blueprint can have its own static files folder ([static_folder]), served under the specified URL ([static_url_path]). This folder contains only that: it has no routes. The file [common/bootstrap/css/bootstrap.min.css] is thus served to URL and [/bootstrap/css/bootstrap.min.css];
  • Lines 26–28: A context processor is a function that [Flask] executes before each view is generated. It returns a dictionary, whose key-value pairs are added to the view’s variables. Here, [path] (the path of the requested URL) and [year] (the current year) are thus available in all views, without the actions having to provide them. The template uses these for its footer.

docs.title: 4.3.2. The template: templates/layout.html
docs.text:
<!doctype html>
{# the layout of the pages: the pages EXTEND it, and fill its blocks #}
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
  {# a block: a slot that the page can fill; here with a default content #}
  <title>{% block title %}Home{% endblock %} - My site</title>
  {# url_for builds the URL of a static file: /bootstrap/css/bootstrap.min.css #}
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="{{ url_for('bootstrap.static', filename='css/bootstrap.min.css') }}">
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="{{ url_for('static', filename='css/styles.css') }}">
</head>
<body>
  <div class="container py-3">
    {# insertion of the fragments/navbar.html file #}
    {% include "fragments/navbar.html" %}
    <main>
      {# the content of the page requested by the action is inserted here #}
      {% block content %}{% endblock %}
    </main>
    {# path, year: added to the model of all the views (see app.py) #}
    <footer class="footer">Page [{{ path }}] - © {{ year }}</footer>
  </div>
</body>
</html>
  • line 6: the [viewport] tag instructs mobile browsers to display the page at the screen’s width, which is what [Bootstrap] expects;
  • line 8: A block is a named container that pages extending the template can fill. The content written between [{% block title %}] and [{% endblock %}] is the block’s default content, used by a page that does not override it;
  • lines 10–11: [url_for], which we are familiar with from actions (example 04), also generates the URL for a static file: [static] refers to the application’s static folder, [bootstrap.static] to that of the blueprint [bootstrap]; [filename] is the file path within that folder. [url_for] is available in all views. Typing URL manually ([/static/css/styles.css]) would also work, but [url_for] adapts if the folder is moved or if the application is installed under a prefix of URL;
  • line 16: [{% include %}] inserts the content of another view, in this case the navigation bar. The included view has access to the variables of the view that includes it;
  • line 19: the block that each page fills with its own content. It is empty by default;
  • line 22: the footer uses the two variables from the context processor.

The class [container] of [Bootstrap] centers the content and limits its width; [py-3] adds vertical padding: [Bootstrap] provides hundreds of classes of this type, which are combined in the [class] attribute.

docs.title: 4.3.3. The navigation bar: templates/fragments/navbar.html
docs.text:
{# a fragment: a piece of page, inserted by {% include %} #}
<nav class="navbar navbar-expand bg-light rounded mb-3 px-3">
  <span class="navbar-brand">My site</span>
  <div class="navbar-nav">
    <a class="nav-link" href="/">Home</a>
    <a class="nav-link" href="/team">Team</a>
    <a class="nav-link" href="/raw">Page without layout</a>
  </div>
</nav>

A fragment: a section of a page that has no meaning on its own. The classes [navbar], [navbar-brand], and [nav-link] are those of the navigation bar in [Bootstrap].

docs.title: 4.3.4. A macro: templates/fragments/card.html
docs.text:
{# a MACRO: a piece of page that has parameters, like a function #}
{% macro card(name, role) %}
<div class="card">
  <div class="card-body">
    <h5 class="card-title">{{ name }}</h5>
    <p class="card-text">{{ role }}</p>
  </div>
</div>
{% endmacro %}
  • Lines 2–9: A macro is a page fragment that has parameters; this is the function of [Jinja2]. Calling it—[{{ card("name", "role") }}]—inserts the page fragment generated with these values. Parameters can have a default value, as in [Python]: [{% macro card(name, role="") %}]. The card ([card]) is a component of [Bootstrap].

docs.title: 4.3.5. The pages
docs.text:
{# this page EXTENDS the layout: it only provides the content of its blocks #}
{% extends "layout.html" %}
{# the [card] macro of the fragments/card.html file #}
{% from "fragments/card.html" import card %}

{% block content %}
  <h1>Welcome</h1>
  <p>This page only contains its own content: the header, the navigation
    bar and the footer come from the <code>layout.html</code> layout.</p>
  {# the call of the macro, with two parameters written on the spot #}
  {{ card("A macro", "called with parameters written on the spot") }}
{% endblock %}
  • Line 2: The page extends the template: [Jinja2] generates the template page, replacing its blocks with those redefined by the page. [{% extends %}] must be the first tag in the view. In a view that extends a template, text written outside the blocks does not appear in the generated page (however, the [{% set %}] instructions retain their effect there; we’ll see this in the chapter on internationalization);
  • line 4: the import of the macro [card], defined in another file;
  • line 6: the template’s [content] block, redefined. The page does not redefine the [title] block: it retains its default content, “Home”;
  • Line 11: the macro call.
{% extends "layout.html" %}
{% from "fragments/card.html" import card %}

{% block title %}Our team{% endblock %}

{% block content %}
  <h1>Our team</h1>
  <div class="row g-3">
    {% for member in members %}
    <div class="col-md-4">
      {# the macro receives the name and the role of the current member #}
      {{ card(member.name, member.role) }}
    </div>
    {% endfor %}
  </div>
{% endblock %}
  • line 4: this page also redefines the title;
  • lines 9–14: one card per team member, in a grid using [Bootstrap] ([row], [col-md-4]: three columns on a medium or large screen, one column on a phone).

The controller contains no new features:

# controllers/pages.py: three pages
from dataclasses import dataclass

from flask import Blueprint, render_template

pages = Blueprint("pages", __name__)


# a member of the team
@dataclass
class Member:
    name: str
    role: str


@pages.get("/")
def home():
    return render_template("pages/home.html")


@pages.get("/team")
def team():
    members = [
        Member("Marie Pélissier", "Director"),
        Member("Jacques Bromard", "Developer"),
        Member("Philippe Jandot", "Graphic designer"),
    ]
    return render_template("pages/team.html", members=members)


@pages.get("/raw")
def raw():
    return render_template("pages/raw.html")

Finally, the third page does not use the template:

<!doctype html>
{# this view does not use the layout: it is a complete page #}
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <title>Raw page</title>
</head>
<body>
  <p>This page does not use the layout: no Bootstrap, no navigation bar.</p>
  <p><a href="/">Back to home</a></p>
</body>
</html>

The browser received a complete page: the template, fragment, page, and macros were assembled on the server. The URL style sheets were calculated by [url_for]. You can verify that the [Bootstrap] file is being served correctly (the [-I] option of [curl] displays only the response headers):

curl -I http://localhost:5000/bootstrap/css/bootstrap.min.css

HTTP/1.1 200 OK

Content-Type: text/css; charset=utf-8
